lessons.title: V3·A1 — Buffers, bytes and encodings
lessons.summary: The byte layer, taken seriously. Pooled memory and why byteOffset ruins naive typed-array views, mixed-endian headers, LEB128 varints, length-prefixed framing across chunk boundaries, UTF-8 truncation that does not split a code point, StringDecoder, strict TextDecoder, base64url and constant-time comparison.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A1 — Buffers, bytes and encodings

`06_buffers_streams` introduced `Buffer` as "the thing streams carry", and
`d14_buffers` drilled the surface: `alloc`, `concat`, `subarray`, hex, base64.
That was enough to move bytes around without corrupting them. It is not enough
to write a protocol, and it is nowhere near enough to explain the two bugs that
every Node engineer eventually ships: a typed-array view that reads someone
else's data, and a string that gets cut in half through the middle of an emoji.

This sector is the byte layer taken seriously. Everything here is in memory and
synchronous, which is deliberate — the mistakes are hard enough without an
event loop underneath them.

## Concept — a Buffer is a view, not a block

Start with the fact that explains most of the surprises:

```ts
class Buffer extends Uint8Array {}
```

That is the whole relationship. A `Buffer` **is** a `Uint8Array`, so every
`TypedArray` method works on it, and `instanceof Uint8Array` is true. What
`Buffer` adds is the number accessors (`readUInt32BE`), the string codecs
(`toString("base64url")`), and — the important one — a **pool**.

`Buffer.allocUnsafe(n)` for `n` smaller than `Buffer.poolSize >>> 1` (4 KiB by
default) does not allocate. It hands you a slice of an 8 KiB `ArrayBuffer` that
Node is handing out to everybody, advancing an offset each time. So:

```ts
const a = Buffer.allocUnsafe(4);
const b = Buffer.allocUnsafe(4);
a.buffer === b.buffer;   // true, quite often
a.byteOffset;            // 0
b.byteOffset;            // 4  (or wherever the pool cursor was)
a.buffer.byteLength;     // 8192 — not 4
```

Two consequences, and both of them are the exercises. First, `allocUnsafe`
returns memory that was recently something else, which is why it is "unsafe":
uninitialised means "the previous tenant's bytes", and shipping one of those to
a client is a genuine information leak. `Buffer.alloc(n)` zero-fills.
`Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow(n)` skips the pool and gives you a dedicated
`ArrayBuffer` — that is what you want for a buffer you intend to keep, because
a 12-byte pooled buffer that lives forever pins 8 KiB.

Second — and this is the bug — `buf.buffer` is the **pool**, not your bytes:

```ts
const view = new Float64Array(buf.buffer);              // wrong: whole pool
const ok = new DataView(buf.buffer, buf.byteOffset, buf.byteLength);  // right
```

Every conversion from a `Buffer` to another view type must carry
`byteOffset` and `byteLength`. Forgetting it is silent: you read plausible
numbers, they are just somebody else's.

## Concept — encodings are lossy in both directions

`"héllo".length` is 5. `Buffer.byteLength("héllo")` is 6. `"👋".length` is 2,
because JavaScript strings are UTF-16 code units and an emoji outside the BMP
is a surrogate pair; its UTF-8 encoding is 4 bytes. There are therefore three
different counts of "how big is this text", and picking the wrong one is how a
`substring(0, 100)` on a column declared `VARCHAR(100)` still overflows.

UTF-8 is self-synchronising, which is the property the exercises lean on. A
lead byte announces its length (`0b0xxxxxxx` = 1, `0b110xxxxx` = 2,
`0b1110xxxx` = 3, `0b11110xxx` = 4) and every continuation byte matches
`0b10xxxxxx`. From any position you can walk backwards to the nearest lead byte
in at most three steps — that is how you truncate safely, and it is also why a
decoder can resynchronise after corruption instead of losing the rest of the
file.

`Buffer.prototype.toString("utf8")` never fails. Invalid bytes become U+FFFD,
silently. `new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true })` throws instead, which is
what you want at a trust boundary.

## Problem 1 — a header with two endiannesses

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement
`readHeader(buf: Buffer): { magic: string; version: number; flags: number; payloadLength: number; checksum: bigint }`
for this 20-byte header: bytes 0-3 the ASCII magic `"IPSK"`, byte 4 a uint8
version, byte 5 a uint8 flag bitfield, bytes 6-7 **reserved and ignored**,
bytes 8-11 a uint32 **big-endian** payload length, bytes 12-19 a uint64
**little-endian** checksum returned as a `bigint`.

`readHeader(Buffer.from("4950534b0107000000000010" + "0102030405060708", "hex"))`
gives `{ magic: "IPSK", version: 1, flags: 7, payloadLength: 16, checksum: 578437695752307201n }`.
Fewer than 20 bytes throws an `Error` mentioning `20`; a wrong magic throws an
`Error` mentioning the magic it actually found.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex1
```

## Problem 2 — truncate without breaking a character

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `truncateUtf8(text: string, maxBytes: number): string`
returning the longest prefix of `text` whose UTF-8 encoding is at most
`maxBytes` bytes, never ending inside a multi-byte sequence and never splitting
a surrogate pair.

`truncateUtf8("héllo", 3)` is `"hé"` (3 bytes), `truncateUtf8("héllo", 2)` is
`"h"`, and `truncateUtf8("a👋b", 4)` is `"a"` — the wave is four bytes and only
three remain. `maxBytes` of `0` gives `""`; a string that already fits is
returned unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex2
```

## Problem 3 — decoding across chunk boundaries

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `decodeChunks(chunks: Buffer[]): string[]`
returning one string per input chunk, such that joining the results is exactly
the UTF-8 decoding of the concatenated chunks — with no U+FFFD introduced by a
character that straddles two chunks.

Given `Buffer.from("héllo")` split as `[0x68, 0xc3]` and `[0xa9, 0x6c, 0x6c,
0x6f]`, the result is `["h", "éllo"]`: the lone `0xc3` is held back. A trailing
incomplete sequence at the very end stays held back and is simply lost — you
are given no flush point.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex3
```

## Problem 4 — LEB128, the variable-length integer

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement unsigned LEB128:

- `encodeVarint(value: number): Buffer` — seven bits per byte, little-endian
  groups, the high bit set on every byte except the last. `0` is `<00>`, `127`
  is `<7f>`, `128` is `<80 01>`, `300` is `<ac 02>`.
- `decodeVarint(buf: Buffer, offset = 0): { value: number; bytesRead: number }`.

A negative or non-integer value throws. A decode that runs off the end of the
buffer throws an `Error` mentioning `truncated`, and so does a varint longer
than 8 bytes (which cannot be a safe integer).

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex4
```

## Problem 5 — framing a byte stream you do not control

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Implement `createFramer(): { push(chunk: Buffer): Buffer[] }`
for a wire format of `uint32be length` followed by that many payload bytes.
`push` returns every message that became complete with this chunk, in order,
and keeps the remainder for next time.

A chunk carrying two whole messages returns both. A chunk carrying half a
length prefix returns `[]` and remembers the two bytes. A payload split across
five chunks returns `[]` four times and then the message. A declared length
above 1 MiB throws an `Error` mentioning the limit — an unbounded allocation
driven by an attacker-supplied length is the classic framing vulnerability.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex5
```

## Problem 6 — views over pooled memory

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Implement:

- `asFloat64Array(buf: Buffer): Float64Array` — the buffer's bytes as
  little-endian doubles, correct even when `buf` is a pooled slice at a
  non-zero `byteOffset`, and correct when that offset is not a multiple of 8.
- `detach(buf: Buffer): Buffer` — a copy that shares nothing with `buf` or its
  pool, so writing to either leaves the other alone.

`buf.length` not divisible by 8 throws. The gate builds its input with
`Buffer.allocUnsafe`, checks `byteOffset`, then mutates the pool underneath
you: a view built from `buf.buffer` alone fails, and so does a `detach` that
returns `buf.subarray(0)`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex6
```

## Problem 7 — base64url, strictly, and a comparison that does not leak

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement:

- `toBase64Url(bytes: Buffer): string` — base64 with `-` and `_` for `+` and
  `/`, and no `=` padding.
- `fromBase64Url(text: string): Buffer` — the inverse, which **rejects**
  anything that is not canonical: a character outside the alphabet, embedded
  padding, whitespace, or a length ≡ 1 (mod 4). Throw an `Error` mentioning
  `base64url`.
- `matches(a: Buffer, b: Buffer): boolean` — equality in time that does not
  depend on where the first differing byte is.

`Buffer.from(text, "base64")` is famously permissive: it ignores invalid
characters rather than failing, so `fromBase64Url` cannot simply delegate to
it. Prove the round trip by re-encoding.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex7
```

## Problem 8 — a UTF-8 validator by hand

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Implement `isValidUtf8(bytes: Buffer): boolean`,
without `TextDecoder`, `toString` or any string conversion. Walk the bytes and
reject:

- a continuation byte where a lead byte belongs, and a truncated sequence at
  the end;
- **overlong** encodings — `c0 80`, `e0 80 80`, `f0 80 80 80` — the historic
  path-traversal exploit, where an ASCII character is smuggled in a multi-byte
  form;
- the surrogate range `U+D800`-`U+DFFF` encoded as three bytes (`ed a0 80`),
  which is CESU-8, not UTF-8;
- anything above `U+10FFFF`, which makes `f5`..`ff` invalid lead bytes outright.

`isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("héllo"))` is `true`; `isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("c080", "hex"))`
is `false`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex8
```

## Challenge — a self-describing record codec

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `encodeRecord(record: Record<string, Value>): Buffer`
and `decodeRecord(buf: Buffer): Record<string, Value>` where
`Value = number | bigint | string | boolean | Buffer`, round-tripping exactly —
including field order, an empty record, an empty string and an empty buffer.

The format: a varint field count, then per field a varint-length-prefixed UTF-8
name, a one-byte type tag, and the value. Tags: `0x01` varint unsigned integer,
`0x02` float64 little-endian, `0x03` varint-length-prefixed UTF-8 string,
`0x04` varint-length-prefixed raw bytes, `0x05` boolean as a single `00`/`01`,
`0x06` int64 little-endian for a `bigint`. A trailing byte after the last field
is an error, and so is an unknown tag.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings challenge
```

## Review

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Implement `hexdump(buf: Buffer, width = 16): string`
producing canonical `xxd`-style output: an 8-digit lowercase hex offset, `": "`,
then `width` bytes as space-separated hex pairs padded out on a short final
line, then `" |"`, then the same bytes as latin1 with every byte outside
`0x20`-`0x7e` shown as `.`, then `"|"`. Lines are joined with `\n` and there is
no trailing newline. An empty buffer gives `""`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/v3na01_buffers_encodings

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The through-line is **a byte is not a character and a Buffer is not a block of
memory**. Both halves are aliasing problems in disguise. A `Buffer` aliases a
pool, so any conversion that drops `byteOffset` reads a neighbour's bytes. A
string aliases code points through UTF-16, so any operation counting the wrong
unit cuts in the wrong place. Every exercise here is one of those two mistakes
in a different costume: the truncation that lands mid-sequence, the decoder
that loses a continuation byte at a chunk edge, the framer that trusts a
length, the validator that accepts an overlong. The recurring instrument is the
accessor with an explicit width and endianness — `readUInt32BE`,
`readBigInt64LE` — because a name that states both is a name you cannot get
subtly wrong.

## ex1 — the header is a contract, and it is not all one endianness

**What it tested:** reading fixed-layout binary with the typed accessors rather
than manual shifting, and treating the length check as part of the parse.

**The classic mistake:** `buf.readUInt32BE(8)` on a 12-byte buffer throws
`ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` from deep inside Node, and the caller gets a message about
an offset instead of "this header is short". Check the length first and say the
number. The second mistake is assuming a format is uniformly big-endian; real
ones are not, and the reserved bytes are there to remind you that skipping
fields is normal.

**Model answer:** `if (buf.length < 20) throw` first, then `toString("latin1",
0, 4)` for the magic, then the four accessors at their documented offsets, with
`readBigUInt64LE` returning a `bigint` because 2⁶⁴ does not fit in a double.

## ex2 — count bytes, cut on code points

**What it tested:** the three-way distinction between UTF-16 code units, code
points and UTF-8 bytes, and the self-synchronising property that lets you back
up.

**The classic mistake:** `text.slice(0, maxBytes)` — right answer for ASCII,
wrong the moment an accent appears — or the almost-right
`buf.subarray(0, maxBytes).toString()`, which lands mid-sequence and appends a
U+FFFD, producing a string that is *longer* in bytes than the limit you were
enforcing.

**Model answer:** encode once, then walk back from `maxBytes` while the byte at
that index is a continuation byte (`(b & 0xc0) === 0x80`); at most three steps.
Iterating the string with `for (const ch of text)` and accumulating
`Buffer.byteLength(ch)` is equally correct and handles surrogate pairs for free,
because string iteration yields code points.

## ex3 — the boundary is not yours to choose

**What it tested:** that a stream hands you arbitrary byte boundaries, and a
stateless decoder cannot survive them.

**The classic mistake:** `chunk.toString("utf8")` per chunk. The trailing
partial sequence becomes U+FFFD in chunk *n* and the leading remainder becomes
another U+FFFD in chunk *n+1*: one character in, two replacement characters
out, and no error anywhere. This is the single most common corruption bug in
Node code that reads sockets.

**Model answer:** one `StringDecoder` instance for the whole run, reused across
chunks. It buffers up to three bytes of an incomplete sequence internally and
prepends them to the next `write`. Building your own would mean re-deriving the
lead-byte table from ex8.

## ex4 — the length is in the data

**What it tested:** bit manipulation with a purpose. LEB128 is how Protocol
Buffers, DWARF, WebAssembly and SQLite store integers whose typical value is
small.

**The classic mistake:** `value >>> 7` in the encoder. JavaScript's bitwise
operators coerce to **32-bit** integers, so anything above 2³¹ silently
wraps — the encoder produces five bytes of nonsense for a value a `double`
holds perfectly well. Use `Math.floor(value / 128)`, or `BigInt`. The decode
side's version of the bug is `result |= byte << shift`, which breaks at
`shift = 28`; multiply by `2 ** shift` instead.

**Model answer:** encode with `value % 128` and `Math.floor(value / 128)`,
setting `0x80` while more remains; decode by accumulating
`(byte & 0x7f) * 2 ** shift` and stopping when the high bit is clear, with the
8-byte guard so a hostile stream cannot spin forever.

## ex5 — never trust a declared length

**What it tested:** the stateful half of protocol work — a parser that survives
being fed one byte at a time — plus the security rule that makes it shippable.

**The classic mistake:** an `if` instead of a `while`. A chunk containing two
complete messages then returns one and leaves the second sitting in the buffer
until the next chunk arrives, which looks fine in tests and deadlocks in
production against a peer that is waiting for your reply. The second mistake is
`Buffer.alloc(length)` on the declared length before checking it: a four-byte
header claiming 4 GiB is one packet, and it is an out-of-memory kill.

**Model answer:** keep a single `Buffer` of leftovers, loop while it holds at
least four bytes *and* the declared length, `subarray` the message out, reslice
the remainder, and bound the length before you touch it.

## ex6 — byteOffset is not optional

**What it tested:** the pool, directly. This is the mechanism from the briefing
turned into a failing assertion.

**The classic mistake:** `new Float64Array(buf.buffer)` — which, for a pooled
16-byte buffer, is a 1024-element view of the entire 8 KiB pool starting at
someone else's data. It does not throw. The values are finite and plausible.
The second mistake is assuming the offset is 8-byte aligned: `Float64Array`
requires it and throws `RangeError` when it is not, so a correct answer copies
whenever alignment fails, or reads through a `DataView`, which has no alignment
requirement at all.

**Model answer:** read with `new DataView(buf.buffer, buf.byteOffset,
buf.length)` and `getFloat64(i * 8, true)` into a fresh `Float64Array` — no
alignment constraint, explicit endianness, no aliasing. `detach` is
`Buffer.from(buf)`, which copies; `Buffer.from(buf.buffer)` would have shared
the pool, and `subarray` shares by definition.

## ex7 — permissive decoders are a security bug

**What it tested:** that base64 has a canonical form and Node's decoder does
not enforce it, plus the one place where an early return is wrong on purpose.

**The classic mistake:** decoding with `Buffer.from(text, "base64")`, which
skips characters it does not recognise — so `"AA=A"` and `"AAA"` decode to the
same bytes. Two tokens with one meaning is a signature-bypass primitive.

**Model answer:** decode, re-encode, require equality with the input; and
`timingSafeEqual` for `matches`, guarded by a length check, because it throws
on unequal lengths and length is not the secret.

## ex8 — the exploits are in the invalid encodings

**What it tested:** the UTF-8 grammar itself, including the three rejections
that exist for security rather than tidiness.

**The classic mistake:** validating only the shape — lead byte, right number of
continuations — and accepting `c0 af`. That decodes to `/` in a naive decoder,
which is how directory traversal walked past a decade of filters that checked
for the literal slash first. Unicode has forbidden overlongs since 3.1
precisely because of this.

**Model answer:** fold the range checks into the lead-byte cases: after `e0`
the next byte must be ≥ `a0`, after `ed` it must be ≤ `9f`, after `f0` ≥ `90`,
after `f4` ≤ `8f`, and `c0`/`c1`/`f5`-`ff` never appear. That is the same table
the WHATWG Encoding Standard's decoder state machine uses.

## challenge — a format is a parser and a serialiser that agree

**What it tested:** composition. Varints from ex4, length prefixes from ex5,
UTF-8 from ex2 and strict framing from ex8, in one artefact that must
round-trip exactly.

**The classic mistake:** measuring a string with `.length` rather than
`Buffer.byteLength` when writing its varint prefix, which is invisible until
the first non-ASCII name and then corrupts every field after it — the failure
that makes people believe binary formats are hard. Second: forgetting that a
decoder must reject trailing bytes. A parser that stops at the field count and
ignores the rest cannot tell a valid record from a valid record with an
attacker's suffix.

**Model answer:** build an array of chunks and `Buffer.concat` once at the end
rather than concatenating per field, thread a single `offset` through the
decoder, and assert `offset === buf.length` before returning.

## review1 — the same bytes, read for humans

**What it tested:** the whole sector from the other direction. A hexdump is
slicing, hex encoding, latin1's one useful property, and padding arithmetic.

**The classic mistake:** `toString("ascii")` for the gutter, which masks the
high bit — byte `0xe9` prints as `i`, so corrupted binary looks like text.
`latin1` maps bytes 0-255 to code points 0-255 exactly, which is why it is
right here and wrong everywhere else.

**Model answer:** step the buffer in `width`-byte `subarray`s,
`toString("hex")` each byte and join with spaces, pad the hex column to
`width * 3 - 1` characters so the final short line still lines up, and build
the gutter with a range test rather than a regex over a decoded string.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: Buffer](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html#buffers-and-typedarrays) — the `Uint8Array` relationship, pooling, and why `buf.buffer` is bigger than `buf`; the mechanism behind ex6.
- [Node.js: `Buffer.allocUnsafe`](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html#static-method-bufferallocunsafesize) — the pool cursor, `poolSize`, and `allocUnsafeSlow`.
- [Node.js: `string_decoder`](https://nodejs.org/api/string_decoder.html) — the stateful decoder ex3 exists to teach.
- [WHATWG Encoding Standard: UTF-8 decoder](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#utf-8-decoder) — the exact state machine and byte ranges ex8 asks you to reproduce.
- [Unicode FAQ: UTF-8 and overlong forms](https://www.unicode.org/faq/utf_bom.html) — why `c0 80` is illegal rather than merely redundant.
- [RFC 4648 §5](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-5) — base64url's alphabet and the canonical-form requirements ex7 enforces.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·A1 — Buffers, bytes and encodings (archive)

## Why this layer keeps producing bugs

Most Node code never sees a byte. You `res.json(user)`, the framework encodes,
and the boundary between text and bytes is somebody else's problem. Then you
write a protocol client, or a file format reader, or a chunked upload handler,
and suddenly the boundary is yours — and the abstractions you have been using
are all designed to hide exactly the things you now need to control.

Two abstractions in particular. `Buffer` looks like a block of memory and is
actually a window onto shared memory. A JavaScript string looks like a sequence
of characters and is actually a sequence of UTF-16 code units. Both work
perfectly until you index them, and then both fail quietly.

## The pool, concretely

```ts
import { Buffer } from "node:buffer";

console.log(Buffer.poolSize);            // 8192

const a = Buffer.allocUnsafe(64);
const b = Buffer.allocUnsafe(64);

console.log(a.buffer === b.buffer);      // true
console.log(a.byteOffset, b.byteOffset); // 0 64
console.log(a.buffer.byteLength);        // 8192
```

Node keeps one 8 KiB `ArrayBuffer` per "pool generation" and a cursor into it.
`allocUnsafe(n)` with `n < poolSize >>> 1` returns `pool.subarray(cursor,
cursor + n)` and advances the cursor, allocating a fresh pool when it runs out.
This makes small allocations nearly free — no `malloc`, no zeroing, no
per-buffer `ArrayBuffer` object for the GC to track.

The costs are the two you now know. Uninitialised memory is real memory that
held real data; `Buffer.alloc` zero-fills for a reason, and `allocUnsafe`
belongs only where you overwrite every byte immediately. And a long-lived
pooled buffer pins its whole pool: cache a hundred 16-byte keys from
`allocUnsafe` and you may be holding a hundred 8 KiB pools. `Buffer.from(x)`
copies into the pool too, so the fix for a retained buffer is
`Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow(n)` plus a copy, or simply accepting the copy from
`Buffer.concat`, which does not pool.

Where it becomes a correctness bug rather than a memory question is
interoperation:

```ts
const buf = Buffer.allocUnsafe(16);
buf.writeDoubleLE(1.5, 0);
buf.writeDoubleLE(2.5, 8);

new Float64Array(buf.buffer);                                  // 1024 elements
new Float64Array(buf.buffer, buf.byteOffset, buf.length / 8);  // 2 — if aligned
```

The second line still throws when `byteOffset % 8 !== 0`, which the pool makes
likely. `DataView` has no alignment requirement and takes an endianness
argument per read, which is why it is the right tool for parsing and
`Float64Array` is the right tool for bulk numeric work on memory you allocated
yourself.

## Numbers, widths and endianness

```ts
const buf = Buffer.alloc(8);
buf.writeUInt32BE(0xdeadbeef, 0);
buf.readUInt32BE(0);          // 3735928559
buf.readUInt32LE(0);          // 4022250974 — same bytes, different number
buf.readBigUInt64BE(0);       // needs 8 bytes; returns a bigint
```

Three rules. Always name the width and the order in the call — `readUInt32BE`,
never a hand-rolled shift chain, because the shift chain is where the 32-bit
coercion bugs live. Anything wider than 2⁵³ must be a `bigint`; a `double`
cannot represent 2⁶⁴ - 1, so `readBigUInt64` is not an inconvenience but the
only correct choice. And the accessors throw `ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` when the read
would pass the end, which is a feature — but a feature whose message names an
offset, not your format, so check lengths yourself and throw something a caller
can act on.

Endianness is not a legacy curiosity. Network protocols are big-endian by
convention ("network byte order"); x86 and ARM are little-endian; so any wire
format is doing a conversion somewhere, and mixed formats are common enough
that ex1 is not contrived.

## Encodings

| encoding | round-trips arbitrary bytes | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `utf8` | no | invalid bytes become U+FFFD, silently |
| `latin1` | **yes** | byte *n* ↔ code point *n*, exactly |
| `hex` | yes | 2 chars per byte; decoding stops at the first non-hex |
| `base64` | yes | permissive on decode; ignores invalid characters |
| `base64url` | yes | RFC 4648 §5; `-_`, no padding |
| `ucs2`/`utf16le` | no | 2 bytes per code unit; odd lengths truncate |
| `ascii` | no | **masks the high bit** — `0xe9` becomes `0x69` |

Two entries deserve emphasis. `latin1` is the only single-byte encoding that
round-trips, which makes it the correct choice for a hexdump gutter, for
`Content-Type` headers carrying raw bytes, and for nothing else — treating
latin1 text as text produces mojibake the moment it leaves your process.
`ascii` is almost never what anyone wants: it is `latin1` with `& 0x7f`, so it
corrupts rather than rejects.

`Buffer.from(str, "base64")` deserves its own warning:

```ts
Buffer.from("AA=A", "base64").toString("hex");   // "00"
Buffer.from("AAA",  "base64").toString("hex");   // "00"
Buffer.from("A A",  "base64").toString("hex");   // "00"
```

Three distinct strings, one output. If any of those strings is a token, a
signature or a cache key, you have an equivalence class where you wanted an
identity. Canonicalise by re-encoding and comparing.

## UTF-8, precisely

```
U+0000  - U+007F   0xxxxxxx
U+0080  - U+07FF   110xxxxx 10xxxxxx
U+0800  - U+FFFF   1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx
U+10000 - U+10FFFF 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx
```

Four properties follow, and they are the whole of ex2, ex3 and ex8:

1. **Self-synchronising.** Continuation bytes are unambiguous (`10xxxxxx`), so
   from any byte you can find the start of the current character in ≤ 3 steps.
2. **Order-preserving.** Byte-wise comparison of UTF-8 equals code-point
   comparison, which is why `ORDER BY` on a `bytea` matches `ORDER BY` on text.
3. **A prefix of a valid string may be invalid.** Hence `StringDecoder`.
4. **Some byte sequences are structurally plausible but forbidden**: overlongs,
   surrogates, and anything past U+10FFFF. A validator that only checks shape
   accepts all three.

Counting, in three flavours:

```ts
const s = "a👋b";
s.length;                    // 4 — UTF-16 code units
[...s].length;               // 3 — code points
Buffer.byteLength(s, "utf8");// 6 — bytes
[...new Intl.Segmenter().segment("👨‍👩‍👧")].length;  // 1 — grapheme
```

Pick the unit your constraint is expressed in. A database column is bytes or
characters depending on the engine; a UI truncation is graphemes; an array
index is code units. Mixing them is the bug.

## Common mistakes

- `new Uint8Array(buf.buffer)` or `new DataView(buf.buffer)` without
  `byteOffset` and `byteLength`. Silent, plausible, wrong.
- `Buffer.allocUnsafe` for a buffer you do not fully overwrite, or one you
  retain.
- `str.slice(0, n)` to enforce a byte limit.
- Per-chunk `chunk.toString("utf8")` when reading a socket or file stream.
- `<<` and `>>>` on values above 2³¹ — JavaScript coerces to int32 first.
- `Buffer.alloc(declaredLength)` before bounding `declaredLength`.
- `a.equals(b)` for secrets. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, after a length check.
- `toString("ascii")` when you meant `latin1`.
- Assuming `Buffer.concat(list)` is cheap in a loop — it is O(total) each time;
  collect and concat once.
- Forgetting that `subarray` (and the deprecated `slice`) **share** memory,
  while `Buffer.from(buf)` copies. Node's `slice` is not `Array#slice`.

## The interview answer

*"What is a Buffer?"* — A `Uint8Array` subclass with number accessors and
string codecs, usually a view into a shared 8 KiB pool rather than its own
allocation. That last clause is the one that gets the follow-up, and the
follow-up is: so any conversion to another view type must pass `byteOffset` and
`byteLength`, and any buffer you keep should not be pooled.

*"How do you safely truncate a UTF-8 string to n bytes?"* — Encode, then walk
back from index *n* while the byte is a continuation byte (`b & 0xc0 === 0x80`)
— at most three steps, because that is the longest tail UTF-8 has. Or iterate
the string by code point, accumulating `Buffer.byteLength` per character, which
also handles surrogate pairs. The wrong answers are `slice(0, n)` and
`buf.subarray(0, n).toString()`.

*"Why does my socket data have question marks in it?"* — You decoded per chunk.
A multi-byte character split across two TCP segments becomes two U+FFFDs. Use
`StringDecoder`, or `setEncoding` on the stream, which uses one internally.

## Check yourself

1. Why can `Buffer.allocUnsafe(64).buffer.byteLength` be 8192?
2. What does `new Float64Array(buf.buffer)` read when `buf` came from
   `allocUnsafe`, and why does it not throw?
3. When does that same expression throw, and what is the fix that never throws?
4. `"👋".length` is 2 and `Buffer.byteLength("👋")` is 4. Explain both numbers.
5. Given the byte `0x93`, is it a lead byte or a continuation byte? How do you
   know from the bits alone?
6. Why is `c0 af` invalid UTF-8 even though its shape is correct, and what did
   accepting it once cost the industry?
7. Which Node encodings round-trip arbitrary bytes, and which silently corrupt?
8. Give two strings that `Buffer.from(s, "base64")` maps to the same bytes, and
   explain why that matters for a session token.
9. Why must `readBigUInt64BE` return a `bigint` rather than a number?
10. What breaks in `encodeVarint` if you write `value >>>= 7`?
11. Why must a length-prefixed framer use `while` rather than `if`?
12. What is the difference between `buf.subarray(0, 4)`, `buf.slice(0, 4)` and
    `Buffer.from(buf.subarray(0, 4))`?
13. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` throws when the lengths differ. Is that a leak?
14. Why is `latin1` correct for a hexdump gutter and wrong for a log message?
15. You must retain ten thousand 20-byte hashes for the process lifetime. How
    do you allocate them, and what goes wrong if you use `allocUnsafe`?
lessons.fullReading:
# The byte layer: how Buffer actually works, and why encodings are a security
# surface

## Where Buffer came from

Node shipped in 2009, four years before `Uint8Array` was in every browser and
five before `ArrayBuffer` was something you could rely on. The runtime needed a
byte container immediately — sockets and files produce bytes — so Ryan Dahl's
early Node used JavaScript strings with the `binary` encoding, one byte per
UTF-16 code unit. It worked, it wasted two bytes per byte, and it made
`String.prototype` methods available on data that was not text, which produced
exactly the class of bug you would expect.

`Buffer` arrived in 0.2 as a purpose-built object backed by external memory
that V8 did not manage. In 0.12 it became a wrapper around a real typed array,
and in Node 4 (V8 4.5, io.js merge era) `Buffer` became a genuine
`Uint8Array` subclass. That history explains the API's shape: `slice` means
`subarray` because it predates the typed-array vocabulary; `latin1` is aliased
as `binary` because that is what the string-based era called it; and the
`Buffer(size)` constructor was deprecated in 6.0 and runtime-deprecated in 10
because `Buffer(50)` returned uninitialised memory while `Buffer("50")`
returned two bytes of ASCII — a type confusion that turned an integer-parsing
bug into a heap disclosure. That CVE class is why `alloc`/`allocUnsafe`/`from`
exist as three separate names.

## The pool, from the C++ side

`Buffer.allocUnsafe` calls `createUnsafeBuffer`, which for sizes under
`poolSize >>> 1` carves from `allocPool`, a module-level `ArrayBuffer` created
by `createPool()`. The relevant lines of `lib/buffer.js` are about fifteen
long: allocate an 8 KiB `ArrayBuffer` with `createUnsafeBuffer`, set
`poolOffset = 0`, and on each request align the offset to 8 bytes, take
`allocPool.subarray(poolOffset, poolOffset + size)`, advance. When the
remaining space is too small, a new pool replaces the old one, and the old pool
stays alive exactly as long as any buffer still views it.

There is a real allocator underneath: V8's `ArrayBuffer::Allocator`, which Node
overrides with `NodeArrayBufferAllocator`, and which calls `malloc` for
`allocUnsafe`-backed pools and `calloc` for zero-filled ones. `Buffer.alloc`'s
zero-fill is therefore not a JavaScript loop; it is `calloc`, and on Linux a
large `calloc` gets zero pages from the kernel for free. That is why the
performance gap between `alloc` and `allocUnsafe` is small for large sizes and
significant for small ones — for small sizes you are comparing "carve from a
pool" against "memset a few bytes plus allocator bookkeeping", and pooling wins
on the bookkeeping, not the zeroing.

Rough orders of magnitude on a modern laptop: `Buffer.allocUnsafe(64)` around
40-60 ns, `Buffer.alloc(64)` around 80-120 ns, `Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow(64)`
several times either because it creates a real `ArrayBuffer` object.
`Buffer.concat` of two 1 KiB buffers is a `memcpy` and costs well under a
microsecond, but doing it inside a loop over *n* chunks is O(n²) bytes copied,
which is the single most common performance bug in stream-parsing code. Collect
chunks into an array, concat once, and pass `totalLength` so the function does
not have to walk the list twice.

Measure with `process.hrtime.bigint()` around a loop of at least a hundred
thousand iterations, and read `process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers` — added in
Node 13 — to see external buffer memory, which does **not** appear in
`heapUsed`. A process leaking retained pooled buffers shows a flat heap and a
climbing `arrayBuffers`, and that signature is worth memorising because it
looks nothing like a normal leak in a heap snapshot.

## Encoding conversions are not free either

`buf.toString("utf8")` is implemented in C++ and, for pure-ASCII content, hits
V8's one-byte string representation directly, which makes it fast — roughly a
gigabyte per second. Non-ASCII forces a two-byte representation and a real
decode. `Buffer.from(str, "utf8")` in the other direction can use
`v8::String::WriteUtf8` and is similarly quick. What is *not* quick is doing
either one per small chunk: the fixed cost per call dominates below a few
hundred bytes, which is another argument for `StringDecoder` over per-chunk
conversion, and for `setEncoding` over manual decoding.

Base64 in Node is a hand-written SIMD-friendly encoder in C++ and runs around
1-2 GB/s; hex is slower per byte because the output is larger. Neither is
usually the bottleneck, but base64 inflates by 4/3, so encoding a 10 MB file
into a JSON payload costs 13.3 MB of string, plus the JSON escape pass, plus
the copy into the socket — the reason people move to multipart uploads is
memory, not CPU.

## The security half

Three of this sector's exercises are security exercises wearing an encoding
costume, and the history is worth knowing because it is short and it repeats.

**Overlong UTF-8.** Before Unicode 3.1 the standard merely said decoders
*should* reject non-shortest forms. Microsoft IIS's decoder accepted them, so
`%c0%af` decoded to `/` after the path-traversal filter had already checked the
string for `/`. That is CVE-2000-0884, and it was worth a worm. The lesson
generalises far past UTF-8: **any input with more than one representation is a
filter bypass waiting for two components that disagree about which
representation is canonical.** It is the same shape as HTTP request smuggling
and as SQL injection through a double-encoded parameter.

**Permissive base64.** Node's decoder skips characters outside the alphabet
instead of failing, so a token and a token with a comma inserted decode
identically. Where the raw string is a database key and the decoded bytes are
the security decision, the two halves of your system disagree about identity.
The defence is always the same: decode, re-encode, compare, reject on
mismatch. JOSE implementations that skip this step have shipped signature
bypasses.

**Timing.** `Buffer.prototype.equals` is `memcmp`, which returns at the first
differing byte. Comparing an attacker-supplied MAC against the real one that
way leaks the position of the first difference through the response time, and
over enough samples that is a byte-at-a-time forgery oracle. `crypto.
timingSafeEqual` XORs and accumulates over the full length. It throws on
unequal lengths, which is correct: the length of a MAC is public, so branching
on it leaks nothing, and returning early for a wrong length is fine.

## When not to reach for this layer

Most code should not. The right default is to stay in strings and objects and
let the framework encode, because every hand-rolled byte path is a place to be
wrong in a way tests do not catch.

Specifically, do not hand-roll a framing protocol when the transport already
has one. HTTP/1.1 chunked encoding, HTTP/2 frames, and WebSocket frames all
solve ex5's problem, and they solve it with a spec, a fuzzer corpus and a
decade of eyes. Do not invent a binary record format when Protocol Buffers,
MessagePack, CBOR or Avro exist; ex-challenge exists to teach you what those
libraries are doing, not to suggest you compete with them, and the moment you
need schema evolution — a field added in version 2, read by a version 1
parser — a hand-rolled format becomes a permanent tax.

Do not use `Buffer` for text you are going to treat as text. Decode once at the
boundary, work in strings, encode once on the way out. Buffers in the middle of
business logic mean you will eventually index one.

And do not micro-optimise allocation without a measurement. `allocUnsafe` over
`alloc` is worth real percentage points in a hot loop that fully overwrites its
buffer, and is worth nothing at all in a request handler that runs twice a
second — where it is only a chance to leak memory contents to a user.

## Further reading

- [Node.js `lib/buffer.js`](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/lib/buffer.js) — `createPool`, `poolOffset` and `allocUnsafeSlow`, in about forty readable lines.
- [Node.js: Buffers and TypedArrays](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html#buffers-and-typedarrays) — the `byteOffset` rule stated in the official words.
- [WHATWG Encoding Standard](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/) — the decoder state machines `TextDecoder` implements, including the exact ranges ex8 asks for.
- [RFC 3629](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3629) — UTF-8's normative definition, including the ban on surrogates and the U+10FFFF ceiling.
- [CVE-2000-0884](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2000-0884) — the overlong-encoding traversal, for when someone asks why validators care about `c0 80`.
- [Node.js security releases index](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability) — where the `Buffer(number)` deprecations and their reasons are documented.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two decisions before you write anything. Which check happens first — the length
or the magic? (Reading four bytes for the magic is itself a read that can go
out of range, so the length check has to come first.) And what does "big-endian
uint32" name in the `Buffer` API? Every accessor spells out its width and its
byte order; find the four you need and the parse is four lines.

## Hint 2

Here is the same idea for a different, smaller format — a 6-byte record of a
little-endian uint16 id followed by a big-endian int32 delta:

```ts
function readRecord(buf: Buffer) {
  if (buf.length < 6) {
    throw new Error(`readRecord: need 6 bytes, got ${buf.length}`);
  }
  return { id: buf.readUInt16LE(0), delta: buf.readInt32BE(2) };
}
```

Note that the offsets are absolute positions in the buffer, not a running
cursor, and that nothing about the accessor names is guessable — look them up.


## Hint 3

Shape: a length guard, a magic guard, then a returned object literal whose five
properties are five accessor calls at fixed offsets. Six lines of body. The
decision left to you is what to do with bytes 6 and 7 — the temptation is to
read them "just in case", but a field you expose is a field you have promised,
and `reserved` in a format specification means "the next version may use this",
not "here is a number for you".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the failure you are being asked to prevent. Call
`Buffer.alloc(4).readUInt32BE(8)` in a scratch file and read the error. It
mentions `ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE`, an attribute name and a bound — nothing that tells
a caller "this header is truncated". Your job is to be the layer that turns
that into a sentence about the format. So the first statement in the function
is a guard, and its message names the number 20.

## Hint 2

The checksum is the field that punishes guessing. Eight bytes is 64 bits;
`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is 2⁵³ - 1. There is no way to return a correct
uint64 as a `number`, which is why the signature says `bigint` and why Node
gives you a separate family of accessors whose names start with `readBig`.
If you find yourself combining two 32-bit reads with a shift, stop: `<<` in
JavaScript truncates to 32 bits and you will get zero.

## Hint 3

Shape: guard on `buf.length`, then `const magic = buf.toString("latin1", 0, 4)`
and guard on that, then four accessor calls at offsets 4, 5, 8 and 12, returned
as an object literal. The decision left to you is which string encoding to use
for the magic — `ascii` masks the high bit, so a corrupted magic byte of `0xd0`
would print as `P` and your error message would lie about what it found.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — truncate without breaking a character

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function truncateUtf8(text: string, maxBytes: number): string;
```

Return the longest prefix of `text` whose UTF-8 encoding occupies at most
`maxBytes` bytes. The result must never end inside a multi-byte sequence and
must never split a surrogate pair.

```ts
truncateUtf8("héllo", 10);  // "héllo"  (6 bytes, fits)
truncateUtf8("héllo", 3);   // "hé"     (3 bytes)
truncateUtf8("héllo", 2);   // "h"      — é is 2 bytes and only 1 remains
truncateUtf8("a👋b", 4);    // "a"      — 👋 is 4 bytes
truncateUtf8("a👋b", 5);    // "a👋"
truncateUtf8("anything", 0);// ""
```

A negative `maxBytes` throws. The gate checks
`Buffer.byteLength(result) <= maxBytes` for every case, and separately checks
that the result contains no U+FFFD that was not in the input.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two honest approaches and they meet in the middle. Top-down: encode
the whole string, cut at `maxBytes`, then back up to a character boundary.
Bottom-up: walk the string one character at a time, adding each character's
byte cost until the next one would not fit. Both need you to answer one
question — *how do I recognise a byte that is in the middle of a character?*
UTF-8 answers it in two bits.

## Hint 2

Continuation bytes all look like `10xxxxxx`. That is the test:

```ts
const isContinuation = (b: number) => (b & 0xc0) === 0x80;

// walking back from an arbitrary index to the start of its character:
let i = someIndex;
while (i > 0 && isContinuation(buf[i])) i--;
```

The mask is `0xc0` (the top two bits) and the expected value is `0x80` (`10`).
`b & 0x80` alone is not enough — that matches continuation bytes *and* every
multi-byte lead byte.


## Hint 3

Shape: reject a negative `maxBytes`, return early when the whole string already
fits (measure with `Buffer.byteLength`, not `.length`), then a loop that
accumulates a byte cost and a stopping index, then one `slice`. The decision
left to you is what index you accumulate — a byte index is useless for slicing a
string, and a code-*point* count is useless too, because `String.prototype.slice`
indexes by code unit. Track the thing `slice` actually understands.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different entry point: forget bytes for a moment and ask what a `for...of` loop
over a string yields. Not code units — `for (const ch of "a👋b")` gives three
iterations, because string iteration is defined over code points and joins
surrogate pairs for you. That single fact turns this exercise into an
accumulator: iterate, ask `Buffer.byteLength(ch)`, stop before you overshoot.
No bit masks at all.

## Hint 2

The trap that costs people this question is the almost-right answer:

```ts
Buffer.from(text, "utf8").subarray(0, maxBytes).toString("utf8");
```

Run it on `truncateUtf8("héllo", 3)` and look at the result's byte length. The
severed `é` decodes to a single U+FFFD, which is *three* bytes in UTF-8, so the
function meant to enforce a 3-byte limit returned 4 bytes. A limit-enforcing
function that can exceed the limit is worse than no function.

## Hint 3

Shape, for the accumulate approach: a `used` counter and a `result` string (or
an array of characters you join). For each code point, compute its cost; if
`used + cost > maxBytes`, `break`; otherwise append and add. Return at the end.
The decision left to you is whether to build the string by concatenation or to
track a code-unit index and `slice` once — the second is faster for long
strings, and getting its index arithmetic right for surrogate pairs is the
actual work.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — decoding across chunk boundaries

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function decodeChunks(chunks: Buffer[]): string[];
```

Return one string per input chunk such that `result.join("")` equals the UTF-8
decoding of `Buffer.concat(chunks)` — with no replacement character introduced
by a character that happened to straddle a chunk boundary.

```ts
// "héllo" is 68 c3 a9 6c 6c 6f; split so that é is cut in half:
decodeChunks([Buffer.from("68c3", "hex"), Buffer.from("a96c6c6f", "hex")]);
// ["h", "éllo"]

decodeChunks([]);                       // []
decodeChunks([Buffer.alloc(0)]);        // [""]
```

A trailing incomplete sequence in the final chunk is held back and lost — you
are given no flush point, and inventing one changes the contract. The gate
splits a string containing 2-, 3- and 4-byte characters at every possible byte
offset and asserts the join is exact each time.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The reason `chunks.map((c) => c.toString("utf8"))` fails is that `toString` is
stateless: it sees a truncated sequence, has nothing to wait for, and emits
U+FFFD. What you need is a decoder that remembers. Node ships exactly one, in a
module you may never have imported, and its whole reason for existing is this
problem.

## Hint 2

The API, on a different example:

```ts
import { StringDecoder } from "node:string_decoder";

const decoder = new StringDecoder("utf8");
decoder.write(Buffer.from([0xe2, 0x82]));  // "" — holding two of three bytes
decoder.write(Buffer.from([0xac]));        // "€"
decoder.end();                             // "" — flushes any remainder
```

The instance is the state. One decoder per stream, not one per chunk — a fresh
decoder per chunk is exactly as broken as `toString`.


## Hint 3

Shape: construct the stateful decoder once, then `chunks.map` through its write
method — genuinely three lines. The decision left to you is the last one: do you
call the flush method after the loop? The prompt says a trailing partial
sequence is dropped, and flushing would emit a U+FFFD that breaks
`join("") === Buffer.concat(chunks).toString()`. Decide it on the contract, not
on tidiness.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a debugging exercise. Write the naive version first:

```ts
chunks.map((c) => c.toString("utf8"));
```

Feed it `["68c3", "a96c6c6f"]` as hex buffers and print the result with
`JSON.stringify`. You will see `"h�"` and `"�llo"` — one broken
character became two replacement characters. Now you know precisely what state
has to be carried across the boundary: the bytes of an incomplete sequence, at
most three of them.

## Hint 2

You could write this yourself, and it is worth understanding what you are being
handed. A decoder needs to know, from a lead byte, how many bytes the character
takes: `0xxxxxxx` → 1, `110xxxxx` → 2, `1110xxxx` → 3, `11110xxx` → 4. At the
end of a chunk, scan back up to three bytes for a lead byte, ask whether its
announced length runs past the end, and if so hold those bytes back. That is
ex8's table doing a second job.

## Hint 3

Shape: create the stateful decoder **once**, outside the loop, then map each
chunk through its `write` method. Three lines. The decision left to you is
whether to call the flush method at the end — the prompt says a trailing
partial sequence is lost, so calling it would append a U+FFFD to the last
string and change `join("")`. Read the contract before you add the tidy-looking
extra line.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — LEB128, the variable-length integer

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement unsigned LEB128, the encoding Protocol
Buffers, DWARF, WebAssembly and SQLite all use for integers that are usually
small: seven payload bits per byte, least-significant group first, the high bit
set on every byte except the last.

```ts
export function encodeVarint(value: number): Buffer;
export function decodeVarint(
  buf: Buffer,
  offset?: number,
): { value: number; bytesRead: number };
```

```ts
encodeVarint(0).toString("hex");        // "00"
encodeVarint(127).toString("hex");      // "7f"
encodeVarint(128).toString("hex");      // "8001"
encodeVarint(300).toString("hex");      // "ac02"
encodeVarint(2 ** 40).toString("hex");  // "8080808080 02" without the space

decodeVarint(Buffer.from("ac02", "hex"));          // { value: 300, bytesRead: 2 }
decodeVarint(Buffer.from("ffac02", "hex"), 1);     // { value: 300, bytesRead: 2 }
```

`encodeVarint` throws for a negative value, a non-integer, or anything above
`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. `decodeVarint` throws an `Error` mentioning
`truncated` when the high bit is set on the last available byte, and also when
the varint would exceed 8 bytes — an unbounded loop driven by remote input is
not a loop, it is a denial of service.

The gate round-trips every value in `[0, 1, 127, 128, 129, 16383, 16384,
2**31, 2**40, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER]`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the algorithm in decimal first and the bit fiddling becomes obvious. To
encode 300 in base 128: 300 = 2×128 + 44, so the digits are 44 then 2,
least-significant first. Now set a marker bit on every digit except the last so
a reader knows when to stop. That marker is `0x80`. Encoding is repeated
division; decoding is a positional sum with place values 1, 128, 16384, ...

## Hint 2

The decode loop, sketched for a fixed two-byte case so you can see the shape
without being given the general answer:

```ts
const lo = buf[0] & 0x7f;          // strip the marker bit
const hasMore = (buf[0] & 0x80) !== 0;
const hi = buf[1] & 0x7f;
const value = lo + hi * 128;       // place value, not a shift
```

Generalise: a `shift` that starts at 0 and grows by 7, a place value of
`2 ** shift`, and a loop that stops on the first byte whose marker is clear.


## Hint 3

Shape for the decoder: a `for(;;)` with two guards at the top (past the end of
the buffer, past the byte limit), a read, an accumulate, and a `break` when the
marker bit is clear. The decision left to you is the order of the two guards
against the accumulate — check before you read the byte, or you will index past
the end, get `undefined`, and discover that `undefined & 0x7f` is `0` rather
than an error, which turns a truncated varint into an infinite loop.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the trap, because it is the whole point of this exercise. Type this
into `node`:

```
> (2 ** 40) >>> 7
0
> 300 << 7
38400
> (2 ** 32) << 1
0
```

JavaScript's bitwise operators convert their operands to **signed 32-bit
integers** first. Above 2³¹ they do not shift, they discard. So every `>>>=`
and `<<=` you were about to write is a bug for exactly the values that make a
varint interesting. Arithmetic — `Math.floor(v / 128)`, `v % 128`,
`n * 2 ** shift` — has no such limit up to 2⁵³.

## Hint 2

The guards are not decoration, they are the difference between a parser and a
vulnerability. Ask what `decodeVarint(Buffer.from("ffffffffffffffffff", "hex"))`
should do: every byte has its marker set, so a naive loop runs off the end of
the buffer, reads `undefined`, and `undefined & 0x7f` is `0`, so the loop never
terminates on its own. Two independent stops are needed: past the end of the
buffer, and past the maximum sensible length.

## Hint 3

Shape for `encodeVarint`: validate, then a `do`/`while` (so that `0` produces
one byte rather than none) pushing `value % 128` into a number array, dividing
by 128, and setting `0x80` on the byte whenever a non-zero remainder is left.
`Buffer.from(bytes)` at the end. The decision left to you is how to detect
"more to come" *after* you have already divided — get that ordering wrong and
`encodeVarint(128)` comes out as one byte instead of two.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 5 — framing a byte stream you do not control

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. A peer sends messages as a `uint32` big-endian length
followed by that many payload bytes. TCP gives you those bytes in whatever
sized pieces it likes. Implement:

```ts
export interface Framer {
  push(chunk: Buffer): Buffer[];
}

export function createFramer(maxMessageBytes?: number): Framer;
```

`push` returns every message that became complete with this chunk, in order,
and retains the rest for the next call. `maxMessageBytes` defaults to
`1024 * 1024`.

```ts
const f = createFramer();
f.push(Buffer.from("00000002" + "6869", "hex"));   // [<Buffer 68 69>]
f.push(Buffer.from("0000", "hex"));                // []  (half a length)
f.push(Buffer.from("0003" + "61", "hex"));         // []  (1 of 3 payload bytes)
f.push(Buffer.from("6263", "hex"));                // [<Buffer 61 62 63>]
```

A chunk carrying two complete messages returns both. A zero-length message is
legal and yields an empty buffer. A declared length above `maxMessageBytes`
throws an `Error` whose message contains the limit — checked **before** any
allocation, because a four-byte header claiming 4 GiB is one packet and an
out-of-memory kill.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The object has exactly one piece of state: the bytes that arrived but have not
yet formed a whole message. Everything else is derived. Each `push` appends the
new chunk to that leftover and then asks, repeatedly, "is there a whole message
at the front?" — repeatedly, because one chunk may complete several.

## Hint 2

The two-stage check, sketched for a single message so the loop is still yours
to write:

```ts
if (buffered.length < 4) return [];                 // not even a length yet
const length = buffered.readUInt32BE(0);
if (buffered.length < 4 + length) return [];        // header but no payload
const message = buffered.subarray(4, 4 + length);
buffered = buffered.subarray(4 + length);           // keep the remainder
```

Two separate insufficiency checks, not one — you can have the length and still
be waiting for the payload, and that is the state most broken framers forget.


## Hint 3

Shape: a closure over `let buffered = Buffer.alloc(0)`; `push` concatenates the
new chunk on, then loops with the two insufficiency guards, collecting messages
into an array. The decision left to you is where the bound check goes. Put it
immediately after `readUInt32BE` and before the "do I have the payload yet?"
test — a hostile length must be rejected on the packet that declares it, not on
the packet that would have completed it, because that second packet never
arrives.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the security requirement, because it constrains the design. The
attack is one packet: `ff ff ff ff` and nothing else. A framer that reads the
length and calls `Buffer.alloc(4294967295)` has already lost, whatever it does
next. So the bound check sits between "I have four bytes" and "I do anything
with the number I just read" — and it must throw rather than return, because a
peer that sends a nonsense length is not a peer you keep talking to.

## Hint 2

Think about what `subarray` costs and what it retains. `subarray` does not
copy; it makes a view onto the same memory. That is what you want for handing
out a message. It is a subtler question for the leftover: a view onto a 64 KiB
chunk that retains two trailing bytes keeps all 64 KiB alive for as long as
you hold it. For this exercise either choice passes, but a production framer
copies the remainder when it is much smaller than its backing store — the same
"a small view pins a large allocation" problem the briefing described for
pooled buffers.

## Hint 3

Shape: a closure over `let buffered = Buffer.alloc(0)` and a `push` that starts
with `buffered = Buffer.concat([buffered, chunk])`, then loops `for (;;)` with
the two guards from the other hint track, pushing completed messages into an
`out` array and `break`ing when neither guard is satisfied. The decision left to
you is where the length bound goes — put it after the read and before anything
else, and remember it must fire even when the payload has not arrived yet.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — views over pooled memory

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function asFloat64Array(buf: Buffer): Float64Array;
export function detach(buf: Buffer): Buffer;
```

`asFloat64Array` reads the buffer's bytes as little-endian doubles. It must be
correct when `buf` is a pooled slice at a non-zero `byteOffset`, and when that
offset is not a multiple of 8. `buf.length` not divisible by 8 throws an
`Error` mentioning `8`.

`detach` returns a buffer with the same contents that shares no memory with
`buf` — not with `buf` itself and not with `buf`'s pool. Writing to either one
must leave the other unchanged.

```ts
const pooled = Buffer.allocUnsafe(16);       // usually byteOffset > 0
pooled.writeDoubleLE(1.5, 0);
pooled.writeDoubleLE(-2.25, 8);
asFloat64Array(pooled);                      // Float64Array(2) [ 1.5, -2.25 ]
asFloat64Array(pooled).length;               // 2, never 1024

const copy = detach(pooled);
pooled.writeDoubleLE(99, 0);
copy.readDoubleLE(0);                        // 1.5
```

The gate builds its input with `Buffer.allocUnsafe`, asserts `byteOffset > 0`,
and then overwrites the surrounding pool. A view derived from `buf.buffer`
alone fails. A `detach` that returns `buf.subarray(0)` or
`Buffer.from(buf.buffer)` fails.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Print three numbers for a pooled buffer before you write anything:
`buf.length`, `buf.byteOffset`, and `buf.buffer.byteLength`. The third is 8192.
That is the whole exercise: `buf.buffer` is not your bytes, it is the pool your
bytes live inside, and every typed-array constructor that takes an
`ArrayBuffer` needs to be told where your window starts and how long it is.

## Hint 2

The three-argument form, on a different type:

```ts
const view = new Uint16Array(buf.buffer, buf.byteOffset, buf.length / 2);
```

This is correct for `Uint16Array` only when `buf.byteOffset` is even —
typed-array constructors throw `RangeError: start offset ... should be a
multiple of 2` otherwise. `Float64Array` wants a multiple of 8, and a pool
cursor makes no such promise. There is one view type in the platform with no
alignment requirement at all; it is also the one that takes an endianness
argument per read.


## Hint 3

Shape for `asFloat64Array`: a divisibility guard, an output `Float64Array`, and
a fill loop. `detach` is one line. The decision left to you is which reader to
fill with — `buf.readDoubleLE(i * 8)` needs no `byteOffset` arithmetic because
the `Buffer` accessors are already relative to the buffer, while a `DataView`
over the three-argument form makes the aliasing explicit and is the thing you
will reach for when the type is not one `Buffer` has an accessor for.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Attack `detach` first, because it is the shorter half and it teaches the same
lesson. Sort these into "shares memory" and "copies":

```ts
buf.subarray(0, buf.length)
buf.slice(0, buf.length)
Buffer.from(buf)
Buffer.from(buf.buffer)
Uint8Array.prototype.slice.call(buf)
```

Two of them copy. `Buffer.prototype.slice` is Node's old alias for `subarray`
and does **not** behave like `Array.prototype.slice`, which is why it is
soft-deprecated. `Buffer.from(buf.buffer)` wraps the entire 8 KiB pool without
copying anything.

## Hint 2

There is a second-order trap in `detach`. `Buffer.from(buf)` copies the bytes —
but into where? Into the pool, because `Buffer.from` uses the same allocator as
`allocUnsafe` for small sizes. The copy is genuinely independent of `buf`, so
it satisfies this exercise; but if the requirement were "hold this for the
lifetime of the process without pinning 8 KiB", the answer would be
`Buffer.allocUnsafeSlow(n)` followed by `buf.copy(target)`. Know which problem
you are solving.

## Hint 3

Shape for `asFloat64Array`: guard on `buf.length % 8`, allocate an output
`Float64Array(buf.length / 8)`, then fill it with reads that carry an explicit
offset and an explicit endianness. The decision left to you is which reader —
`buf.readDoubleLE(i * 8)` uses the `Buffer` accessors and needs no `byteOffset`
arithmetic at all, while a `DataView` over `(buf.buffer, buf.byteOffset,
buf.length)` makes the aliasing question explicit. Both are correct; pick one
and be able to say why the naive `new Float64Array(buf.buffer)` is neither.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — base64url, strictly, and a comparison that does not leak

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function toBase64Url(bytes: Buffer): string;
export function fromBase64Url(text: string): Buffer;
export function matches(a: Buffer, b: Buffer): boolean;
```

`toBase64Url` produces RFC 4648 §5 output: the standard alphabet with `-` for
`+` and `_` for `/`, and no `=` padding.

`fromBase64Url` is the inverse and rejects anything non-canonical with an
`Error` whose message contains `base64url`: a character outside
`[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, any `=`, any whitespace, and a length ≡ 1 (mod 4), which no
byte string can produce.

`matches` reports equality in time that does not depend on the position of the
first differing byte. Different lengths are `false`, not a throw.

```ts
toBase64Url(Buffer.from("hello world"));      // "aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ"
fromBase64Url("aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ").toString();  // "hello world"
toBase64Url(Buffer.alloc(0));                 // ""
fromBase64Url("");                            // <Buffer >

fromBase64Url("aGVsbG8=");   // throws — padding
fromBase64Url("aGVs bG8");   // throws — whitespace
fromBase64Url("aGVsbG8+");   // throws — standard-base64 character
fromBase64Url("A");          // throws — impossible length
```

`Buffer.from(text, "base64")` silently ignores characters it does not
recognise, so it cannot be your validator. The gate feeds `fromBase64Url` five
distinct strings that Node's permissive decoder maps to the same bytes and
requires four of them to throw.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two of the three functions are one line each — Node's `toString` and
`Buffer.from` both accept `"base64url"` as an encoding, so you are not writing
a base64 encoder. The whole exercise is the third thing: proving that the
string you were handed is the *only* string that could have produced those
bytes. Ask yourself how you would check that without a table of rules.

## Hint 2

The general technique, on a different format:

```ts
function parseCanonicalHex(text: string): Buffer {
  const bytes = Buffer.from(text, "hex");
  if (bytes.toString("hex") !== text.toLowerCase()) {
    throw new Error("parseCanonicalHex: not canonical hex");
  }
  return bytes;
}
```

Decode, re-encode, compare. It catches every non-canonical input at once
without your having to enumerate them — including the ones you did not think
of. A syntactic pre-check for the alphabet is still worth having, because it
gives a better error, but the round-trip is the guarantee.


## Hint 3

Shape: `toBase64Url` is one line; `fromBase64Url` is an alphabet test, a length
test, a decode, a re-encode comparison, a return; `matches` is a length guard
and a call. The decision left to you is whether the alphabet regex earns its
place once the round-trip check exists. Strictly it does not — the round trip
catches everything. Keep it or drop it deliberately, and consider which version
gives a useful message when a real token fails at three in the morning.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come in through `matches`, which is the shortest function and the one with the
sharpest reason. `a.equals(b)` compiles down to `memcmp`, which stops at the
first differing byte. Comparing a submitted HMAC to the real one that way makes
the response time a function of how many leading bytes were right — a few
thousand requests and an attacker has forged the tag byte by byte. Node ships
the fix in `node:crypto`, and it throws rather than returning `false` when the
lengths differ, which is why your function needs a length guard first.

## Hint 2

The length rule is arithmetic, not taste. Base64 packs 3 bytes into 4
characters; a remainder of 1 byte becomes 2 characters and a remainder of 2
bytes becomes 3. So unpadded lengths mod 4 can be 0, 2 or 3 — **never 1**. A
string of length 5 is therefore not a truncated encoding of anything, and
accepting it means `fromBase64Url("AAAAA")` and `fromBase64Url("AAAA")` return
the same bytes: two tokens, one identity.

## Hint 3

Shape: `toBase64Url` is `bytes.toString("base64url")`. `fromBase64Url` runs a
regex test for the alphabet, a `length % 4 === 1` check, then
`Buffer.from(text, "base64url")`, then re-encodes and compares before
returning. `matches` guards on length and calls the constant-time comparator.
The decision left to you is whether the regex is still needed once you have the
round-trip check — it is not, strictly, but decide deliberately rather than by
omission, and consider which one produces the error message you would want at
3 a.m.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — a UTF-8 validator by hand

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function isValidUtf8(bytes: Buffer): boolean;
```

without `TextDecoder`, `toString`, `Buffer.from(string)` or any other string
conversion. Walk the bytes and apply the UTF-8 grammar yourself. Reject:

- a continuation byte (`10xxxxxx`) where a lead byte belongs;
- a sequence truncated by the end of the buffer;
- **overlong** forms — `c0 80`, `c1 bf`, `e0 80 80`, `f0 80 80 80` — where a
  character is encoded in more bytes than it needs;
- the surrogate range U+D800-U+DFFF encoded as three bytes (`ed a0 80`), which
  is CESU-8, not UTF-8;
- anything above U+10FFFF, which makes `f5`..`ff` invalid lead bytes.

```ts
isValidUtf8(Buffer.alloc(0));                   // true
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from([0x68, 0x69]));         // true — "hi"
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("c3a9", "hex"));        // true — é
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("f09f918b", "hex"));    // true — 👋
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("c080", "hex"));        // false — overlong "/"-style
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("eda080", "hex"));      // false — surrogate
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("f4908080", "hex"));    // false — above U+10FFFF
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("c3", "hex"));          // false — truncated
isValidUtf8(Buffer.from("80", "hex"));          // false — stray continuation
```

The gate cross-checks a few hundred random buffers against
`new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true })` and requires agreement on every
one, so "close enough" is not close enough.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Structure it as a loop over lead bytes: read one byte, decide from it how many
continuation bytes should follow, check that they are all there and all look
like `10xxxxxx`, then jump the index past the whole sequence. That gets you a
validator that is right about *shape*. The three extra rejections in the prompt
are all range checks, and — this is the key realisation — every one of them is
a constraint on the **second** byte given a particular first byte.

## Hint 2

Here is the shape-only version for two-byte sequences, which you then have to
tighten:

```ts
if (b >= 0xc2 && b <= 0xdf) {
  if (i + 1 >= bytes.length) return false;
  if ((bytes[i + 1] & 0xc0) !== 0x80) return false;
  i += 2;
  continue;
}
```

Notice the range starts at `0xc2`, not `0xc0`. `c0` and `c1` can only ever
encode a value below U+0080, which is by definition an overlong — so they are
excluded by the lead byte alone, and that is one of the three rejections
handled with no extra code at all.


## Hint 3

Shape: `while (i < bytes.length)` with four accept branches keyed on the lead
byte and a final `return false` that sweeps up `80..c1` and `f5..ff` in one
line. The decision left to you is how to express the extra second-byte bound —
four `if` statements for `e0`, `ed`, `f0` and `f4`, or a `[lo, hi]` pair
computed per lead byte. The pair is fewer lines and is what the WHATWG decoder
does; it is also the version people get subtly wrong on the first attempt, so
fuzz it against `TextDecoder` before you believe it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Derive the ranges instead of memorising them. A three-byte sequence carries
4 + 6 + 6 = 16 payload bits and must encode a value of at least U+0800. With a
lead byte of `e0` the top four bits are zero, so the value is at most
U+0FFF — meaning the second byte has to be large enough to push it to U+0800 or
above. Work out the smallest second byte that does: it is `a0`. That is where
the magic numbers come from, and doing this derivation once for `e0`, `ed`,
`f0` and `f4` gives you the whole table.

## Hint 2

Write the oracle before the implementation. Two lines get you a reference:

```ts
const ref = (b: Buffer) => {
  try { new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true }).decode(b); return true; }
  catch { return false; }
};
```

Then fuzz: generate a few thousand random 1-6 byte buffers, compare, and print
the first disagreement as hex. This finds the four boundary cases faster than
reading a table, and it is exactly what the gate does. You may not ship
`TextDecoder` in your answer — but nothing stops you using it to grade yourself
while you work.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `while (i < bytes.length)` with four branches keyed on the lead byte —
`<= 0x7f`, `0xc2..0xdf`, `0xe0..0xef`, `0xf0..0xf4` — and a final `return
false` for everything else, which sweeps up `80..c1` and `f5..ff` in one line.
Inside the three- and four-byte branches, check the continuation bytes first,
then apply the extra bound on byte two. The decision left to you is whether to
special-case `e0`/`ed`/`f0`/`f4` with `if`s or to compute a per-lead-byte
`[min, max]` for the second byte — the second is fewer lines and harder to get
right on the first attempt.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a self-describing record codec

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Build the encoder and decoder for a small binary
record format, using the varint from ex4, the length prefixes from ex5 and the
UTF-8 care from ex2.

```ts
export type Value = number | bigint | string | boolean | Buffer;

export function encodeRecord(record: Record<string, Value>): Buffer;
export function decodeRecord(buf: Buffer): Record<string, Value>;
```

The format, in order:

1. a varint field count;
2. then, per field: a varint byte-length, that many bytes of UTF-8 field name,
   a one-byte type tag, then the value.

Tags and their value encodings:

| tag | type | encoding |
|---|---|---|
| `0x01` | unsigned integer | varint |
| `0x02` | float64 | 8 bytes little-endian |
| `0x03` | string | varint byte-length, then UTF-8 |
| `0x04` | bytes | varint byte-length, then raw |
| `0x05` | boolean | one byte, `00` or `01` |
| `0x06` | bigint | 8 bytes little-endian, signed |

Encoding rules: a `number` that is a non-negative safe integer uses tag `0x01`,
any other `number` uses `0x02`. A `bigint` always uses `0x06`. Field order in
the output is the object's own key order, and `decodeRecord` must reproduce it.

Decoding rules: an unknown tag throws. A field name that is not valid UTF-8
throws. **Trailing bytes after the last field throw** — a decoder that stops at
the field count cannot distinguish a valid record from a valid record with an
attacker's suffix appended.

```ts
const buf = encodeRecord({ id: 7, name: "héllo", ok: true, ratio: 0.5 });
decodeRecord(buf);   // { id: 7, name: "héllo", ok: true, ratio: 0.5 }

decodeRecord(encodeRecord({}));                    // {}
decodeRecord(encodeRecord({ e: "", b: Buffer.alloc(0) })); // { e: "", b: <Buffer > }
decodeRecord(encodeRecord({ big: -5n }));          // { big: -5n }

decodeRecord(Buffer.concat([buf, Buffer.from([0])])); // throws
```

The gate round-trips a hundred generated records containing non-ASCII names,
zero-length values, `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, negative floats and negative
bigints, and compares with a deep-equality check that distinguishes `7` from
`7n`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the two functions as mirror images and keep them adjacent in the file.
Every encoder step has exactly one decoder step, in the same order; if you find
yourself writing a decoder branch with no matching encoder line, one of them is
wrong. Do the empty record first — count 0, no fields, one byte total — and get
that round-tripping before you add a single tag.

## Hint 2

For the encoder, collect and concatenate once:

```ts
const parts: Buffer[] = [];
parts.push(encodeVarint(entries.length));
for (const [name, value] of entries) {
  const nameBytes = Buffer.from(name, "utf8");
  parts.push(encodeVarint(nameBytes.length), nameBytes);
  // ... tag byte and value
}
return Buffer.concat(parts);
```

The important line is `nameBytes.length`, not `name.length` — a name containing
a single accented character makes those two numbers differ, and the decoder
then reads one byte too few and desynchronises for the whole rest of the
record.


## Hint 3

Shape: `encodeRecord` collects a `Buffer[]` and concatenates once at the end; a
private `encodeValue(value): Buffer[]` returning tag-plus-payload keeps the
field loop to three lines. `decodeRecord` threads one `offset` through
bounds-checking readers, loops the field count, switches on the tag, and ends
with `if (offset !== buf.length) throw`. The decision left to you is whether to
import the varint from ex4 or vendor a copy — the gate runs this file in
isolation, so it has to be self-contained, and noticing how much of protocol
work is exactly this kind of copying is part of the exercise.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review — the same bytes, read for humans

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function hexdump(buf: Buffer, width?: number): string;
```

Canonical `xxd`-style output, `width` defaulting to 16. Each line is:

1. the offset of the line's first byte as 8 lowercase hex digits;
2. `": "`;
3. the line's bytes as two-digit lowercase hex, space-separated, **padded on
   the right** so that a short final line still lines up — the column is always
   `width * 3 - 1` characters wide;
4. `" |"`;
5. the same bytes as text, with every byte outside `0x20`-`0x7e` shown as `.`;
6. `"|"`.

Lines are joined with `\n`, with no trailing newline. An empty buffer produces
`""`.

```ts
hexdump(Buffer.from("hi\nthere, world!!"), 8);
```

```
00000000: 68 69 0a 74 68 65 72 65 |hi.there|
00000008: 2c 20 77 6f 72 6c 64 21 |, world!|
00000010: 21                      |!|
```

The gate checks the exact bytes of the output for several widths, including a
buffer whose length is an exact multiple of `width` (no trailing empty line)
and a buffer containing `0x00`, `0x7f`, `0x80` and `0xff`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na01_buffers_encodings review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three independent problems, and solving them separately is much easier than
solving them together: chop the buffer into lines, render one line's hex
column, and render one line's text gutter. Write the middle one first and check
it against `Buffer.from("hi").toString("hex")` — note that `toString("hex")`
gives you `6869` with no separators, so the spacing is yours to add.

## Hint 2

Padding arithmetic, sketched:

```ts
const HEX_COLUMN = width * 3 - 1;   // "68 69 0a" for width 3 is 8 characters
const hex = [...slice].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join(" ");
const padded = hex.padEnd(HEX_COLUMN, " ");
```

`width * 3 - 1` because each byte contributes two characters plus a separator,
except the last, which has no separator after it. `padStart(2, "0")` matters:
byte `0x0a` must print as `0a`, and `(10).toString(16)` is `"a"`.


## Hint 3

Shape: `const lines: string[] = []`, a stride loop over the buffer, a
`subarray` per line (it clamps at the end, so no `Math.min`), three rendered
pieces joined by a template literal, and `lines.join("\n")` at the end. The
decision left to you is how to walk a line's bytes: `[...slice]` works, because
a `Buffer` is a `Uint8Array` and spreads into numbers, at the cost of an
intermediate array per line. Know that it works and why before you decide
against it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at the gutter first, because it is the part with a real decision in it.
You need bytes 0x20-0x7e as themselves and everything else as `.`. Two
approaches: decode the slice to a string and replace, or map bytes to
characters directly. If you decode, which encoding? `utf8` is wrong — byte
`0xe9` is not a valid standalone sequence and becomes U+FFFD. `ascii` is worse:
it masks the high bit, so `0xe9` becomes `0x69` and prints as `i`, quietly
turning binary into fake text. There is exactly one encoding that maps byte *n*
to code point *n*.

## Hint 2

Get the boundary cases into your head before you write the loop. A buffer of
length 32 with `width` 16 produces two lines, not three — a `for` loop with
`i <= buf.length` gives you an empty third line, and the gate checks for
exactly that. A buffer of length 0 produces the empty string, not a single
blank line. Both fall out of `for (let i = 0; i < buf.length; i += width)`
plus a `join("\n")` at the end, and neither needs a special case.

## Hint 3
