Shape: a `lines: string[]`, a stride loop, `const slice = buf.subarray(i, i +
width)` (which clamps for you at the end — no `Math.min` needed), then the
three pieces assembled with a template literal and pushed. The decision left to
you is how to iterate the slice's bytes: `[...slice]` spreads a `Buffer` into
numbers because it is a `Uint8Array`, which is neat, while a plain indexed loop
avoids the intermediate array. Either is fine; know that the spread works and
why.

lessons.title: V3·A2 — Readable and Writable from first principles
lessons.summary: The stream state machines, not the stream recipes. The readable event and read(n), unshift for pushback, _construct and _destroy for resource lifetime, _writev and cork, finish versus close, AbortSignal, a push-API bridge that honours demand, and a tee whose slow branch does not lose data.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A2 — Readable and Writable from first principles

`d15_readable_writable` had you build sources and sinks: a range stream, a
bounded sink, a duplex pair. Those exercises treated a stream as a thing you
construct and then hand to `for await` or `pipeline`. That is the right default
and it is most of the code you will write.

This sector is about the layer underneath, which you need exactly when the
default stops working: when you must read a fixed number of bytes and then
change your mind, when the resource behind a stream must not be opened until
somebody actually reads, when a sink wants to batch, when a stream has to be
cancellable, or when you have to tell — from outside — whether a stream is
finished, failed, or merely idle. Every one of those is a question about a
state machine, and the answer is always a property or a hook you may not have
noticed existed.

## Concept — a Readable has three states, not two

`readable.readableFlowing` is not a boolean. It is `null`, `false`, or `true`,
and the difference between `null` and `false` is where most stream confusion
lives.

- **`null`** — the initial state. Nobody has asked for data. No `data` events
  will fire, `read()` has not been called, and for a well-behaved source
  nothing has been produced. A stream you construct and then forget is here,
  and it holds its resources open forever.
- **`true`** — flowing. Data is pushed at you via `data` events as fast as the
  source produces it. Entered by adding a `data` listener, by calling
  `resume()`, or by `pipe()`.
- **`false`** — paused after having flowed. Entered by `pause()`, or by
  `unpipe()`. Distinct from `null` because the machinery has already started.

The `data` event and the `readable` event are two different protocols and you
must pick one:

```ts
// push protocol: the stream calls you
readable.on("data", (chunk) => { /* flowing = true */ });

// pull protocol: the stream says "there is something", you decide how much
readable.on("readable", () => {
  let chunk;
  while ((chunk = readable.read(4)) !== null) { /* exactly 4 bytes, or null */ }
});
```

`read(n)` is the one that makes protocol work possible. It returns exactly `n`
bytes or `null` — never a short read — so "wait until I have a 4-byte header"
is a single call rather than a buffer-accumulating loop. `read()` with no
argument returns whatever is buffered. And `read(0)` returns `null` while
triggering a refill, which is the documented way to nudge a stream without
consuming anything.

The reverse operation is `unshift`:

```ts
const first = readable.read(2);
if (first !== null && !looksLikeGzip(first)) readable.unshift(first);
```

`unshift` pushes bytes back onto the front of the internal buffer, so a later
consumer sees the stream as if you had never looked. That is how content
sniffing works — HTTP upgrade detection, magic-number dispatch, BOM stripping —
and it is the only sanctioned way to un-read.

## Concept — construction and destruction are hooks

A stream's lifetime has two ends and both are overridable.

```ts
new Readable({
  construct(callback) {                 // runs before the first _read
    open(this.path, (err, fd) => { this.fd = fd; callback(err); });
  },
  read(size) { /* ... */ },
  destroy(err, callback) {              // runs exactly once, on any ending
    if (this.fd === undefined) return callback(err);
    close(this.fd, (closeErr) => callback(err ?? closeErr));
  },
});
```

`_construct` (Node 15+) exists so a stream can be *created* without acquiring
anything. Reads are queued until its callback fires. That matters because
constructing a hundred file streams to process them one at a time should not
open a hundred file descriptors, and before `_construct` the only way to get
that was a lazy wrapper.

`_destroy` is the single teardown path. It runs once — Node guarantees it —
for every ending: normal completion with `autoDestroy` (the default since Node
14), an explicit `destroy()`, an error, or a `pipeline` unwinding. Cleanup
belongs there and nowhere else, because `end`, `finish` and `close` are all
avoidable in at least one failure mode.

## Concept — the writable side batches

`writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean, and the sink implementation sees one
of two methods. `_write(chunk, encoding, cb)` is called once per chunk.
`_writev(chunks, cb)` — if you implement it — is called with an **array** of
`{ chunk, encoding }` whenever more than one write is buffered. That happens
naturally under load, and deliberately when you `cork()`:

```ts
socket.cork();
socket.write(header);
socket.write(body);
process.nextTick(() => socket.uncork());   // one _writev, one syscall
```

`cork` buffers; `uncork` releases. Node's own HTTP implementation does this to
turn headers-plus-body into a single write. The trap is that `uncork` must
actually happen — a `cork` without a matching `uncork` is a stream that never
delivers anything, and an exception between the two leaves it corked forever.

Finally, the endings. `end()` says "no more writes"; `destroy()` says "stop
now". `finish` fires when everything written has been flushed by `_final`;
`close` fires when the stream is done with its resources, after `destroy`. They
are not the same event and neither implies the other in every path — which is
why `stream.finished()` exists, and why the last exercise asks you to reason
about `writableEnded`, `writableFinished`, `destroyed` and `errored` as a
precedence order rather than a set of flags.

## Problem 1 — exactly n bytes

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `readExactly(readable, n)` resolves with a `Buffer` of
exactly `n` bytes, using the `readable`/`read(n)` protocol rather than
accumulating `data` events. A stream that ends with fewer than `n` bytes
available rejects with an `Error` mentioning how many bytes it did get.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex1
```

## Problem 2 — look, then put it back

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `sniff(readable, n)` reads up to `n` leading bytes,
returns them, and `unshift`s them so that a later consumer sees the complete,
unmodified stream. A stream shorter than `n` returns what exists.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex2
```

## Problem 3 — open nothing until asked

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createLazySource(open)` builds an object-mode Readable
over a resource acquired by `await open()`, using `_construct` so that `open`
is not called at construction time, and `_destroy` so that the resource's
`close` runs exactly once on every ending — normal, early `destroy`, or error.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex3
```

## Problem 4 — a sink that batches

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createBatchSink()` returns `{ writable, batches() }`.
Implement `_writev` so that buffered writes arrive as one batch, `_write` for
the single-chunk case, and `_final` to record a terminal marker. `batches()`
returns the batches in order.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex4
```

## Problem 5 — did it finish, or did it just stop?

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `settled(stream)` resolves `"finished"` when a stream
completes normally, rejects with the stream's error when it fails, and rejects
with a `"destroyed before completing"` error when it is destroyed without one —
including when the stream is *already* in that state before you are called.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a push API behind a pull interface

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createPushSource(subscribe)` wraps an API that hands
you events whenever it likes. Honour `push()`'s return value: when it returns
`false`, stop pulling from the source until `_read` is called again. Call the
returned unsubscribe function exactly once, in `_destroy`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex6
```

## Problem 7 — cancellation

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `withAbort(readable, signal)` returns the same stream,
destroyed with an `AbortError` (an `Error` whose `name` is `"AbortError"`) when
the signal fires — immediately if it is already aborted — and with its abort
listener removed once the stream settles, on every path.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex7
```

## Problem 8 — two consumers, one source

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `tee(source)` returns two object-mode Readables that
each receive every item in order, where a slow branch does not lose data and a
destroyed branch does not stall the other one.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex8
```

## Challenge — a frame reader driven by read(n)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createFrameReader(bytes)` turns a byte Readable
of `uint32be`-length-prefixed messages into an object-mode Readable of message
buffers, driven by the `readable`/`read(n)` protocol and `unshift` — not by
accumulating a leftover buffer.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable challenge
```

## Review

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. `describeStream(stream)` classifies any stream as
`"idle" | "flowing" | "paused" | "ending" | "ended" | "errored" | "destroyed"`
from its introspection properties, with a precedence you have to get right.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable review1
```

# Reading - node/v3na02_readable_writable

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The through-line is **a stream is a state machine with hooks, and the hooks are
where correctness lives**. Every problem here fails the same way when it fails:
somebody handles the happy path with an event listener and forgets that the
state machine has three or four other exits. The `readable` event without the
`end` case hangs. The `_read` without `_destroy` leaks a handle. The `_writev`
without `_write` drops the single-chunk path. The abort listener without a
cleanup path keeps a signal alive for the process lifetime.

The second theme is **demand**. `read(n)` returning `null` means "not yet";
`push()` returning `false` means "stop". Code that treats either as terminal
truncates, and code that ignores both buffers without limit. Everything here is
downstream of taking those two return values literally.

## ex1 — read(n) is all-or-nothing

**What it tested:** the pull protocol, and the fact that `read(n)` never
short-reads.

**The classic mistake:** treating a `null` return as "the stream is empty" and
resolving with whatever has arrived. `null` from `read(n)` means only that
fewer than `n` bytes are buffered right now; the answer is to wait for the next
`readable` event, not to give up. The second mistake is forgetting that `end`
also fires a final `readable`, so the "ended with too few bytes" rejection must
be checked on the `end` path or the promise never settles.

**Model answer:** a `readable` handler that tries `read(n)` and resolves on a
non-null result, an `end` handler that rejects with the count it did manage,
an `error` handler, and — on every one of those three paths — removal of all
three listeners.

## ex2 — unshift is the only un-read

**What it tested:** that inspecting a stream's prefix without consuming it is a
supported operation, and how content sniffing is actually implemented.

**The classic mistake:** reading the prefix and then trying to hand the
consumer a `Readable.from([prefix, ...rest])` reconstruction. It works for the
data and loses everything else: the source's error propagation, its `destroy`
semantics, and its resource lifetime. `unshift` puts the bytes back into the
same stream, so the object you return is the object you were given.

**Model answer:** `read(n)`, and if the result is `null` because fewer than `n`
bytes exist, `read()` with no argument to take what there is; then
`unshift(prefix)` before returning it. Unshifting an empty buffer is a no-op
worth guarding, because unshifting after `end` throws.

## ex3 — the resource is not the stream

**What it tested:** `_construct` and `_destroy` as the acquisition and release
points, and the guarantee that `_destroy` runs exactly once.

**The classic mistake:** opening the resource in the constructor body. That
makes construction a side effect, so a stream you build and never read still
holds a file descriptor — and a batch job that maps a thousand paths to a
thousand streams before processing them exhausts the descriptor table before
reading a byte. The second mistake is closing in an `end` listener, which never
runs when the consumer destroys the stream early.

**Model answer:** `construct(cb)` awaits `open()` and stores the handle,
calling `cb(err)` on failure so the stream errors before any read;
`destroy(err, cb)` closes if a handle exists and forwards the original error
ahead of any close error, because the first failure is the interesting one.

## ex4 — _writev is an optimisation with a correctness clause

**What it tested:** that a sink sees batches only when it opts in, and that
opting in does not remove the single-chunk path.

**The classic mistake:** implementing `_writev` alone. Node calls `_writev`
only when more than one write is buffered; a lone `write()` followed by `end()`
goes to `_write`, and a sink without one throws `ERR_METHOD_NOT_IMPLEMENTED` at
runtime, on the quiet path, in production. The other mistake is reading
`chunks[i]` as the data — each element is `{ chunk, encoding }`, and the extra
indirection is easy to miss because `console.log` of a Buffer inside an object
still looks like data.

**Model answer:** `_write` records a one-element batch, `_writev` records
`chunks.map((c) => c.chunk)`, `_final` records the terminal marker and calls
back — and nothing records anything before calling back, so a batch is only
counted once accepted.

## ex5 — finish and close are different questions

**What it tested:** the terminal-state vocabulary, including the case where the
stream reached its terminal state before you were asked.

**The classic mistake:** `new Promise((res) => stream.on("finish", res))`.
Three failures in one line: a destroyed stream never emits `finish`, so the
promise hangs; an errored stream emits `error` with nobody listening, so the
process throws; and a stream that already finished before the listener was
attached hangs too, because events are not replayed.

**Model answer:** check the synchronous state first — `errored`, then
`destroyed`, then the ended flags — and only then attach listeners. `errored`
is a property, not just an event, and reading it is how you learn about a
failure that happened before you arrived.

## ex6 — push() returning false is an instruction

**What it tested:** the bridge every real integration needs — a source that
produces on its own schedule, behind an interface that produces on demand.

**The classic mistake:** ignoring `push()`'s return value and pushing every
event as it arrives. The stream's internal buffer then grows without bound, and
because it is a buffer rather than an array in your code, the leak is invisible
in a heap snapshot until you know to look at `readableLength`. The second
mistake is unsubscribing in an `end` listener rather than `_destroy`, so a
consumer that gives up early leaves the subscription live.

**Model answer:** a `paused` flag set when `push` returns `false` and cleared
in `_read`, a queue for events that arrive while paused, and a single
`unsubscribe` call in `_destroy` guarded by a boolean, because `_destroy` is
guaranteed once but the subscription may already have been torn down by an
error.

## ex7 — cancellation is a lifetime problem

**What it tested:** `AbortSignal` integration, including the already-aborted
case and listener cleanup.

**The classic mistake:** `signal.addEventListener("abort", ...)` with no
removal. An `AbortController` that outlives the stream — a request-scoped one
reused across many operations — accumulates a listener per operation, each
retaining the stream. This is the `EventEmitter` leak from `04_events_errors`
with a different class name. The second mistake is skipping the
`signal.aborted` check, which makes cancellation before the first tick a no-op.

**Model answer:** the already-aborted branch first, then `addEventListener`
with `{ once: true }` for the abort side, and an unconditional
`removeEventListener` in a `finished()` callback so the non-aborted path cleans
up too.

## ex8 — a tee is a fan-out with two rates

**What it tested:** that duplicating a stream means duplicating demand, and
that the two branches will not consume at the same speed.

**The classic mistake:** pushing each item into both branches and ignoring the
`push` results. The slow branch's buffer grows to the size of the entire source
— which is fine for tests and fatal for a large file, and is exactly the
failure mode that makes people believe teeing is impossible. The other mistake
is ending both branches when one is destroyed; the prompt asks for the
opposite.

**Model answer:** a per-branch flag for "destroyed", a shared pull loop that
runs only when at least one live branch has demand, and per-branch queues so a
lagging branch buffers explicitly rather than inside the stream machinery,
where you cannot see it.

## challenge — a parser written in reads

**What it tested:** ex1 and ex2 composed into a real protocol reader, and the
insight that `read(n)` removes the need for a leftover buffer entirely.

**The classic mistake:** reverting to the accumulate-and-slice pattern from the
previous sector inside a `data` handler. It works, and it throws away the point
of the exercise: the pull protocol lets you say "give me four bytes" and then
"give me *length* bytes", which is the protocol written as code rather than as
a state variable. The subtler bug is calling `read(length)` before checking
that `length` is bounded.

**Model answer:** an async pull loop that awaits a `readable` event whenever
`read(n)` returns `null`, checks `readable.readableEnded` to distinguish "not
yet" from "never", and pushes each completed frame into the object-mode output.

## review1 — the flags have a precedence

**What it tested:** the state machine, named. Anyone can list the properties;
the exercise is deciding which one wins when several are true at once.

**The classic mistake:** checking `destroyed` before `errored`. Every errored
stream is also destroyed, so that ordering reports every failure as a clean
shutdown — and a monitoring dashboard built on it shows zero errors forever.
The same trap sits between `ended` and `ending`.

**Model answer:** most-specific first — `errored`, then `destroyed`, then the
ended flags, then the flowing tri-state — with `readableFlowing === null`
mapping to `"idle"` rather than `"paused"`, because a stream nobody has read
from has not been paused, it has never started.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `readable.read([size])`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#readablereadsize) — the all-or-nothing contract behind ex1 and the challenge.
- [Node.js: `readable.unshift()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#readableunshiftchunk-encoding) — the content-sniffing use case ex2 reproduces.
- [Node.js: `_construct` and `_destroy`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#readable_constructcallback) — the acquisition and release hooks for ex3.
- [Node.js: `writable._writev()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#writable_writevchunks-callback) — the batch signature ex4 implements, including the `{ chunk, encoding }` shape.
- [Node.js: `stream.finished()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streamfinishedstream-options-callback) — the terminal-state helper ex5 asks you to reason about by hand.
- [Node.js: two reading modes](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#two-reading-modes) — the `readableFlowing` tri-state that review1 classifies.

# V3·A2 — Readable and Writable from first principles (archive)

## The model that makes the API make sense

A Node stream is a bounded queue with two callbacks attached. The Readable side
owns a buffer, a `_read(size)` implementation that is asked to fill it, and a
`push()` that fills it. The Writable side owns a buffer, a `_write` or
`_writev` implementation that is asked to drain it, and a `write()` that fills
it. Everything else — flowing mode, `pipe`, async iteration, `pipeline` — is a
scheduling policy layered on those two queues.

Hold that model and the surprising bits become predictable. `push()` returns
`false` because the readable buffer is at its `highWaterMark`; `write()`
returns `false` for the writable one. `_read` is called when the readable
buffer is below the mark and a consumer wants data; it is *not* called again
until you `push` something, which is why a `_read` that returns without pushing
and without arranging a later push produces a stream that hangs with no error.

## The reading modes, precisely

```ts
const r = getReadable();
r.readableFlowing;            // null — nothing has asked yet

r.on("readable", () => {});   // still null-ish: pull protocol, not flowing
r.on("data", () => {});       // true
r.pause();                    // false
r.resume();                   // true
```

Three consequences worth internalising:

1. **A stream in the `null` state produces nothing and releases nothing.**
   Construct a hundred and you hold a hundred sockets. This is why `_construct`
   exists.
2. **Adding a `data` listener is a side effect**, not an observation. It starts
   the stream. Adding one "just to log" changes program behaviour, and adding
   one after data has already flowed misses everything before it.
3. **Mixing protocols is a bug.** A `data` listener plus a `readable` listener
   on the same stream means two consumers competing for one buffer; the
   documentation says do not, and the failure is silently interleaved chunks.

`read(n)` deserves its own paragraph because it is the least-known useful thing
in the module:

```ts
readable.read(4);   // exactly 4 bytes, or null — never 3
readable.read();    // everything buffered, or null
readable.read(0);   // always null, but triggers a refill and a later 'readable'
```

In object mode, `read(n)` ignores `n` and returns one object. In byte mode, a
size larger than the `highWaterMark` raises the mark for that stream, which is
occasionally what you want and more often a sign you should raise it
explicitly.

## Lifetime hooks

```ts
import { Readable } from "node:stream";

class Source extends Readable {
  #handle?: Handle;

  _construct(callback: (err?: Error | null) => void): void {
    open().then((h) => { this.#handle = h; callback(); }, callback);
  }

  _read(size: number): void {
    this.#handle!.next().then((v) => this.push(v ?? null), (e) => this.destroy(e));
  }

  _destroy(err: Error | null, callback: (err?: Error | null) => void): void {
    if (!this.#handle) return callback(err);
    this.#handle.close().then(() => callback(err), (e) => callback(err ?? e));
  }
}
```

Four rules that this shape encodes:

- `_construct`'s callback gates the first `_read`. Reads issued before it fires
  are queued, so you never see a half-constructed stream.
- `_destroy` runs **once**, for every ending. It is the only place cleanup
  belongs.
- `_destroy` receives the error that caused the destruction, or `null`. Pass it
  through; do not replace it with a close error, because the first failure
  explains the second.
- Never `throw` from `_read` or `_write`. Call `destroy(err)` or the callback
  with an error. A synchronous throw from inside the machinery escapes into
  whatever was calling `read()`, which is usually Node itself.

## The writable side

```ts
const w = new Writable({
  highWaterMark: 64 * 1024,
  write(chunk, encoding, cb) { sink.append(chunk); cb(); },
  writev(chunks, cb) { sink.appendAll(chunks.map((c) => c.chunk)); cb(); },
  final(cb) { sink.flush().then(() => cb(), cb); },
  destroy(err, cb) { sink.close(); cb(err); },
});
```

`_final` is the flush hook: it runs after `end()` and after every buffered
write has been handed to `_write`/`_writev`, and `finish` fires when its
callback does. That is where a batching sink writes its partial batch, where a
file writer fsyncs, and where a network client sends a terminator.

`cork()`/`uncork()` are the manual batching lever:

```ts
res.cork();
res.write(statusLine);
res.write(headers);
res.write(body);
process.nextTick(() => res.uncork());
```

The `nextTick` is idiomatic: it lets the current synchronous run finish
queueing before the flush. Node's HTTP layer corks around header-and-body
writes for exactly this reason, turning two syscalls into one. Two warnings:
`cork` nests (n corks need n uncorks), and an exception between cork and uncork
leaves the stream corked forever, so anything non-trivial belongs in a
`try`/`finally`.

## Terminal states

| property | meaning |
|---|---|
| `writableEnded` | `end()` has been called |
| `writableFinished` | everything has been flushed; `finish` has fired |
| `readableEnded` | `end` event has fired |
| `destroyed` | `destroy()` has run |
| `closed` | the `close` event has fired |
| `errored` | the error the stream died of, or `null` |

`errored` is the one people miss. It is a property holding an `Error`, added in
Node 18, and it means you can learn that a stream failed without having had a
listener attached at the time. Every terminal-state check should start there.

## Common mistakes

- Treating `read(n) === null` as end-of-stream. It means "not yet".
- Adding a `data` listener to inspect a stream, thereby starting it.
- Mixing the `data` and `readable` protocols on one stream.
- Acquiring a resource in a stream's constructor instead of `_construct`.
- Cleaning up in an `end`/`finish` listener instead of `_destroy`.
- Implementing `_writev` without `_write`.
- Reading `chunks[i]` in `_writev` instead of `chunks[i].chunk`.
- `cork()` without a guaranteed `uncork()`.
- Waiting on `finish` for a stream that may be destroyed instead.
- `signal.addEventListener("abort", ...)` with no matching removal.
- Throwing from `_read` or `_write` rather than destroying or calling back.
- Calling `push()` after `push(null)` — it emits `ERR_STREAM_PUSH_AFTER_EOF`.

## The interview answer

*"What is backpressure and where does a Readable express it?"* — Backpressure
is the consumer's ability to slow the producer. On the writable side it is
`write()` returning `false` and the `drain` event. On the readable side it is
`push()` returning `false`: the buffer is full, so stop producing until `_read`
is called. A source that ignores that return value has no backpressure at all,
regardless of what is downstream.

*"Why would you use the `readable` event instead of `data`?"* — When you need
to control how much you take. `read(n)` is all-or-nothing, so protocol parsing
— a fixed header then a variable body — is two calls instead of a leftover
buffer and a state variable. Also when you need to `unshift`, which flowing
mode cannot do.

*"Where do you release a file descriptor held by a custom stream?"* —
`_destroy`, because it is the only hook Node guarantees runs exactly once for
every ending: normal end with `autoDestroy`, explicit destroy, error, or a
`pipeline` unwinding. `end` and `finish` are each skippable.

## Check yourself

1. What are the three values of `readableFlowing` and what causes each?
2. Why is adding a `data` listener not a read-only operation?
3. `read(4)` returns `null` on a stream with 3 bytes buffered and more coming.
   What should your code do next, and what should it not conclude?
4. What does `read(0)` do, and when is it useful?
5. When is `unshift` illegal, and what happens if you call it then?
6. Give a concrete scenario where opening a resource in the constructor rather
   than `_construct` costs you an outage.
7. `_destroy` receives an error argument. When is it non-null, and what should
   you do with it if closing also fails?
8. Under what circumstances does Node call `_writev` rather than `_write`?
9. What is the shape of an element of the `chunks` array in `_writev`?
10. What does `_final` run after, and what fires when its callback fires?
11. Why is `cork()` usually paired with `process.nextTick(() => uncork())`?
12. Distinguish `writableEnded`, `writableFinished` and `closed`.
13. Why should a terminal-state check read `errored` before `destroyed`?
14. What does `push()` returning `false` oblige a custom Readable to do?
15. What goes wrong if an `AbortSignal` outlives the streams that listen to it?
