# Streams as state machines: the design, the rewrites, and the parts that still
# leak

## Four generations of the same idea

Node's stream module has been rewritten more times than any other part of the
platform, and each rewrite is legible in the API.

**Streams1** (0.x) was `data`/`end`/`pause`/`resume` and nothing else. `pause()`
was advisory — a source could ignore it — so backpressure was a suggestion.
Data was delivered as it arrived, and if you attached your listener a tick too
late, it was gone. That last property, "the stream starts when you look at it",
survives today as flowing mode and is still the single most common source of
lost data in Node programs.

**Streams2** (0.10, 2013) introduced the internal buffer, `highWaterMark`, the
`readable` event, and `read(n)`. This is the rewrite that made backpressure
real: a source now pushes into a buffer, `push()` reports when the buffer is
full, and consumers pull. Flowing mode was retained as a compatibility layer
implemented on top of the pull model, which is why `readableFlowing` is a
tri-state — `null` is "we have not decided which compatibility path you are
on".

**Streams3** (0.12) unified the two so that a single stream could be used
either way without an explicit mode switch, at the cost of the rule that you
must not use both protocols at once.

Since then the changes have been additive and each one closed a specific
recurring bug: `pipeline()` in 10 (because `pipe` leaks on error),
`autoDestroy` defaulting on in 14 (because streams stayed alive after
finishing), `_construct` in 15 (because lazy acquisition needed a wrapper),
`errored`/`closed` as properties in 18 (because terminal state was only
observable through events), and `AbortSignal` support throughout (because
cancellation was ad hoc).

Knowing this history is practical, not decorative: it tells you that anything
awkward in the API is a compatibility seam, and that the newest mechanism is
usually the one that fixed the bug you are about to hit.

## What happens on a read, in order

Call `readable.read(4)` on a stream with 2 bytes buffered:

1. `read` computes `howMuchToRead`. Fewer bytes are available than requested,
   so the answer is 0 and the return value will be `null`.
2. Because the buffer is below the `highWaterMark`, `read` sets
   `state.needReadable = true` and calls `_read(highWaterMark)`.
3. Your `_read` does whatever it does. If it pushes synchronously, `push`
   appends to the buffer and — because `needReadable` is set — schedules an
   `emitReadable` on the next tick. If it pushes asynchronously, the same thing
   happens later.
4. `read` returns `null`. Your `readable` handler exits.
5. On the next tick, `readable` fires. You call `read(4)` again. This time
   `howMuchToRead` returns 4, the buffer is sliced, and you get a Buffer.

Two things fall out. First, the loop `while ((chunk = read(n)) !== null)` in a
`readable` handler is not a busy-wait; it drains what is available and exits,
and the event brings you back. Second, `_read` is a *request*, not a
requirement — Node will not call it again until you push, so a `_read` that
neither pushes nor schedules a push is a permanent stall, and it produces no
error because from the machinery's perspective you simply have not answered
yet. That is the number one cause of "my custom stream hangs".

## The buffer is a linked list, and that matters

Since Node 12 the internal buffer is a singly linked list (`BufferList`) with
`head`, `tail` and `length`. `push` appends in O(1); `read` consumes from the
head. The `consume(n)` path has a fast case when the head chunk is exactly the
right size and a slow case that walks and copies.

The performance consequence: **chunk size dominates**. A stream delivering
64 KiB chunks does a fraction of the bookkeeping of one delivering 64-byte
chunks for the same bytes, because the per-chunk cost — list node, event
scheduling, a `_read` round trip — is fixed. This is why `fs.createReadStream`
defaults to a 64 KiB `highWaterMark` and why raising it for network sockets
rarely helps (the kernel is handing you MTU-sized pieces regardless) but
raising it for files often does.

Object mode inverts the arithmetic. `highWaterMark` counts *items*, defaulting
to 16, and each item can be any size. Sixteen 10 MB rows is 160 MB of "buffer",
and the machinery reports it as a length of 16. When an object-mode pipeline
blows up on memory, this is nearly always why, and the fix is an explicit
`highWaterMark` of 1 or 2 on the object-mode stages.

Measuring: `stream.readableLength` and `stream.writableLength` are live
counters, and sampling them under load is the only honest way to see where a
pipeline is queueing. `process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers` catches byte-mode
buffering that `heapUsed` misses. Do not measure with timers; measure with the
counters, because timing tells you a stage is slow and the counters tell you
which one.

## Where the design still leaks

**Errors are not values.** A stream can fail after you have stopped looking,
and until Node 18 the only way to know was to have been listening. `errored` as
a property fixed the observability, not the ergonomics: you still cannot ask a
stream "did you succeed" without a helper. `stream.finished()` is that helper
and most code should use it instead of hand-rolling ex5.

**`close` is not guaranteed to be last, and `finish` is not guaranteed at
all.** `emitClose: false` exists; some third-party streams never emit it. Code
that waits for a specific event rather than using `finished()` is code that
works against the streams it was tested with.

**Half-open duplexes are genuinely hard.** The readable and writable halves
have independent states, so `destroyed` on a Duplex means "both", `end()` means
"the writable half", and a socket where one side has shut down its write
direction is a state the property table describes only awkwardly.

**Mixing protocols is unenforced.** Attaching `data` and `readable` listeners
to one stream is documented as unsupported and does not throw. It interleaves.

## When not to work at this level

Most of the time. If your problem is "read this file, transform each line,
write that file", the answer is `pipeline` with an async generator in the
middle, and every hook in this sector is somebody else's implementation detail.
Reach for `_construct`, `_writev`, `read(n)` and `unshift` when you are
*building* a stream that others will consume — a client library, a codec, a
framework adapter — and not when you are consuming one.

Specifically: do not hand-roll a tee when the data fits in memory; collect it
into an array and iterate twice. Do not hand-roll cancellation when
`pipeline(..., { signal })` exists. Do not implement `_writev` before measuring
that per-chunk overhead is your bottleneck. And if you find yourself
implementing a Readable whose `_read` is a queue drain, check whether
`Readable.from(asyncGenerator)` expresses the same thing in a quarter of the
code — it usually does, and it gets `_destroy` right for free.

The exceptions are real, though, and they are the reason this sector exists. A
protocol client cannot avoid `read(n)`. A file-backed stream cannot avoid
`_construct` without leaking descriptors. A sink over a batching API cannot
avoid `_writev`. And nothing at all can avoid `_destroy`.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: API for stream implementers](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#api-for-stream-implementers) — the authoritative description of every hook in this sector.
- [Node.js: two reading modes](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#two-reading-modes) — the tri-state and the rule against mixing protocols.
- [Node.js backpressure guide](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) — the official walkthrough of `push()` and `write()` return values.
- [`lib/internal/streams/readable.js`](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/lib/internal/streams/readable.js) — `howMuchToRead`, `emitReadable` and `needReadable`, which explain the tick-by-tick trace above.
- [Streams2 announcement, nodejs.org (2012)](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/feature/streams2) — why the internal buffer and `read(n)` were added, in the words of the people who added them.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — exactly n bytes

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function readExactly(readable: Readable, n: number): Promise<Buffer>;
```

Resolve with a `Buffer` of exactly `n` bytes taken from the front of the
stream, using the `readable` event and `read(n)` — not by accumulating `data`
events. Bytes beyond `n` stay in the stream for the next consumer.

```ts
const src = Readable.from([Buffer.from("abc"), Buffer.from("defgh")]);
await readExactly(src, 5);          // <Buffer 61 62 63 64 65>  ("abcde")
await readExactly(src, 3);          // <Buffer 66 67 68>        ("fgh")
```

A stream that ends with fewer than `n` bytes available rejects with an `Error`
whose message contains both `n` and the number of bytes it actually had. A
stream that errors rejects with that error. `n` of `0` resolves with an empty
buffer without waiting.

Every listener you attach must be removed on every settling path — the gate
asserts `readable.listenerCount("readable") === 0` afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex1
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the failure. Write the naive version — a single `readable`
handler that resolves whatever `read(n)` gives it — and feed it
`Readable.from(["ab", "cde"])` with `n = 5`. It hangs. Now instrument: log
inside the handler each time it fires and log the return value. You will see
`null` on the first firing, and then the process exits with the promise
unsettled. The bug is not in the reading; it is that you have no plan for the
firing where the answer is "not yet".

## Hint 2

The end path is subtler than it looks. When a stream ends, it emits one last
`readable` *and then* `end`. So your `readable` handler will run one final time
with the tail of the buffer available. If you need 5 bytes and 3 arrive, that
final `read(5)` still returns `null` — the bytes are there but not enough of
them — and only the `end` event tells you no more are coming. To report how
many bytes there *were*, call `read()` with no argument in the end handler:
it returns the whole remaining buffer.

## Hint 3

Shape: guard `n === 0`, then a promise with three listeners and a single
`settle` helper that detaches all three before resolving or rejecting. The
decision left to you is how the `end` path computes its count. Reading the
remainder with `read()` gives you the exact number for the message, but it also
*consumes* those bytes — decide whether a stream that failed to satisfy the
request should be left holding its tail, and be able to defend the choice.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — look, then put it back

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function sniff(readable: Readable, n: number): Promise<Buffer>;
```

Read up to `n` leading bytes, return them, and put them back so that the stream
is left exactly as you found it. The same `readable` object is then consumed by
somebody else, who must see every byte including the ones you inspected.

```ts
const src = Readable.from([Buffer.from("\x1f\x8brest of the gzip")]);
const magic = await sniff(src, 2);           // <Buffer 1f 8b>
magic.readUInt16BE(0) === 0x1f8b;            // true — it is gzip
(await text(src));                            // "\x1f\x8brest of the gzip"
```

A stream with fewer than `n` bytes in total returns what exists (an empty
buffer for an empty stream) and still leaves the stream intact. Nothing may be
unshifted after the stream has ended — that throws `ERR_STREAM_UNSHIFT_AFTER_END_EVENT`
— so an empty prefix must not be pushed back.

The gate sniffs, then drains, and compares the drained bytes to the original
input. It also asserts the stream still reports `readableEnded === false`
immediately after `sniff` resolves for a non-empty stream.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two operations, and the second is the one you may not know exists. Reading is
ex1's problem with one relaxation — you want *up to* `n` bytes, so a short
stream is not an error. Putting them back is a single method on `Readable`
whose entire purpose is this: to make a consumed prefix un-consumed, so that
the next reader sees the original stream.

## Hint 2

The two-step read, because `read(n)` will not short-read for you:

```ts
let prefix = src.read(n) as Buffer | null;
if (prefix === null) {
  // fewer than n bytes buffered — take whatever is there
  prefix = (src.read() as Buffer | null) ?? Buffer.alloc(0);
}
```

The fallback matters at two different times: when the stream is short overall,
and when it has simply not buffered `n` bytes yet. Only the first is a real
"short stream" — distinguishing them is what makes this harder than it looks.


## Hint 3

Shape: the listener triangle from ex1, relaxed so that `end` resolves with
whatever remains instead of rejecting, then `unshift` guarded on a non-empty
prefix and a stream that has not ended, then return. The decision left to you
is whether the guard on `readableEnded` is the right one or whether you should
be tracking "did I learn about the shortness from the end event" explicitly —
they are the same thing here, and they stop being the same thing the moment
somebody calls `sniff` twice.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through what you are *not* allowed to do. The obvious alternative —
read the prefix, then return a new stream that replays it in front of the rest
— fails for reasons that have nothing to do with data:

```ts
Readable.from([prefix, ...])   // wrong object identity
```

The caller holds a reference to the original stream. A new stream has its own
error propagation, its own `destroy`, and no connection to the underlying
resource, so destroying the wrapper leaks the file descriptor. The requirement
"the same object, unmodified" is the requirement that forces `unshift`.

## Hint 2

The illegal case will bite you. `unshift` after the `end` event throws
`ERR_STREAM_UNSHIFT_AFTER_END_EVENT`. That happens exactly when the stream was
shorter than `n` and you waited long enough to learn it — you now hold the tail
of a finished stream and cannot give it back. The prompt's contract handles
this by saying an empty prefix is not unshifted, but consider what your code
does with a *non-empty* prefix from an ended stream, and whether the gate's
"drain and compare" would notice.

## Hint 3

Shape: await enough data (ex1's listener triangle, relaxed to accept a short
result on `end`), then `if (prefix.length > 0) readable.unshift(prefix)`, then
return the prefix. The decision left to you is whether to return the caller's
buffer or a copy. `unshift` puts the very same `Buffer` object back into the
stream's internal list, so the caller now holds a live reference to memory a
later consumer will read — harmless if they only inspect it, a spectacular
heisenbug if they write to it.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — open nothing until asked

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface Resource<T> {
  next(): Promise<T | null>;   // null means end of data
  close(): Promise<void>;
}

export function createLazySource<T>(open: () => Promise<Resource<T>>): Readable;
```

An object-mode Readable over a resource that must not be acquired until
somebody reads, and must be released exactly once however the stream ends.

- `open` is **not** called during `createLazySource`. It is called from
  `_construct`, before the first `_read`.
- A rejected `open` makes the stream emit that error, and `close` is never
  called because nothing was opened.
- `close` runs exactly once on every ending: normal end, early `destroy()`, a
  rejected `next()`, or a consumer's `break` out of `for await`.
- A rejected `next()` destroys the stream with that error, and the error the
  consumer sees is that one — not a subsequent failure from `close`.

```ts
let opened = 0;
const src = createLazySource(async () => { opened++; return makeResource([1, 2]); });
opened;                          // 0 — nothing has been read
await src.take?.(0);             // (the gate uses its own probe)
for await (const v of src) { /* 1, 2 */ }
opened;                          // 1, and the resource is closed
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex3
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it by writing the tests you would want, before the code. There are
four endings, and each is a separate assertion:

- read to completion → `close` called once;
- `src.destroy()` after one item → `close` called once;
- `next()` rejects → `close` called once, and the consumer sees `next`'s error;
- `open()` rejects → `close` called **zero** times.

Now look at where you were going to put the cleanup. An `end` listener covers
one of those four. A `finally` in an async loop covers two. Only one hook
covers all four, and Node documents it as running exactly once.

## Hint 2

The error-precedence rule has a reason worth internalising. When `next()`
rejects and then `close()` also rejects — which is common, because the resource
is already broken — you have two errors and one slot. Report the first. The
second is almost always a consequence of the first, and a stack trace that says
"close failed" when the real event was "the connection dropped" costs somebody
an hour. This is the same reasoning as `try { … } finally { … }` swallowing a
secondary throw, and the same as an error `cause` chain.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `let resource: Resource<T> | undefined` in the closure, `construct`
awaiting `open()` into it, `read()` calling `next()` and pushing the value or
`null`, `destroy` closing if the resource exists. The decision left to you is
what `read` does about concurrency: Node will not call `_read` again until you
push, so a single in-flight `next()` is guaranteed *if* every path through
`read` ends in exactly one `push` or one `destroy`. Trace your error branch and
check that it does not both destroy and push.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The exercise is mostly about believing the documentation on one point: Node
calls `_writev` only when more than one write is *already buffered* when the
stream drains. It is an optimisation the machinery applies when it can, not a
replacement for `_write`. So a sink is not finished until both exist, and the
path that catches people is the boring one — a single write, no cork, nothing
under load.

## Hint 2

The `_writev` signature is the detail that surprises people:

```ts
writev(chunks, callback) {
  // chunks is Array<{ chunk: Buffer; encoding: BufferEncoding }>
  const buffers = chunks.map((c) => c.chunk);
  callback();
}
```

Each element is a wrapper object, not a Buffer. Logging `chunks` prints
something that looks buffer-ish enough to fool you, and the failure downstream
is a batch of `[object Object]`.


## Hint 3

Shape: two closure variables and a `new Writable({ write, writev, final })`,
returned inside an object literal with three accessor functions. Fifteen lines.
The decision left to you is whether `batches()` returns the internal array or a
copy of it. Handing out a live reference to internal state is the bug from
`04_events_errors` ex1 in a new costume: a caller who sorts the result has just
reordered your sink's history.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through `cork`, because that is how you make `_writev` fire on
demand rather than waiting for load. `cork()` tells the stream to buffer;
`uncork()` releases everything at once, which is exactly the "more than one
write buffered" condition. Node's own HTTP layer corks around the header and
body writes to turn two syscalls into one. Two rules come with it: corks nest,
so *n* corks need *n* uncorks; and an exception between the two leaves the
stream corked with no error anywhere, which looks exactly like a hung request.

## Hint 2

Think about ordering inside each method. The instinct is to record first and
call back second, and for this exercise either order passes — but a real sink
does the work first and calls back only on success, because `callback(err)` is
how a sink *refuses*. Recording before deciding gives you a log that claims to
have accepted data the sink rejected. That reconciliation mismatch is the bug
that makes people distrust their own metrics, so build the habit here where it
is free.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `batches: Buffer[][]` and a `finalised` boolean in the closure, a
`new Writable({ write, writev, final })` referring to them, and an object
literal exposing the three members. The decision left to you is what `_write`
records — a one-element array keeps `batches()` uniformly `Buffer[][]`, which
makes the caller's life simple, at the cost of hiding whether a batch of one
came from `_write` or from `_writev` with a single element. Decide whether that
distinction matters to your consumer before you erase it.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 5 — did it finish, or did it just stop?

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function settled(stream: Readable | Writable): Promise<"finished">;
```

without using `stream.finished` or `stream/promises`. Resolve with
`"finished"` when the stream completes normally; reject with the stream's own
error when it fails; reject with an `Error` whose message contains
`destroyed before completing` when it is destroyed without an error before
ending.

The hard requirement: it must give the right answer for a stream that reached
its terminal state **before** `settled` was called, because events are not
replayed.

```ts
const w = new Writable({ write(_c, _e, cb) { cb(); } });
w.end();
await settled(w);                        // "finished"

const dead = new Writable({ write(_c, _e, cb) { cb(); } });
dead.destroy(new Error("disk full"));
await settled(dead).catch((e) => e.message);   // "disk full"

const late = new Writable({ write(_c, _e, cb) { cb(); } });
late.destroy();
await settled(late).catch((e) => e.message);   // "...destroyed before completing"
```

The gate calls `settled` both before and after the terminal event for each of
the three outcomes, and requires the same answer either way. Remove your
listeners on every path.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split the problem in two and the shape appears: *has it already happened?* and
*what happens next?* The first half is answered synchronously by properties —
Node exposes the terminal state, not just the terminal events — and the second
half is the ordinary listener triangle. Write the synchronous half first and
return early from it; everything after that line is the not-yet case.

## Hint 2

The property vocabulary, worth printing on a scratch stream to see for
yourself:

```ts
w.errored;            // the Error it died of, or null
w.destroyed;          // destroy() has run
w.writableEnded;      // end() was called
w.writableFinished;   // everything flushed; 'finish' fired
r.readableEnded;      // 'end' fired
```

`errored` is the one that changes the design: it means a failure that happened
before you arrived is still discoverable, so you never have to guess.


## Hint 3

Shape: a synchronous prelude of early returns, then a promise with four
listeners — `finish`, `end`, `close`, `error` — and one detaching settle. The
decision left to you is what `close` means when it arrives first. It fires for
both good and bad endings, so it cannot decide the outcome on its own; the
model answer treats it as "if nothing better has arrived, consult `errored` and
fall back to the destroyed-early error". Convince yourself that ordering cannot
resolve success twice.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the bug you are being paid to avoid. This line appears in a great
deal of production code:

```ts
await new Promise((resolve) => stream.on("finish", resolve));
```

It has three distinct failure modes. A destroyed stream never emits `finish`,
so the await never returns and the request hangs until a proxy timeout. An
errored stream emits `error`, which — with no listener — throws and can take
the process down. And a stream that finished one tick before this line runs
also hangs, because `finish` fired to an empty room. Every requirement in the
prompt is one of those three.

## Hint 2

Order matters more than coverage. Ask what is true of a stream destroyed with
an error: `errored` is set, `destroyed` is `true`, and `writableFinished` is
`false`. All three checks match something, so whichever you test first decides
the answer. Check the most specific state first — the error — or every failure
in your system will be reported as a clean shutdown, and the dashboard will be
green while the queue backs up.

## Hint 3

Shape: a synchronous prelude returning early for `errored`, then `destroyed`,
then the ended-and-finished flags; after that a promise with `finish`/`end`,
`close` and `error` listeners and one detaching settle function. The decision
left to you is which event means success for each half of a Duplex — `finish`
is the writable side, `end` is the readable side, and a stream may legitimately
have only one. Listening for both and settling on either is the pragmatic
answer; be able to say why `close` alone is not sufficient.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come in through the leak. Write the version that ignores `push()`'s return
value — three lines, works perfectly on the tests you would write first — and
then run it against a source emitting a million values into a consumer that
processes one per tick. Watch `src.readableLength` climb. That number is the
stream's internal buffer, it has no upper bound once you ignore the return
value, and it does not look like an array in a heap snapshot. The whole
exercise is the two lines that stop it.

## Hint 2

Think carefully about `end()` arriving while your queue is non-empty. The
source has finished producing but the consumer has not finished consuming, so
pushing `null` immediately truncates the stream — silently, with no error, and
only under load, because in a fast test the queue is always empty when `end`
arrives. Set a flag instead, and push `null` at the one place that knows the
queue is empty: the drain loop.

## Hint 3

Shape: closure state of `queue`, `paused`, `ended`, `unsubscribe` and a
`subscribed` flag; `_read` subscribes on first call, then clears `paused`,
drains, and pushes `null` if `ended` and empty; `_destroy` calls `unsubscribe`
once and nulls it. The decision left to you is whether `emit` after `end()` is
an error or is ignored. The stream will throw `ERR_STREAM_PUSH_AFTER_EOF` if
you forward it, so you must decide deliberately — a badly behaved source is not
a reason to crash a consumer.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — cancellation

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function withAbort<T extends Readable>(stream: T, signal: AbortSignal): T;
```

Return the same stream, wired so that aborting the signal destroys it with an
`AbortError` — an `Error` whose `name` is `"AbortError"` and whose message
mentions the operation was aborted.

- An **already-aborted** signal destroys the stream before `withAbort` returns
  control to the event loop.
- The abort listener is removed once the stream settles for any reason, so a
  long-lived `AbortController` does not accumulate listeners.
- Aborting after the stream has already ended does nothing.
- `signal.reason` is used as the error when it is an `Error`; otherwise the
  `AbortError` is constructed.

```ts
const ac = new AbortController();
const src = withAbort(Readable.from([1, 2, 3]), ac.signal);
ac.abort();
await once(src, "error");      // AbortError

const before = new AbortController();
before.abort(new Error("too late"));
const s2 = withAbort(Readable.from([1]), before.signal);
s2.errored?.message;           // "too late"
```

The gate creates one `AbortController`, wires a hundred streams to it, lets
them all finish normally, and asserts
`getEventListeners(signal, "abort").length === 0` afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An `AbortSignal` is an `EventTarget`, and everything you learned about
`EventEmitter` leaks in `04_events_errors` applies unchanged: a listener added
per operation to a target that outlives the operation is a growing array of
closures. The only difference is the method names — `addEventListener` and
`removeEventListener` rather than `on` and `off` — and the fact that the leak is
easier to miss, because a signal does not warn you at eleven listeners.

## Hint 2

The already-aborted branch is not an optimisation, it is a correctness case:

```ts
if (signal.aborted) {
  stream.destroy(toError(signal.reason));
  return stream;
}
```

A listener added to an already-fired signal never runs — `abort` is a one-shot
event that has already happened — so without this branch, cancelling before you
start is the one case where cancellation silently does nothing. This is the
same shape as ex5's "terminal state before you looked" problem.


## Hint 3

Shape: a `toError(reason)` helper, an early return for the already-aborted
case, `addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true })`, and `finished()`
for the removal. The decision left to you is what happens if the *same* stream
is passed to `withAbort` twice with different signals — nothing in the
signature prevents it, both listeners are legitimate, and both cleanups must
still run. Decide whether that is a supported use or something you would
document against.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the error object, because "an `AbortError`" is a convention rather
than a class and getting it wrong makes your stream un-catchable by the code
that expects it. There is no `AbortError` constructor in Node's public API. The
convention — shared with `fetch`, `fs/promises` and the DOM — is an `Error`
whose `name` property is exactly `"AbortError"`, and consumers branch on
`err.name === "AbortError"` to distinguish "we cancelled this" from "this
failed". Node also gives you `signal.throwIfAborted()`, whose thrown value has
that shape when the reason was not set explicitly.

## Hint 2

The cleanup half needs a hook that fires for every ending, and this time it is
not `_destroy` — you did not build this stream, you were handed it. What you
have is the module-level helper that takes any stream and calls you back when
it is done, whatever "done" turned out to mean. It also returns a cleanup
function of its own, which is the detail people miss: the helper itself
attaches listeners, and abandoning it is a second leak on top of the one you
were fixing.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `toError(reason)` helper, the already-aborted early return, an
`onAbort` closure, `signal.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true })`,
and a `finished(stream, () => signal.removeEventListener("abort", onAbort))`
for the cleanup. The decision left to you is what the abort handler does when
the stream has already ended — `destroy()` on an ended stream is documented as
a no-op, so the guard is arguably redundant; decide whether you want to depend
on that, and note that `stream.destroyed` makes the intent visible either way.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — two consumers, one source

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function tee(source: Readable): [Readable, Readable];
```

Two object-mode Readables that each receive every item of `source`, in order.

- The source is pulled only when at least one live branch wants data, so a
  branch that is not being read does not cause the source to be drained into
  memory without limit.
- A slow branch buffers rather than losing items; the gate reads branch A to
  completion first, then branch B, and requires both to see everything.
- Destroying one branch does not end or stall the other; the source keeps
  flowing for the survivor.
- Destroying **both** branches destroys the source.
- An error on the source destroys both branches with that error.

```ts
const [a, b] = tee(Readable.from([1, 2, 3]));
await toArray(a);   // [1, 2, 3]
await toArray(b);   // [1, 2, 3]
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3na02_readable_writable ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The thing that makes teeing hard is that "how much have you consumed" is now
two numbers instead of one, and the source can only be at one position. Two
designs follow from that: keep one shared buffer plus a read cursor per branch,
or keep a queue per branch and push every item into both. The second is simpler
and is what the prompt describes; the first is what you would build if memory
mattered more than clarity.

## Hint 2

The pull trigger, sketched for a single branch so the two-branch version is
still yours:

```ts
const pump = async () => {
  if (pumping) return;
  pumping = true;
  for await (const item of source) {
    branch.push(item);
    if (branch.readableLength > 8) await once(branch, "resume"); // crude
  }
  pumping = false;
};
```

That `if` is the crude version of the real condition, which is "at least one
live branch has asked for more". Replace it with a per-branch `wants` flag set
in `_read` and cleared when `push` returns `false`, and the pump becomes
correct rather than approximate.


## Hint 3

Shape: a branch factory producing `{ stream, live, wants }`, one async `pump`
guarded by a `pumping` flag, and a `demand()` promise the pump awaits when no
live branch wants more. `_destroy` clears `live`, destroys the source when the
live count hits zero, and nudges the pump so it is not left waiting on a
promise nobody will resolve. The decision left to you is the branch
`highWaterMark`: it is the size of the gap you are willing to let the two
consumers drift apart by, and choosing it is the whole design.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the failure the prompt is guarding against. Write the naive
tee — a `data` listener on the source pushing into both branches — and read
branch A to completion before touching branch B. Everything works, and
`b.readableLength` is now the entire source. For three integers that is
nothing; for a 4 GB file it is the process. The lesson generalises: **a tee
whose branches are consumed at different rates buffers the difference, and
somebody has to own that buffer.** Your job is to make it explicit rather than
accidental.

## Hint 2

The destroy matrix is where the marks are. Four cases, and the naive
implementation gets two of them wrong:

| event | branch A | branch B | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A destroyed | dead | keeps going | keeps going |
| A and B destroyed | dead | dead | destroyed |
| source errors | destroyed with err | destroyed with err | — |
| source ends | pushes null | pushes null | — |

The two people miss are row one — ending B when A dies, because the pump loop
had a single exit — and row two, leaving the source open forever because
nothing counted the survivors.

## Hint 3

Shape: two `Readable`s built by a small factory that records a `live` flag and
a `wants` flag per branch; a single async pump that iterates the source and
pushes to every live branch, awaiting a "somebody wants more" promise when all
live branches are full; `_destroy` on each branch clearing its flag and
destroying the source when the live count reaches zero. The decision left to
you is how the pump waits: a promise resolved by the next `_read`, or a poll on
the next tick. One of those is correct and one only usually works.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The insight to lean on: with `read(n)` you do not need a parser state machine
at all. A state machine exists to remember "I am part-way through a length
prefix" — but `read(4)` already remembers that for you by refusing to return
anything until four bytes exist. So the parser becomes two sequential
statements in a loop, which is what the protocol actually says.

## Hint 2

You need one primitive: "await exactly `n` bytes, or learn that the stream
ended". That is ex1, with the ending distinguished rather than thrown:

```ts
async function readN(src: Readable, n: number): Promise<Buffer | null> {
  for (;;) {
    const chunk = src.read(n) as Buffer | null;
    if (chunk !== null) return chunk;
    if (src.readableEnded) return null;
    await once(src, "readable");   // may also settle on 'end'
  }
}
```

Build the whole challenge on top of that and the frame loop is six lines. Note
that `once(src, "readable")` from `node:events` rejects on `error`, which is
how source failures reach you without a third listener.


## Hint 3

Shape: a `readN(src, n)` helper returning `Buffer | null`, then an object-mode
`Readable` with `highWaterMark: 1` whose `read()` runs an async IIFE — header,
bound check, payload, push — with a `reading` re-entrancy flag and a `destroy`
that destroys the source. The decision left to you is what to do with the
`unshift` the prompt offers you. The model answer never needs it, because
`read(n)` never short-reads; work out for yourself which alternative design
would need it, and you will understand what `unshift` is actually for.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come in through the read-ahead requirement, because it is the one that
constrains the architecture rather than the code. If you write the obvious
`Readable` with an async `_read` that reads a frame and pushes it, you get
laziness for free — Node will not call `_read` again until you push. If you
instead write a background loop that reads frames and pushes them as fast as it
can, you have to check `push()`'s return value and suspend, which is ex6 again.
Both are legitimate; only one of them is short. Decide before you type.

## Hint 2

The two endings are easy to confuse and the gate separates them. A source that
ends *between* frames is a clean end: push `null`. A source that ends after
delivering a length prefix but not the payload is corruption: destroy with an
error. Your `readN` helper returns `null` in both cases, so the caller must
know which one it asked for — the first `readN(4)` returning `null` is fine,
the second `readN(length)` returning `null` is not. That asymmetry is the whole
error path.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `readN` helper as above, then a `new Readable({ objectMode: true,
highWaterMark: 1, read() { ... }, destroy() { ... } })` whose `read` is an
async IIFE doing prefix-then-payload-then-push. Guard against re-entrancy with
a `reading` flag even though `_read` should not overlap — an async `_read` that
awaits makes the guarantee harder to reason about than it is worth. The
decision left to you is where the length bound goes relative to the payload
read, and what it means that a hostile peer can make you allocate before it
sends a single payload byte.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is a classification problem where the hard part is not knowing the
properties but ordering the tests. Many of them are true at once — an errored
stream is destroyed and closed; an ended stream has `writableEnded` set as well
as `writableFinished`. So write the list of states down first, mark which
properties are true in each, and read off the ordering that distinguishes them.
The answer is always "most specific first".

## Hint 2

The tri-state is the one that needs care:

```ts
if (r.readableFlowing === true)  return "flowing";
if (r.readableFlowing === false) return "paused";
return "idle";   // null
```

Strict comparison against `true` and `false` rather than truthiness, because
`null` is falsy and would collapse `"idle"` into `"paused"`. That distinction
is not pedantry: `null` means nobody has ever read, which for a file-backed
stream means the descriptor is open and nothing is happening — a leak, not a
pause.


## Hint 3

Shape: one widened local type, six ordered `if`s, and the tri-state. Under
twenty lines. The decision left to you is what a Writable with none of the
terminal flags set should be called. The prompt says `"idle"`, which is honest
but lossy — a writable that is mid-flush with a full buffer is not idle in any
useful sense, and `writableLength` would tell you so. Note where the
classification is coarser than the reality, because that is the kind of thing
that matters when the function's output becomes a metric.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a monitoring problem, which is what it is. Imagine this function
labelling a metric. Get step 1 and 2 the wrong way round and every failure in
the fleet is counted as a clean shutdown, so the error rate is a flat zero
while the queue backs up and nobody is paged. The ordering is not a style
question; it is the difference between an observable system and a green
dashboard on a burning building.

## Hint 2

Duplex streams are where a naive implementation falls over, and the gate
includes one. A Duplex has both halves, so `writableEnded` can be true while
`readableFlowing` is `true` — the write direction has shut down and data is
still arriving, which is exactly a socket after `shutdown(SHUT_WR)`. Decide
which half your classification describes and be consistent. The prompt's
ordering answers it for you: the writable-side terminal states are checked
before the readable-side flowing states.

## Hint 3

Shape: a widened local type so TypeScript lets you read properties that only
exist on one side, then six `if`s in the prompt's order, then the tri-state.
The decision left to you is how to detect "this is a readable" for step 5 —
`"readableFlowing" in stream` is honest and cheap, `stream instanceof Readable`
fails for duck-typed streams from other libraries, and reading the property and
comparing against `undefined` conflates "not a readable" with "a readable in an
odd state". Pick one and know its failure mode.

lessons.title: V3·A3 — Transform streams and object mode
lessons.summary: Transform as a pair of independent queues with a callback in between. Buffered remainders and _flush, byte-in object-out and back again, the two object-mode flags set separately, PassThrough as a meter, bounded stateful transforms, compose with async generators, and a concurrent map that preserves order.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A3 — Transform streams and object mode

`d16_transform_pipeline` had you write transforms that map one chunk to one
chunk: uppercase, JSON-parse, filter. That is the easy half, and it hides the
thing that makes transforms interesting — a Transform is not a function applied
to a stream. It is a Writable and a Readable glued together, with **two
independent buffers, two independent object-mode flags and two independent
high-water marks**, and the glue is a callback you are trusted to call exactly
once.

Almost every hard transform bug is a consequence of that structure. The line
splitter that loses its last line has forgotten that the writable side ended
while the readable side still owed a chunk. The parser that turns 64 KiB of
bytes into ten thousand objects has an object-mode readable side with a
high-water mark of 16 and no idea it is now the bottleneck. The async transform
that processes one record at a time when the API could take ten is not slow
because of the network; it is slow because the callback is a concurrency gate
of exactly one.

## Concept — the two halves

```ts
import { Transform } from "node:stream";

const parse = new Transform({
  writableObjectMode: false,   // bytes in
  readableObjectMode: true,    // objects out
  writableHighWaterMark: 64 * 1024,
  readableHighWaterMark: 8,

  transform(chunk, encoding, callback) {
    for (const obj of decode(chunk)) this.push(obj);
    callback();                // "I am ready for the next chunk"
  },

  flush(callback) {
    if (remainder) this.push(finish(remainder));
    callback();                // "nothing more will be pushed"
  },
});
```

Read that as two contracts rather than one. `push()` speaks to the **readable**
side: it appends to the output buffer and returns `false` when that buffer is
full. `callback()` speaks to the **writable** side: it says the input chunk has
been consumed and the next may arrive. They are not the same statement and you
need both.

The rules that follow, in the order people break them:

1. **Call the callback exactly once per `transform` call.** Twice is
   `ERR_MULTIPLE_CALLBACK` and takes the process down; zero times is a stream
   that stops with no error at all, which is worse.
2. **Do not push after calling the callback for the last time** — that is what
   `_flush` is for. Pushing after `_flush`'s callback is
   `ERR_STREAM_PUSH_AFTER_EOF`.
3. **`callback(err)` is how a transform fails.** Throwing from inside
   `transform` escapes into the machinery; in an async `transform` a throw
   becomes an unhandled rejection instead, which is worse again.
4. **`callback(null, value)` is shorthand for `push(value); callback()`** and
   is only usable in the one-in-one-out case. Where the ratio is anything else,
   use `push` explicitly.

## Concept — object mode is two flags, and a count

`objectMode: true` sets both sides. Setting them separately is what makes a
parser or a serialiser expressible:

| stream | writable side | readable side |
|---|---|---|
| line splitter | bytes | objects (strings) |
| NDJSON serialiser | objects | bytes |
| batcher | objects | objects |
| gzip | bytes | bytes |

The high-water mark means different things on each side. In byte mode it is
bytes and defaults to 64 KiB (16 KiB before Node 22 for some stream types); in
object mode it is a **count of items** and defaults to 16. Sixteen items can be
sixteen bytes or sixteen 10 MB rows, and the stream machinery cannot tell the
difference. Every object-mode memory blow-up traces back to that sentence, and
the fix is an explicit `readableHighWaterMark` of 1 or 2 on stages whose items
are large.

## Concept — the callback is the concurrency gate

```ts
transform(record, _enc, callback) {
  enrich(record).then((out) => { this.push(out); callback(); }, callback);
}
```

This is correct and it is strictly serial: Node will not call `transform` again
until `callback` fires, so one record is in flight at a time. If `enrich` is a
50 ms network call, ten thousand records take eight minutes regardless of how
much the remote service could have absorbed.

Getting concurrency means calling the callback *before* the work finishes and
tracking the outstanding work yourself, which immediately raises the question
the last two exercises are about: what happens to ordering, and what happens to
errors that arrive after you said you were ready?

## Problem 1 — a line splitter that keeps its remainder

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createLineSplitter()` is a byte-in, object-out
Transform emitting complete lines without their terminators, handling `\n` and
`\r\n`, holding a partial trailing line across chunks and emitting it from
`_flush`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex1
```

## Problem 2 — many in, one out

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createBatcher(size)` groups object-mode input into
arrays of exactly `size`, emitting a final short batch from `_flush` and
emitting nothing at all for an empty stream.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex2
```

## Problem 3 — objects in, bytes out

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createNdjsonSerialiser()` takes objects and emits
UTF-8 bytes, one JSON document per line. A value that cannot be serialised —
a circular reference, a `bigint` — fails that write through the callback rather
than throwing.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex3
```

## Problem 4 — zero out, sometimes

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createAsyncFilter(predicate)` keeps items for which an
**async** predicate resolves true, drops the rest, and destroys the stream with
the predicate's error when it rejects — without ever calling the callback
twice.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a meter that changes nothing

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createMeter()` returns a `PassThrough` plus a `stats()`
reporting chunk count, byte count and the largest chunk seen — an
instrumentation stage that is transparent to the data.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex5
```

## Problem 6 — state, bounded

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createDedupe(keyOf, maxKeys)` passes through the first
item for each key and drops repeats, remembering at most `maxKeys` keys and
evicting the least recently seen — because an unbounded `Set` in a long-running
transform is a memory leak with a business justification attached.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex6
```

## Problem 7 — the same thing, without a Transform

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `composeStages(stages)` builds a single Duplex from an
array of async generator functions using `stream.compose`, with the errors of
any stage propagating and the whole thing usable inside `pipeline`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex7
```

## Problem 8 — concurrency without reordering

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createConcurrentMap(fn, concurrency)` runs up to
`concurrency` async mappings at once and emits results in **input order**,
propagating the first error and not starting work after it.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex8
```

## Challenge — parse, enrich, batch

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createEnrichingBatcher(options)` is one Duplex:
NDJSON bytes in, arrays of enriched objects out, with bounded concurrency,
preserved order and correct failure semantics on malformed input.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode challenge
```

## Review

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. `createSplitter(separator)` splits a byte stream on
an **arbitrary multi-byte separator** that may itself straddle a chunk
boundary — ex1's problem with the easy assumption removed.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/v3na03_transform_objectmode

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The through-line is **the ratio**. A Transform is defined by how many outputs
each input produces, and every hard case in this sector is a ratio that is not
one. Many-to-one needs `_flush`, because the last group is incomplete when the
input ends. One-to-many needs explicit `push` calls, because
`callback(null, value)` can only emit one thing. Zero-to-one needs care with
the callback, because "drop this" and "fail this" are one keystroke apart.
And the async ratio — one input, one output, later — needs you to notice that
the callback is a semaphore of size one.

The second theme is **where the state lives**. A remainder, a batch in
progress, a set of seen keys, a window of pending results: all are closure
variables surviving between `transform` calls, and each needs a plan for the
end of the stream and a bound on its growth. A transform with unbounded state
is a leak that only appears in production, because tests end.

## ex1 — the last line has no newline

**What it tested:** the buffered-remainder pattern and `_flush`.

**The classic mistake:** `chunk.toString().split("\n").forEach(push)`. It emits
a spurious empty string for every chunk ending in a newline, splits any
multi-byte character that straddles the chunk boundary into two replacement
characters, and loses the final line entirely when the file does not end in a
newline. That last one is the bug that ships, because most test fixtures do end
in a newline.

**Model answer:** keep a string remainder, `split` the concatenation, `pop` the
last element back into the remainder, push the rest, and in `_flush` push the
remainder if it is non-empty. Decode with a `StringDecoder` so the multi-byte
boundary problem never arises.

## ex2 — the incomplete group is not an error

**What it tested:** the many-to-one ratio, where `_flush` is not an edge case
but half the algorithm.

**The classic mistake:** emitting the partial batch unconditionally in `_flush`,
so an empty stream yields one empty array. Downstream code that treats "a
batch" as "at least one record" then does a zero-row insert on every idle
minute. The `if (batch.length > 0)` is the whole difference.

**Model answer:** push when the batch reaches `size`, allocate a fresh array
rather than reusing one — handing out a live reference and then mutating it is
the aliasing bug from V3·A1 in object form — and guard the flush.

## ex3 — a failed serialisation is a failed write

**What it tested:** the object-in, byte-out direction, and the difference
between failing a chunk and crashing.

**The classic mistake:** letting `JSON.stringify` throw out of `transform`. A
circular reference in one record then takes down the process instead of
rejecting one row, and a batch job that could have skipped a bad line dies at
90% completion. The second mistake is `writableObjectMode: true` alone with no
thought for the readable side, which is correct here but only by accident —
knowing *why* the readable side stays in byte mode is the point.

**Model answer:** `try`/`catch` around the serialisation, `callback(err)` on
failure with the offending key named, and `\n` appended rather than prepended
so that concatenating two serialised streams is still valid NDJSON.

## ex4 — drop, keep, or fail

**What it tested:** the zero-or-one ratio combined with an async decision, and
the callback-exactly-once rule under a rejection.

**The classic mistake:** `if (await predicate(x)) this.push(x); callback();`
inside an `async transform`. It reads correctly and it is a trap: an async
function that throws does not throw *into* the machinery, it returns a rejected
promise the machinery is not awaiting, producing an unhandled rejection and a
stream that hangs. Node's stream implementation does support an async
`transform` — but only when you let its returned promise be the signal and do
not also call the callback.

**Model answer:** the callback style, `predicate(x).then(...)` with both
branches ending in exactly one `callback` call — `callback()` for keep or drop,
`callback(err)` for failure.

## ex5 — measure without perturbing

**What it tested:** `PassThrough` as what it actually is — a Transform whose
`transform` pushes its input unchanged — and the idea that instrumentation is a
stage.

**The classic mistake:** attaching a `data` listener to an existing stream to
count bytes. That switches the stream into flowing mode, which for a stream
that was about to be piped somewhere changes its behaviour and can lose data to
the eventual consumer. A `PassThrough` inserted into the pipeline observes
without changing the mode of anything.

**Model answer:** `new PassThrough()` with a `data` listener on the
PassThrough itself — safe, because that stream exists only to be piped through
— or a `transform` that records and forwards. Both are fine; the second is
honest about being a Transform.

## ex6 — a Set is a leak with good intentions

**What it tested:** bounded state. Deduplication is trivially correct and
trivially unbounded, and the exercise is entirely about the second half.

**The classic mistake:** `const seen = new Set()` and nothing else. On a
finite file it is perfect. In a long-running service processing a message
stream it grows until the process dies, and the failure looks like a slow leak
with no obvious owner. The subtler mistake in the bounded version is evicting
on insertion order rather than *recency*, which discards exactly the keys most
likely to recur.

**Model answer:** a `Map` used as an LRU — `delete` then `set` on every hit to
move the key to the end, and `delete` the first key from `map.keys()` when the
size exceeds the bound. `Map` preserves insertion order, which is what makes
this four lines instead of a data structure.

## ex7 — the generator is usually the better transform

**What it tested:** that `stream.compose` and async generators express most
transforms more clearly than the class, and that they compose into something
`pipeline` accepts.

**The classic mistake:** expecting a generator stage to receive one item per
call. It receives the *whole source* as an async iterable and yields any number
of outputs, which means the ratio problems from ex1 and ex2 disappear —
a many-to-one batcher is a `for await` with an array and a trailing `if`, and
`_flush` becomes "the code after the loop".

**Model answer:** `compose(...stages)` where each stage is
`async function* (source) { ... }`. Errors propagate because a throw inside a
generator rejects the iterator, and the composed Duplex destroys accordingly.

## ex8 — order is a promise you have to keep

**What it tested:** the hardest ratio — one-to-one, out of order, back into
order — and the bookkeeping that makes it safe.

**The classic mistake:** starting the work, calling the callback immediately,
and pushing results as they resolve. That gives you concurrency and loses
ordering, and the reordering is data-dependent, so it passes tests with uniform
latency and scrambles production. The second mistake is unbounded concurrency:
calling the callback immediately with no window means ten thousand records
become ten thousand concurrent requests.

**Model answer:** a queue of promises in input order, `callback()` deferred
while the queue is at `concurrency`, and a drain loop that pushes results from
the head of the queue only when the head has settled — so a slow item at
position three holds back four and five, which is exactly what "preserve order"
costs.

## challenge — three ratios in one stage

**What it tested:** composition of everything above, with the error semantics
that fall out of combining them.

**The classic mistake:** treating a malformed JSON line as fatal. A single bad
line in a ten-million-line feed should be reportable and skippable, and making
that a policy option rather than a hard-coded choice is the difference between
a component and a script. The other mistake is losing the final partial batch
when the enrichment queue is still draining — the flush must wait for the
in-flight work before it decides the batch is complete.

**Model answer:** three generator stages composed — split, enrich with a
bounded ordered window, batch — because the class-based version of the same
thing needs three `_flush` implementations and an explicit hand-off between
them.

## review1 — the separator can be split too

**What it tested:** ex1 with the convenient assumption removed. A single-byte
separator can never straddle a chunk boundary; a multi-byte one can, and the
naive remainder logic silently misses every occurrence that does.

**The classic mistake:** keeping only "everything after the last separator" as
the remainder. When the chunk ends with the first two bytes of a three-byte
separator, those two bytes are not after any separator, so they are kept — and
then the search on the next chunk starts from the beginning of the joined
buffer and finds it correctly. The version that fails is the one that searches
only the *new* chunk.

**Model answer:** keep the whole unmatched tail as a Buffer, `indexOf` the
separator in the joined buffer on every chunk, and never decode to a string —
because a string decode reintroduces the multi-byte boundary problem that
`Buffer.indexOf` does not have.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: implementing a Transform](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#implementing-a-transform-stream) — `_transform`, `_flush` and the callback contract behind every exercise here.
- [Node.js: `transform._flush()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#transform_flushcallback) — the end-of-input hook that ex1, ex2 and the challenge depend on.
- [Node.js: object mode](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#object-mode) — why the high-water mark is a count and what the two flags do separately.
- [Node.js: `stream.compose()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streamcomposestreams) — the generator-based composition ex7 uses.
- [Node.js: streams and async generators](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streams-compatibility-with-async-generators-and-async-iterators) — the source-as-async-iterable model that makes ratios disappear.

# V3·A3 — Transform streams and object mode (archive)

## What a Transform is

A `Transform` is a `Duplex` whose readable side is fed by its writable side. It
holds two buffers. Data written to it lands in the writable buffer; the
machinery hands chunks to your `_transform`; whatever you `push` lands in the
readable buffer; a consumer drains that. Backpressure works in both directions
automatically, because the readable side being full stops the machinery calling
`_transform`, which stops the writable side draining, which makes `write()`
return `false` upstream.

That automatic chain is the reason to use a Transform at all. It is also why
breaking the callback contract is so destructive: the callback is the only
signal the machinery has that you are ready for more.

```ts
new Transform({
  transform(chunk, encoding, callback) { /* exactly one callback call */ },
  flush(callback) { /* last chance to push */ },
});
```

## The four ratios

**One to one.** `callback(null, transformed)` and nothing else.

```ts
transform(chunk, _enc, cb) { cb(null, chunk.toString().toUpperCase()); }
```

**One to many.** Push repeatedly, then call back with nothing.

```ts
transform(chunk, _enc, cb) {
  for (const line of split(chunk)) this.push(line);
  cb();
}
```

**Many to one.** Accumulate, push when full, and handle the leftover in
`_flush`. The `_flush` half is not optional — without it, the last group is
silently discarded.

```ts
transform(item, _enc, cb) {
  batch.push(item);
  if (batch.length === size) { this.push(batch); batch = []; }
  cb();
}
flush(cb) { if (batch.length) this.push(batch); cb(); }
```

**One to zero-or-one.** A filter. The trap is that both branches must call the
callback, and neither may call it twice.

## Object mode, both flags

```ts
new Transform({
  writableObjectMode: true,    // I accept objects
  readableObjectMode: false,   // I emit bytes
  writableHighWaterMark: 16,   // 16 objects
  readableHighWaterMark: 65536 // 65536 bytes
});
```

`objectMode: true` is shorthand for setting both. Set them separately whenever
your stage is a parser or a serialiser, and set the high-water marks separately
whenever the two sides have different natural units — which is exactly when the
object-mode flags differ.

Three properties of object mode worth memorising:

- `highWaterMark` counts **items**, default 16. It is not a memory bound.
- `push(null)` still means end-of-stream, so `null` can never be a data value.
  `undefined` is fine, which surprises people.
- Strings and Buffers are passed through untouched; no encoding conversion
  happens, so a `Buffer` written to an object-mode stream arrives as that same
  `Buffer` object, not a copy.

## Async transforms

Node supports three styles and mixing them is the bug:

```ts
// 1. callback style
transform(x, _e, cb) { work(x).then((y) => cb(null, y), cb); }

// 2. async method — the returned promise IS the signal; do not call cb
async transform(x) { return await work(x); }        // one-to-one only

// 3. async generator, via compose or Readable.from
async function* stage(source) { for await (const x of source) yield await work(x); }
```

Style 1 is the most flexible and the only one that expresses every ratio.
Style 3 is the most readable and is what you should reach for by default. Style
2 is a trap in disguise: `async transform(x, enc, cb)` with an `await` and a
`cb()` call gives you a promise the machinery *also* watches, so an exception
after the callback becomes an unhandled rejection while the stream continues.

## Concurrency

The callback is a semaphore of size one. To exceed it you must call back early
and manage the outstanding work yourself:

```ts
transform(item, _enc, cb) {
  const promise = fn(item);            // start now
  pending.push(promise);
  promise.catch(() => {});             // no unhandled rejection while queued
  if (pending.length < concurrency) cb();     // room for more
  else pending[0].then(() => cb(), cb);       // wait for the oldest
  void drain();                        // push settled heads, in order
}
```

Three details that are easy to miss and expensive to debug. Attach a no-op
`catch` to every promise the moment you create it, or a rejection that is not
awaited for a few ticks becomes an unhandled rejection and kills the process.
Drain strictly from the head of the queue, or ordering is lost. And on the
error path, stop starting new work — otherwise a failing upstream produces a
thousand doomed requests before the stream notices.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting `_flush`, so the last partial line, batch or window vanishes.
- Emitting the partial group from `_flush` even when it is empty.
- Calling the callback twice (`ERR_MULTIPLE_CALLBACK`) or not at all.
- Pushing after the final callback (`ERR_STREAM_PUSH_AFTER_EOF`).
- Throwing from `_transform` instead of `callback(err)`.
- Mixing an `async transform` with a `callback` call.
- `objectMode: true` when only one side should be in object mode.
- Leaving an object-mode `highWaterMark` at 16 when items are large.
- Reusing the batch array instead of allocating a fresh one after each push.
- An unbounded `Set`/`Map` of seen keys in a long-running transform.
- Decoding a Buffer chunk to a string before splitting, which corrupts
  multi-byte characters that straddle chunk boundaries.
- Unbounded concurrency from calling the callback immediately with no window.

## The interview answer

*"When would you write a Transform rather than an async generator?"* — When you
need a stream object with an identity: something to insert into an existing
`pipeline`, to expose from a library, or to attach events and introspection to.
For code you control end to end, `compose` with async generators is shorter and
handles `_flush` implicitly as "the code after the loop". The generator also
cannot get the callback contract wrong, because there is no callback.

*"Why does my transform lose the last record?"* — Because the state is in a
closure and the input ended. `_flush` is the only hook that runs between the
last `_transform` and the readable side ending, and any many-to-one ratio needs
it.

*"How do you make a stream stage concurrent without losing order?"* — Keep a
queue of promises in input order, bound its length to the concurrency you want,
call the transform callback when there is room for another, and push results
only from the head of the queue. The cost is head-of-line blocking, which is
the price of ordering and should be a documented property of your stage.

## Check yourself

1. Name the two contracts `push()` and `callback()` speak to.
2. What error does calling the callback twice produce, and what happens if you
   never call it?
3. Which ratios cannot be expressed with `callback(null, value)`?
4. Why does a batching transform need `_flush`, and what must its guard be?
5. What is the default `highWaterMark` in object mode, and in what unit?
6. Give a stage where `writableObjectMode` and `readableObjectMode` differ.
7. Why is `null` unusable as a value in an object-mode stream, and is
   `undefined`?
8. What goes wrong when an `async transform` also calls the callback?
9. How many items are in flight in the naive async transform, and why?
10. What is the memory profile of `const seen = new Set()` in a long-running
    dedupe, and how do you bound it while keeping the right keys?
11. Why does a `Map` make an LRU four lines long?
12. Why is `chunk.toString()` before splitting a correctness bug and not just a
    performance one?
13. What does a `PassThrough` do that a `data` listener on the source does not?
14. In a concurrent ordered map, why must every pending promise get an
    immediate no-op `catch`?
15. What does "preserve order" cost you when item three is slow?
