# Transforms: the middle of the pipe, and the three ways to write one

## Where Transform came from

Streams1 had no transform. A "filter" was a function you called in a `data`
handler, and composing two of them meant two handlers and manual `pause`
calls. Streams2 in 0.10 introduced `Duplex` and then `Transform` on top of it,
and the design decision that still shapes the API is that a Transform is *not*
a mapping function — it is a Duplex whose two halves are wired together, with
the user's `_transform` sitting in the wire.

That choice bought a real property: backpressure composes for free. When you
`pipeline(a, b, c)`, `c` being slow makes `b`'s readable buffer fill, which
makes the machinery stop calling `b._transform`, which makes `b`'s writable
buffer fill, which makes `a`'s pushes return `false`. The chain is not
coordinated by anything; it is four independent buffers each doing the local
thing. Any hand-rolled "map over a stream" that does not reproduce this ends up
with an unbounded queue somewhere in the middle.

The cost is the callback contract. Because the machinery cannot see inside your
function, the only signal that a chunk has been consumed is your call, and the
only signal that output exists is your `push`. Every `ERR_MULTIPLE_CALLBACK`
and every mysteriously stalled pipeline is that ignorance surfacing.

`_flush` was added at the same time for the same structural reason: the
writable side ending and the readable side ending are different events, and
something has to run in between.

## What actually happens per chunk

Writing one chunk into a Transform costs, roughly:

1. `write()` → `writeOrBuffer` → a `WriteReq` object, appended to the writable
   buffer list.
2. The machinery calls `_transform(chunk, enc, cb)`.
3. Your `push(value)` → `readableAddChunk` → a node in the readable buffer
   list, plus possibly an `emitReadable` scheduled on the next tick.
4. Your `cb()` → `afterTransform` → `_write`'s callback → the next buffered
   write, or a `drain` emission if the writable buffer just dropped below its
   mark.

That is on the order of a hundred nanoseconds of bookkeeping plus one or two
microtask hops, per chunk, per stage. It is irrelevant for 64 KiB chunks and it
dominates for 20-byte ones. A four-stage pipeline processing a million small
records is doing four million rounds of that machinery — which is why a
`compose` of async generators is often measurably faster than the equivalent
chain of Transform objects: the generators hand items to each other directly
without allocating write requests or scheduling emissions.

Concrete orders of magnitude on a modern laptop: a trivial Transform passes
roughly 1-3 million small objects per second per stage; an async generator
stage doing the same mapping manages 5-10 million; a plain synchronous
`for` loop over an array does tens of millions. Streams are not the fast path
and were never meant to be — they are the *bounded-memory* path. Choose them
when the data does not fit, not when it does.

Measure with `readableLength` and `writableLength` sampled under load rather
than with timers. A stage whose `writableLength` sits at its high-water mark is
the bottleneck; a stage whose `readableLength` sits at its mark is being
throttled by whatever is downstream. That two-number diagnosis is faster than
any profiler for stream work.

## Object mode and the memory cliff

The 16-item default is the single most expensive default in the module. Four
object-mode stages with default marks and 5 MB items is 320 MB of buffer at
steady state, invisible in a heap snapshot as anything but "a lot of retained
objects", and reachable only through internal `BufferList` nodes.

The rule of thumb that survives contact with production: **if an item can
exceed about 100 KB, set `readableHighWaterMark` and `writableHighWaterMark`
explicitly, and set them to 1 or 2.** A mark of 1 does not serialise your
pipeline; it means one item buffered plus one in flight, which is enough to
keep every stage busy while bounding memory to a small multiple of one item.

The other object-mode subtlety is that `null` is reserved. `push(null)` ends
the stream, so a record whose value is legitimately null must be wrapped —
`{ value: null }` — or the stream truncates at the first one. This has bitten
every ORM streaming integration at least once.

## Three ways to write a stage, and when each wins

**The Transform class** wins when the stage is a *thing*: a library export, a
stage inserted into a pipeline built elsewhere, something that needs
introspection or events, or something whose state you want to expose. It is
also the only option when you need `_construct`, `_destroy` or `_writev` on the
same object.

**`compose` with async generators** wins for everything you own end to end. The
ratio problems dissolve: many-to-one is a loop with an array and a trailing
`if`; one-to-many is `yield` in a loop; `_flush` is the code after the loop;
error propagation is `throw`. The generated Duplex works everywhere a Transform
does. Since Node 16.9 (`stream.compose`, still marked experimental but widely
used) this is the default answer.

**A plain function over an async iterable** wins when the stage does not need
to be a stream at all. `for await (const x of source) yield f(x)` is a
generator, not a stream, and if both ends of your pipeline are already async
iterables you never need to construct a stream object. Node 22's iterator
helpers (`.map`, `.filter`, `.take` on `Readable`) cover a surprising amount of
this with no library at all.

## When not to use a Transform

When the data fits in memory. `const rows = await toArray(source); rows.map(f)`
is faster, clearer, easier to test and easier to debug, and "the data fits" is
true far more often than stream enthusiasm suggests. A 200 MB CSV on a service
with 4 GB of heap does not need a pipeline.

When the transformation needs global information — a sort, a join against
another full dataset, a median. Streams are one-pass and forward-only; anything
requiring the whole set either buffers it (at which point you have written a
worse array) or belongs in a database.

When you need per-item error handling with continuation. A stream stage that
fails destroys the stream, so "skip the bad rows and keep going" means catching
inside the stage and emitting an error *value* rather than throwing — a design
that is often clearer as an explicit `Result` type mapped over an iterable.

And when the concurrency you need is not order-preserving. If results may be
emitted in any order, a bounded worker pool over an async iterable is simpler
than ex8's queue, and it does not pay the head-of-line blocking cost.

The honest summary is that Transform is a coordination primitive, not a
computation one. Reach for it when the interesting property of your problem is
*bounded memory over an unbounded input*, and reach for an array, a generator,
or a database when it is anything else. The three exercises in this sector that
felt like plumbing — the remainder, the flush guard, the eviction — are all
consequences of that one property, and they are the price of not knowing how
much data is coming.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: implementing a Transform stream](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#implementing-a-transform-stream) — the callback contract, `_flush`, and the error rules.
- [Node.js: `stream.compose()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streamcomposestreams) — composing generators and streams into one Duplex.
- [Node.js: object mode](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#object-mode) — the item-counting high-water mark and the reserved `null`.
- [`lib/internal/streams/transform.js`](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/lib/internal/streams/transform.js) — under 200 lines; `afterTransform` is the whole wiring.
- [Node.js: Readable iterator helpers](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#readablemapfn-options) — `.map`, `.filter`, `.take` and friends, which replace many hand-written stages.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — a line splitter that keeps its remainder

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function createLineSplitter(): Transform;
```

A byte-in, object-out Transform emitting one string per line, without the line
terminator. It handles `\n` and `\r\n`, holds an incomplete trailing line
across chunk boundaries, and emits that remainder from `_flush` if it is
non-empty.

```ts
// written as: "alpha\nbe", "ta\r\ngamma"
// emitted as: "alpha", "beta", "gamma"

// written as: "one\ntwo\n"
// emitted as: "one", "two"        — no trailing empty string

// written as: nothing
// emitted as: nothing             — an empty stream produces no lines
```

Multi-byte UTF-8 characters split across chunk boundaries must not be
corrupted: the gate writes `"héllo\n"` as the two chunks `68 c3` and
`a9 6c 6c 6f 0a` and requires `"héllo"`.

A blank line in the middle of the input **is** a line and is emitted as `""`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state cross a chunk boundary here, not one. The obvious one is
the text after the last newline. The less obvious one is the two bytes of a
half-delivered `é`. Handle the second with the tool from V3·A1 ex3 and the
first with a string variable, and the transform body becomes four lines.

## Hint 2

The split-and-pop pattern, which is the whole algorithm:

```ts
const parts = (remainder + text).split("\n");
remainder = parts.pop()!;      // always the incomplete tail; may be ""
for (const line of parts) this.push(line);
```

`split` always returns at least one element, and the last element is by
definition whatever followed the final separator — which is exactly the
remainder. That is why `pop` is unconditional and why a chunk ending in `\n`
leaves an empty remainder rather than emitting an empty line.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `StringDecoder` and a `remainder` string in the closure, a `transform`
that decodes, splits, pops and pushes, and a `flush` that pushes the remainder
if it is non-empty. The decision left to you is where `\r` is stripped. Doing
it in the split (a regex on `\r?\n`) and doing it per line
(`line.endsWith("\r")`) are both defensible; only one of them behaves correctly
when a `\r\n` is itself split across two chunks, so work out which.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through the failing fixture. Write the naive version —
`chunk.toString().split("\n").forEach((l) => this.push(l))` — and run it on
`["one\ntwo\n"]`. You get `"one"`, `"two"`, `""`. Now run it on
`["al", "pha\n"]`. You get `"al"`, `"pha"`. Two different bugs from one missing
idea: the last element of a split is not a line, it is a *maybe-line*, and only
the end of the stream can tell you which.

## Hint 2

The `_flush` guard has a business consequence worth stating. If you push the
remainder unconditionally, a file ending in a newline produces a trailing empty
line, and downstream `JSON.parse("")` throws on every well-formed file you own.
If you never push it, a file *not* ending in a newline silently loses its last
record — and POSIX says text files end in a newline, so your fixtures will all
have one and production will not. The guard is `if (remainder.length > 0)`.

## Hint 3

Consider what happens without the decoder before you decide it is optional.
`Buffer.prototype.toString("utf8")` on a chunk ending mid-character emits
U+FFFD and drops the partial bytes; the next chunk starts with an orphaned
continuation byte and emits another. Both replacement characters land inside
your remainder string, so the corruption is invisible until somebody reads the
output. The gate's `héllo` split is there specifically to catch the version
that works on ASCII.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two lines of algorithm and one line of endgame. Accumulate; when the
accumulator reaches `size`, emit it and start a new one; and when the input
ends, emit whatever is left — *if* there is anything left. The third line is
the one that does not fit in `_transform`, which is what `_flush` is for.

## Hint 2

The reset is where the aliasing bug lives:

```ts
if (batch.length === size) {
  this.push(batch);
  batch = [];        // a NEW array, not batch.length = 0
}
```

`batch.length = 0` and `batch.splice(0)` empty the array you just handed
downstream. The consumer holds a reference to it, so their first batch becomes
empty and then refills with the second batch's contents — a bug that looks like
the stream is emitting the wrong data rather than the same data.

## Hint 3

Shape: validate `size`, close over `let batch: T[] = []`, an object-mode
`Transform` whose `transform` pushes-and-resets and whose `flush` guards on
`batch.length > 0`. The decision left to you is what `size` of `0` or `1.5`
should do. Throwing from the factory means the caller finds out at wiring time
with a clean stack; failing inside `transform` means they find out at 3 a.m.
with a stack that goes through the stream machinery.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from downstream. Whatever consumes your batches is going to do something
like `await db.insertMany(batch)`. Now ask what an unguarded `_flush` costs
that consumer: every empty input produces one empty array, so an idle minute
becomes a zero-row insert, a log line, and a metrics data point that says work
happened. Multiply by a stream that runs continuously and you have built a
system that is busiest when nothing is happening.

## Hint 2

Think about the `highWaterMark` before you leave the exercise. The writable
side accepts objects and the readable side emits arrays of `size` objects, so
with the default of 16 on both sides the stage can be holding 16 input items
plus 16 output batches — that is `16 + 16 * size` items resident. For `size` of
1000 and rows of 10 KB, one "batching" stage is holding 160 MB. Setting
`readableHighWaterMark: 1` costs nothing in throughput and removes the cliff.

## Hint 3

Consider the type signature honestly. The declaration says `<T>` but a
`Transform` is not generic — the stream machinery has no idea what flows
through it, and `T` exists purely to document intent at the call site. That is
worth noticing rather than glossing: everything you know about the contents of
an object-mode stream is a convention held by the code on both ends, and the
type parameter is a comment the compiler happens to check at exactly one place.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — objects in, bytes out

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function createNdjsonSerialiser(): Transform;
```

Objects in, UTF-8 bytes out: one JSON document per line, each terminated by
`\n` (not separated by it — concatenating two serialised streams must still be
valid NDJSON).

```ts
// in:  { id: 1 }, { id: 2, name: "héllo" }
// out: '{"id":1}\n{"id":2,"name":"héllo"}\n'   as UTF-8 bytes
```

A value that `JSON.stringify` cannot handle fails **that write** through
`callback(err)` rather than throwing:

- a circular reference → an `Error` mentioning `circular` or the stringify
  failure;
- a `bigint` → an `Error`, because `JSON.stringify(1n)` throws `TypeError`;
- a value that stringifies to `undefined` (a bare `undefined`, a function) →
  an `Error` mentioning `not serialisable`.

The gate pipes a stream containing one bad record between two good ones and
requires the pipeline to reject with that error, with the first record's bytes
already delivered.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Set the two object-mode flags separately, and be able to say why: the writable
side takes objects, the readable side emits bytes, and `objectMode: true` would
put the readable side in object mode too — which happens to work, because a
string pushed into an object-mode stream is passed through untouched, and then
breaks the moment somebody pipes you into a file.

## Hint 2

The failure surface of `JSON.stringify` is wider than it looks:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ a: 1n });        // throws TypeError
JSON.stringify(undefined);        // returns undefined — no throw
JSON.stringify(() => {});         // returns undefined — no throw
const o: any = {}; o.self = o;
JSON.stringify(o);                // throws TypeError: Converting circular...
```

Two of those throw and two return `undefined`. A `try`/`catch` alone catches
half the problem; the other half needs a check on the returned value.

## Hint 3

Shape: `writableObjectMode: true`, a `transform` wrapping the stringify in
`try`/`catch`, an explicit `undefined` check, and
`callback(null, Buffer.from(json + "\n", "utf8"))` on success. The decision
left to you is whether to push a `Buffer` or a string. Pushing a string into a
byte-mode stream is legal — it is encoded with the stream's default encoding —
so the difference is whether you want the encoding decision to be explicit at
the point where you know it is UTF-8, or implicit at a point where you do not.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the operational question: what should a ten-million-line export
do when line 4,000,000 has a circular reference? Crashing the process loses the
first four million lines of work. Silently skipping the record produces a file
that is missing a row nobody will notice for a year. Failing the *write* — this
exercise's contract — destroys the stream with a specific error, which lets the
caller decide, and lets a wrapper implement "skip and count" if that is the
policy. Design for the decision to be made one layer up.

## Hint 2

The terminator-versus-separator distinction is not pedantry. With `\n` as a
separator you write `a\nb\nc`, and appending a second file's `x\ny` gives you
`a\nb\ncx\ny` — the last record of the first file and the first of the second
have fused into one malformed line. With `\n` as a terminator every record ends
the same way, files concatenate, `tail -f` works, and a reader that splits on
`\n` and skips empty trailing fragments is correct. This is why NDJSON, JSON
Lines and syslog all terminate.

## Hint 3

Think about what `callback(err)` actually does before you rely on it. It
destroys the transform with that error, which propagates to the `pipeline` that
fed it and to the destination. The chunks already pushed are already gone
downstream — the gate checks exactly that — so "fail the write" is not
"transactional". If your consumer needs all-or-nothing, that has to happen at a
layer that can undo, and no stream can offer it.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The whole exercise is one sentence: three outcomes, one callback. Keep the
item, drop the item, or fail — and each path must end in exactly one call.
Write the three calls first, as three literal lines, and then work out what
goes above them. `callback()`, `callback()`, `callback(err)`.

## Hint 2

The `.then` form makes the exactly-once property visible:

```ts
predicate(item).then(
  (keep) => {
    if (keep) this.push(item);
    callback();
  },
  (err) => callback(err as Error),
);
```

One handler per outcome, one `callback` in each. Compare that with a
`try`/`catch` wrapping an `await` and a single trailing `callback()` — which is
also correct, but only if the `catch` returns, and only if nothing after the
`await` can throw.

## Hint 3

Shape: `objectMode: true` and a `transform` that calls the predicate and
dispatches. Ten lines. The decision left to you is `async transform(item, enc,
callback)` versus the `.then` form. Node treats an `async` transform's returned
promise as a completion signal *as well as* your callback, so the async version
only works if you never call the callback — and the moment you need the
drop-versus-keep distinction, you will want to. Pick one style and do not mix
them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the concurrency claim in the prompt: "the predicate is never
called concurrently". You are not asked to implement that — you get it for
free, and understanding why is the point. The machinery does not call
`_transform` again until your callback fires, so the callback *is* a semaphore
of size one. Every serial-async-transform performance complaint on the internet
is that sentence, discovered the hard way. ex8 is the exercise that removes the
limit; here, notice that you have it.

## Hint 2

The failure to guard against is subtle enough to name. Consider:

```ts
async transform(item, _enc, callback) {
  if (await predicate(item)) this.push(item);
  callback();
}
```

When `predicate` rejects, the `async` function returns a rejected promise. The
callback is never called, so the stream stalls; and depending on how the
machinery is treating that promise you also get an unhandled rejection. The
stream does not error — it simply stops, with no message, which is the worst
diagnostic in the module.

## Hint 3

Think about what "the original error object, not a wrapper" is protecting. The
caller almost certainly branches on it: `err.code === "ENOENT"`,
`err instanceof ValidationError`, `err.name === "AbortError"`. Wrapping it in
`new Error("filter failed: " + err.message)` destroys every one of those
branches and keeps only the text. If you want to add context, ES2022 gives you
`new Error("...", { cause: err })` — but then the caller has to unwrap, so for
a pass-through stage the right answer is to pass it through.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The identity transform already exists in the module, and it exists precisely so
you can insert a stage that does nothing. Find it, then decide whether you are
going to observe it from the outside or subclass the behaviour. Both are
defensible; one is two lines shorter and the other is more honest about being a
Transform.

## Hint 2

Observing from the outside looks like this:

```ts
const stream = new PassThrough();
stream.on("data", (chunk: Buffer) => { bytes += chunk.length; });
```

That is safe here — and only here — because the `PassThrough` is a stream you
created for the purpose. Attaching the same listener to somebody else's source
would switch it into flowing mode and change their program. Know which of those
two situations you are in every time you write `.on("data", ...)`.

## Hint 3

Shape: three counters in the closure, the stage, and a `stats()` returning a
fresh object literal. The decision left to you is whether `stats()` returns a
snapshot or a live view. Returning the same mutable object every time is
cheaper and turns every consumer into a subscriber of a value that changes
under them — which is either exactly what you want for a progress bar or a
race condition, depending on who is reading.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through what "transparent" has to mean, because it is stricter than
"the bytes are the same". A stage that concatenates its input and pushes it in
64 KiB pieces delivers identical bytes and is not transparent: it changes chunk
boundaries, which changes latency for a downstream consumer that acts per
chunk, and it changes the memory profile. The gate compares boundaries for this
reason. Whatever you write, one chunk in must be one chunk out, immediately.

## Hint 2

Think about where a meter belongs in a pipeline and what it can therefore tell
you. Placed after the source it measures what the source produced; placed
before the sink it measures what survived the transforms; placed on both sides
of one stage it measures that stage's compression ratio. That is the actual
use — `pipeline(src, meterIn.stream, gzip, meterOut.stream, dst)` gives you a
ratio for free, and it is a good habit for any transform whose output size is
not predictable.

## Hint 3

Consider byte mode versus object mode. This meter counts `chunk.length`, which
is bytes for a `Buffer` and characters for a string — two different things the
moment anything non-ASCII arrives, and meaningless for an object-mode stream
carrying rows. A production meter either forces byte mode, or measures
`Buffer.byteLength(chunk)` when handed a string, or counts items and says so.
Decide which one you are building and let the field name say it.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — state, bounded

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function createDedupe<T>(
  keyOf: (item: T) => string,
  maxKeys: number,
): Transform;
```

An object-mode Transform that passes through the first item for each key and
drops repeats — while remembering at most `maxKeys` keys, evicting the **least
recently seen** when it must.

```ts
const dedupe = createDedupe<{ id: string }>((x) => x.id, 3);
// in:  a, b, a, c, d, b
// out: a, b, c, d, b
//                  ^ "b" reappears because remembering d evicted the
//                    least recently seen key, which was b.
```

Trace for `maxKeys` of 3: after `a, b` the map is `[a, b]`; the second `a`
is a hit and moves `a` to the most-recent end, giving `[b, a]`; `c` gives
`[b, a, c]`; `d` overflows and evicts `b`, giving `[a, c, d]`; so the final `b`
is unseen and passes through.

`maxKeys` must be a positive integer. The gate feeds 100,000 items with 50,000
distinct keys through a dedupe with `maxKeys` of 1000 and asserts the internal
map never exceeds 1000 entries.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Deduplication is one line and is not the exercise. The exercise is the second
sentence: *at most `maxKeys`*. Write the unbounded version, then ask what a
long-running service does with it — a message stream with unique ids grows a
`Set` forever, and the leak has a plausible business justification attached to
it, which is why it survives code review.

## Hint 2

The data structure you want is already in the language:

```ts
const lru = new Map<string, true>();
// on a hit, move to the most-recent end:
lru.delete(key);
lru.set(key, true);
// on overflow, drop the least recent:
if (lru.size > maxKeys) lru.delete(lru.keys().next().value as string);
```

`Map` iterates in insertion order and `set` on an existing key does **not**
change that order — which is why the `delete` before the `set` is load-bearing
rather than decorative.

## Hint 3

Shape: validate `maxKeys`, close over the `Map`, and a `transform` that
computes the key, checks membership, touches or inserts, evicts if oversized,
and pushes only on a miss. The decision left to you is whether a *hit* should
also refresh recency. The prompt says yes — that is what makes it an LRU rather
than a FIFO — but notice what it costs: a hot duplicate key stays resident
forever, which is the intended behaviour for a dedupe and the wrong behaviour
for a rate limiter.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the honest admission this exercise contains: a bounded dedupe is
**wrong**, on purpose. Evict a key and a later duplicate passes through, so the
output is not deduplicated — it is deduplicated within a window. That is a
trade you are making deliberately, and the reason it is acceptable is that
duplicates in real streams cluster in time: a retry arrives seconds after the
original, not months. Any component that bounds its memory is making a claim
about the shape of its input, and being able to state that claim is the
difference between engineering and hoping.

## Hint 2

Think about `keyOf` throwing. It is caller-supplied and it runs on every item,
so a record missing the field it reads takes down the stream from inside your
`transform`. That is a throw out of `_transform`, which is the thing V3·A3
keeps telling you not to do — except here it is not your code that throws. A
`try`/`catch` around the key computation with `callback(err)` turns somebody
else's bug into your stream's error, which is the correct place for it to
surface.

## Hint 3

Consider the alternative implementations before settling. A `Set` plus a
separate array of insertion order is the version people write first: two
structures to keep in sync, O(n) removal from the array, and a bug the first
time a key is touched twice. A `Map` to timestamps and a periodic sweep is what
people write second: O(n) sweeps and a memory ceiling that is only enforced
sometimes. The insertion-ordered `Map` is four lines and exactly bounded. Know
why the other two are worse so you can defend the choice.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A generator stage does not receive one item per call. It receives the entire
upstream as an async iterable, once, and yields as many outputs as it likes.
That single difference dissolves every ratio problem in this sector: one-to-many
is two `yield`s in a loop, many-to-one is an accumulator, and the end-of-input
hook is the statement after the `for await`.

## Hint 2

`compose` accepts a mixture of streams, generator functions and iterables:

```ts
import { compose } from "node:stream";

const duplex = compose(
  async function* (src) { for await (const x of src) yield x + 1; },
  new Transform({ objectMode: true, transform(x, _e, cb) { cb(null, x * 2); } }),
);
```

The result is a Duplex: writable at the front, readable at the back. Note that
`compose()` with no arguments throws, which is why the empty-array case in the
prompt needs a decision rather than a spread.

## Hint 3

Shape: guard the empty case by returning a `PassThrough({ objectMode: true })`,
otherwise `compose(...stages)`. Four lines. The decision left to you is the
type. `compose` returns a `Duplex` and TypeScript cannot connect the stages'
input and output types to each other — the `Stage<any, any>[]` in the signature
is an admission of that. A properly typed variadic `compose` is possible with
overloads or a recursive conditional type; write down whether you think the
complexity would earn its place.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it by rewriting ex1 as a generator before you touch this exercise:

```ts
async function* lines(source: AsyncIterable<Buffer>) {
  let rest = "";
  for await (const chunk of source) {
    const parts = (rest + chunk.toString("utf8")).split("\n");
    rest = parts.pop()!;
    yield* parts;
  }
  if (rest) yield rest;
}
```

Eight lines, no callback contract, no `_flush`, no way to push after EOF, and
the error handling is `throw`. Sit with the fact that this is the same program
as your ex1 answer, and then decide when the class is still worth it.

## Hint 2

Think about backpressure, because the reasonable worry is that generators lose
it. They do not: `for await` pulls one item at a time and does not run ahead of
its consumer, so a slow sink suspends the generator at its `yield` exactly as a
full readable buffer stops the machinery calling `_transform`. What you *do*
lose is the buffer — a generator holds one item, not sixteen — which usually
improves the memory profile and occasionally costs throughput on a stage with
bursty latency.

## Hint 3

Consider what you give up. A composed Duplex has no `_construct` and no
`_destroy` of its own, so lazily acquiring a resource per stage and releasing it
on early termination has to be `try`/`finally` inside the generator — which
works, and only works if the consumer's early exit propagates as an iterator
`return()`. It does, for `pipeline` and `for await` with `break`. It does not
if somebody stores the iterator and abandons it, which is the one failure mode
the class-based version handles better.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate jobs and they need two separate mechanisms. Limiting concurrency
is about *when you call the transform callback* — call it immediately and more
work starts, defer it and the machinery waits. Preserving order is about *when
you push* — you must push from the front of a queue, not as results arrive.
Solve them one at a time; conflating them is why this exercise is the hardest
in the sector.

## Hint 2

The queue is of promises, in input order:

```ts
const pending: Promise<O>[] = [];

transform(item, _enc, callback) {
  const p = fn(item);
  p.catch(() => {});          // no unhandled rejection while it waits in line
  pending.push(p);
  void drain();
  if (pending.length < concurrency) callback();
  else pending[0].then(() => callback(), callback);
}
```

The last line is the throttle: when the window is full, do not accept another
item until the **oldest** one has settled. `drain` then pushes from the head
while the head is settled — which needs a way to ask "has this promise
settled?", and promises do not answer that question, so you must record it.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `pending` array of `{ promise, done, value, error }` records, a
`drain()` that shifts and pushes while `pending[0].done`, a `transform` that
enqueues and throttles, and a `flush` that awaits everything remaining and
drains again. The decision left to you is how the error path stops further
work: a `failed` flag checked at the top of `transform` is the simple answer,
and you should convince yourself it is checked *after* the awaits as well, or a
rejection racing with an in-flight callback starts one more call than it should.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through what you are trading away. Preserving order means that when
item three is slow, items four and five are finished and *waiting* — held in
memory, not delivered. That is head-of-line blocking, the same phenomenon that
motivated HTTP/2's multiplexing and then HTTP/3's move off TCP. Your queue's
maximum length is your concurrency, so the memory cost is bounded and
predictable, but the latency cost is not: one pathological item stalls
everything behind it. Document that, because a caller who cannot tolerate it
wants an unordered variant instead.

## Hint 2

The `p.catch(() => {})` line is not defensive noise and skipping it will kill
your process. A promise that rejects while nothing is attached to it triggers
`unhandledRejection` on the next turn of the loop — and under Node's default
that is a fatal error. Your queued promises may sit for many turns before
`drain` reaches them. Attaching a no-op handler the moment you create the
promise marks it as handled; the real handling still happens later in `drain`,
because a promise can have any number of handlers.

## Hint 3

Think about `_flush` before you write `_transform`, because it constrains the
design. When the input ends there may be `concurrency - 1` mappings still
running, and every one of their results must be emitted before the readable
side ends. So `flush` is "await everything in the queue, drain, then call
back", and that means `drain` has to be callable when no new item is arriving —
which rules out any design where pushing is a side effect of `transform`.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the bad-line policy, because it is the design decision the rest
hangs off. Three plausible behaviours: fail the stream, skip silently, or
report and skip. Hard-coding any one of them makes the component unusable for
somebody — a payments feed must fail, an analytics feed must not — and the
`onBadLine?` in the signature is the shape that lets both callers exist. Notice
also what it does *not* offer: there is no way to say "stop after 100 bad
lines", and adding one would mean the callback returning a decision. Think
about which API you would rather maintain.

## Hint 2

The line number is harder than it looks and the gate checks it. Counting inside
the loop over `parts` is right; counting chunks is wrong; and the trailing
remainder in the flush is one more line, not zero. Get it wrong by one and
every error report in production points at the wrong record, which is worse
than no line number at all because people trust it.

## Hint 3

Think hard about the interaction between concurrency and batching at the end of
the input. The batcher's flush runs when the enrich stage's iterable finishes —
and with generators that is automatic, because `for await` in the batcher does
not complete until `enrich` returns, which does not happen until its own queue
has drained. That is the strongest argument for the generator decomposition:
the three end-of-input behaviours sequence themselves. Write the same thing as
three chained `Transform`s and you have to reason about three `_flush`
callbacks firing in the right order.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review — the separator can be split too

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function createSplitter(separator: Buffer | string): Transform;
```

A byte-in, object-out Transform (each output is a `Buffer`) splitting on an
**arbitrary** separator, which
may be several bytes long and may itself straddle a chunk boundary. Each
emitted item is the content between separators, without the separator. The
readable side is in object mode for one reason: byte mode cannot represent an
empty chunk, and an empty field must survive.

```ts
// separator "--", written as: "a--b", "c--d"
// emitted:                    "a", "bc", "d"

// separator "END", written as: "oneE", "NDtwo"
// emitted:                     "one", "two"      — the separator was split

// separator "|", written as: "a||b"
// emitted:                   "a", "", "b"        — an empty field is a field
```

The trailing segment is emitted from `_flush`, including an empty one when the
input ends with a separator — `"a|"` emits `"a"` and then `""`. An empty input
emits nothing. An empty separator throws from `createSplitter`.

Work in `Buffer`s throughout: decoding to a string reintroduces the multi-byte
boundary problem that `Buffer.indexOf` does not have.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na03_transform_objectmode review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Ex1 got away with something. A single-byte separator cannot be split across a
chunk boundary, so "everything after the last newline" was a safe remainder.
With a multi-byte separator, a chunk can end with the first two bytes of a
three-byte marker, and those bytes are not after any separator — so the
remainder has to be *the whole unmatched tail*, and the search has to run over
the joined buffer, not over the new chunk.

## Hint 2

`Buffer.indexOf` takes a Buffer needle and a start offset:

```ts
let from = 0;
for (;;) {
  const at = buffered.indexOf(sep, from);
  if (at === -1) break;
  this.push(buffered.subarray(from, at));
  from = at + sep.length;
}
buffered = buffered.subarray(from);
```

One loop, one reslice at the end. The subtle part is not in these lines — it is
in what `buffered` was before them, and whether a separator spanning the seam
can be found at all.

## Hint 3

Shape: validate the separator, close over `let buffered = Buffer.alloc(0)`, a
`transform` that concatenates and then runs the scan loop, and a `flush` that
pushes what remains — unconditionally, because a trailing empty field is a
field. The decision left to you is whether to keep the entire unmatched tail or
only its last `sep.length - 1` bytes plus a running offset. The second is what a
memory-conscious implementation does, and getting its offset arithmetic right
is the actual exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through the failing case, which is easy to construct and easy to
miss. Separator `"END"`; write `"oneE"` then `"NDtwo"`. Run your ex1-shaped
answer: it searches the new chunk `"NDtwo"` for `"END"`, finds nothing, and
emits `"oneE"` and `"NDtwo"` as two fields. Nothing errors. The output is
plausible. This is the corruption that only appears at particular chunk sizes,
which is to say: never on your machine and always in production behind a proxy
that fragments differently.

## Hint 2

The empty-field question is a real semantic decision, not an edge case to make
go away. `"a||b"` split on `"|"` is three fields, the middle one empty — CSV,
`split()` in every language, and `IFS` in the shell all agree. But `"a|"` is
two fields, the second empty, and *that* is where implementations diverge:
`"a|".split("|")` in JavaScript gives `["a", ""]`, while `awk` and many parsers
give `["a"]`. The prompt picks the JavaScript semantics; know that you picked
them, because the consumer counting rows will care.

## Hint 3

Consider the memory shape of the naive answer under adversarial input. If the
separator never appears, `buffered` grows to the entire stream — you have
written a `concat` with extra steps, and a 4 GB file is a process death. The
fix is the same one as V3·A1 ex5: a maximum segment length, past which you
destroy the stream. Nothing in the prompt asks for it, which is exactly how
real code ends up without it.

lessons.title: V3·A4 — Backpressure and pipeline()
lessons.summary: Backpressure as a contract rather than a feeling: the write/drain protocol by hand, why pipe leaks and pipeline does not, aborts that tear a whole chain down, high-water marks including zero, a token bucket that throttles instead of dropping, a bounded push-to-pull bridge, and pipeline reimplemented.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A4 — Backpressure and pipeline()

`d17_backpressure` established the rule: `write()` returning `false` means stop
and wait for `drain`. This sector is about what that rule costs, what enforces
it, and what happens in the four places it silently does not apply.

Start with the thing worth being precise about, because "backpressure" is used
loosely enough to be useless. Backpressure is **not** the system getting
slower. A system with working backpressure and a slow consumer runs at the
consumer's speed with bounded memory. A system without it runs at the
*producer's* speed, in memory, until the process is killed. The difference is
not performance; it is whether the failure mode is latency or death.

## Concept — the write/drain contract, written out

```ts
for (const chunk of chunks) {
  if (!writable.write(chunk)) {
    await once(writable, "drain");
  }
}
writable.end();
```

Four facts hide in those five lines.

**`write()` always accepts the chunk.** The `false` return is advice, not
refusal. Ignoring it is legal and the data is not lost — it is buffered, in the
stream's internal list, with no upper bound. That is why the failure is a
memory graph and not an exception.

**`false` means "the buffer is now at or above `highWaterMark`."** Not "full",
because there is no full. The mark is a threshold at which the stream asks you
to stop, and it defaults to 64 KiB in byte mode and 16 items in object mode.

**`drain` fires when the buffer falls back below the mark**, not when it is
empty. So the loop above keeps the buffer oscillating around the mark, which is
the point: you want the consumer never starved and the buffer never unbounded.

**`await once(writable, "drain")` hangs forever if the stream errors** while
you are waiting. That is the bug that makes hand-rolled pumps unsafe, and the
reason `pipeline` exists.

## Concept — pipe leaks, pipeline does not

```ts
source.pipe(gzip).pipe(dest);           // do not
await pipeline(source, gzip, dest);     // do
```

`pipe()` wires data and backpressure and *nothing else*. When `dest` emits an
error, `pipe` unpipes — and leaves `source` and `gzip` open, flowing, holding
file descriptors and sockets, forever. The `error` events on the other streams
have no listeners, so they either do nothing or crash the process. This is the
single most common resource leak in Node services, and it is why every style
guide from about 2018 onward says the same thing.

`pipeline` (use the promise form from `node:stream/promises`) adds the three
things `pipe` lacks: an error listener on every stage, destruction of every
stage when any one fails, and a single completion signal. It also ends the
destination for you, which is why there is no `{ end: false }` option — if you
need the destination to stay open, you are not doing a pipeline, and the last
exercise in this sector is exactly that case.

Stages can be streams, async generator functions, or — since Node 16 — a plain
async function at the end acting as the sink:

```ts
const total = await pipeline(
  source,
  async function* (src) { for await (const c of src) yield transform(c); },
  async function (src) { let n = 0; for await (const c of src) n += c.length; return n; },
);
```

## Concept — cancellation is part of the contract

```ts
await pipeline(source, gzip, dest, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5_000) });
```

Every stage is destroyed on abort and the promise rejects with an `AbortError`.
Compare that with the naive alternative — a `setTimeout` that calls
`source.destroy()` — which stops the source and leaves the transform and
destination to finish whatever they had buffered, then hang waiting for input
that will not arrive.

## Problem 1 — the contract by hand

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `writeAll(writable, chunks)` writes every chunk,
waiting for `drain` whenever `write` returns `false`, ends the stream, and
resolves with the number of times it had to wait — while rejecting rather than
hanging if the stream fails mid-write.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex1
```

## Problem 2 — what pipe leaves behind

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `transfer(source, destination)` moves all data and
guarantees that a failure anywhere destroys **both** streams — the property
`pipe` does not have and the gate checks by failing the destination and
asserting `source.destroyed`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a chain that can be cancelled

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `runWithTimeout(streams, ms)` runs a pipeline that
tears the whole chain down when the time limit passes, rejecting with an
`AbortError` and leaving every stage destroyed.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex3
```

## Problem 4 — throttling, not dropping

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createTokenBucket({ capacity, perTick, tick })` is a
Transform that applies real backpressure — it delays its callback until tokens
are available — driven by an injected clock so the gate can grade it without a
timer.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex4
```

## Problem 5 — proving the throttle

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `observePressure(source, sink)` runs a transfer while
sampling `writableLength` and counting `drain` events, returning evidence that
a slow consumer bounded a fast producer.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a bridge that pushes back

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createBoundedBridge(limit)` turns a push API into a
pull stream where `push()` returns a promise that does not resolve until there
is room — the shape that makes an upstream callback API respect a downstream
consumer.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex6
```

## Problem 7 — the high-water mark, exactly

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createLazySource(items, highWaterMark)` builds a
Readable from an async generator that must not produce ahead of demand, and
`countProduced` proves it — including the `highWaterMark: 0` case, which does
not mean what most people assume.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex7
```

## Problem 8 — write pipeline yourself

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `myPipeline(...streams)` reimplements the promise form:
wire the chain, propagate errors in both directions, destroy every stage on any
failure, and resolve only when the last stage has genuinely finished.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex8
```

## Challenge — an ingest with a bounded queue

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `runIngest(subscribe, sink, options)` connects a
push-based source to a Writable through a bounded queue, with abort support and
a report of how often it had to apply backpressure upstream.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline challenge
```

## Review

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. `pump(source, destination, { end })` is the manual
transfer `pipeline` refuses to do: backpressure honoured, errors propagated,
and the destination deliberately left open when asked.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/v3na04_backpressure_pipeline

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The through-line is that **backpressure is a contract with three parties and
everybody has to keep it**. The producer must stop when told. The consumer must
say `drain` when it can take more. And the code in the middle must not silently
absorb the difference. Every failure in this sector is one party defecting:
the pump that ignores `false`, the bridge that queues without a bound, the
transform that drops instead of delaying, the `pipe` that stops relaying
failures.

The second theme is **teardown**. A pipeline is not finished when the data ends;
it is finished when every stage has released what it held. `pipe` gets the data
right and the teardown wrong, which is why it is the wrong default despite
working perfectly in every example.

## ex1 — the wait must be interruptible

**What it tested:** the write/drain loop, written out, including the failure
path most implementations forget.

**The classic mistake:** `await once(writable, "drain")` with no error
handling. When the sink fails while you are waiting — a disk filling, a socket
resetting — `drain` never fires, and the promise never settles. The process
does not crash and does not exit; it simply stops, which is the hardest failure
to diagnose because there is nothing in the logs. `events.once` accepts a
stream and rejects on `error` for exactly this reason.

**Model answer:** loop, `write`, and on `false` await a race between `drain`
and `error` — `once(writable, "drain")` already is that race — counting the
waits, then `end()` and await `finished`.

## ex2 — the leak is the lesson

**What it tested:** that `pipeline` is not sugar for `pipe`. It is the error
plumbing.

**The classic mistake:** `source.pipe(dest)` plus `dest.on("error", ...)`,
which handles the error and still leaks. The listener stops the crash; it does
nothing about `source`, which is still open, still flowing, and still holding
whatever it holds. In a request handler that is one leaked file descriptor per
failed upload, and the process dies of `EMFILE` an hour later with a stack
trace pointing somewhere irrelevant.

**Model answer:** `await pipeline(source, destination)` from
`node:stream/promises` — one line, and the reason to know the long version is
so that you can explain to a reviewer why the one line is not optional.

## ex3 — cancelling one stage cancels nothing

**What it tested:** `AbortSignal` at the pipeline level rather than the stream
level.

**The classic mistake:** a `setTimeout` that destroys the source. The source
stops, and the transform sits holding a partial buffer waiting for input, and
the destination waits for the transform, and the promise from `pipeline` never
settles — a timeout that produces a hang is worse than no timeout. Destroying
the *destination* is equally partial in the other direction.

**Model answer:** `pipeline(streams, { signal })` with
`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`, because the abort handling lives where the knowledge
of all the stages lives. Note that the rejection is an `AbortError`, so callers
distinguish "we gave up" from "it broke".

## ex4 — a limiter that drops is not a limiter

**What it tested:** that rate limiting inside a stream means *delaying the
callback*, which propagates backpressure upstream automatically.

**The classic mistake:** dropping chunks when over budget. That is a sampler,
not a throttle, and it silently loses data — the worst outcome a middle stage
can produce. The second mistake is `setTimeout` with a real clock, which makes
the component untestable; injecting the tick source is what turns a flaky test
into a deterministic one.

**Model answer:** decrement tokens, and when there are not enough, hold the
callback until the injected clock refills. Holding the callback is the entire
mechanism: the machinery will not deliver another chunk, so the writable buffer
fills, so `write()` upstream returns `false`.

## ex5 — measure the counters, never the clock

**What it tested:** how you *prove* backpressure exists, which is a different
skill from implementing it.

**The classic mistake:** timing the transfer and asserting it took longer than
some threshold. That test is flaky on a loaded CI box and proves nothing about
memory anyway. The observable facts are `writableLength` staying near the
high-water mark and the `drain` count being greater than zero; both are exact
integers.

**Model answer:** sample `writableLength` after each write, count `drain`
events, and assert the maximum sample never exceeded the mark by more than one
chunk — a statement about memory, which is what backpressure is actually for.

## ex6 — the bound is the point

**What it tested:** the push-to-pull adapter, with the queue bounded by making
the producer wait rather than by discarding.

**The classic mistake:** an unbounded array with a synchronous `push` that
always returns. Every push succeeds, the producer never slows down, and the
array is now the unbounded buffer you removed from the stream. Returning a
promise is what gives the producer something to await — and a producer that
ignores the returned promise is a producer you cannot help, which is worth
stating in the component's documentation.

**Model answer:** a queue with a limit, a list of waiting resolvers, and a
`push` that resolves immediately when there is room and otherwise parks; the
consumer's `_read` shifts an item and releases exactly one waiter.

## ex7 — highWaterMark 0 is not "no buffering"

**What it tested:** the exact semantics of the mark, and the difference between
"lazy" and "unbuffered".

**The classic mistake:** assuming `highWaterMark: 0` means the source produces
strictly on demand. It does not: a mark of 0 makes `push()` always return
`false`, but the machinery still calls `_read` once to prime the stream, so the
first item is produced before anyone asks. A mark of 1 is what "one item of
lookahead" actually means. For an object-mode stage where an item is a database
round trip, the difference is one wasted query per stream — small, and
multiplied by every stream you create.

**Model answer:** `Readable.from(generator, { objectMode: true, highWaterMark: 1 })`
and a production counter incremented inside the generator, which is the only
place that can honestly report what was produced.

## ex8 — pipeline is twelve subtle lines

**What it tested:** everything above, assembled. Writing it once is how the
argument for using the built-in becomes concrete.

**The classic mistake:** treating the chain as a sequence of `pipe` calls with
a single `error` handler on the last stage. Errors travel forward through
`pipe` only as an absence of data; a failure in stage two must destroy stage
one (which is upstream, the direction `pipe` never looks) as well as stage
three. The other mistake is resolving on the destination's `finish` rather than
waiting for `close`, which returns before the sink has released its resources.

**Model answer:** attach `finished()` to every stage, destroy all of them on
the first error, and resolve when the last one is done — with the first error
winning, because subsequent ones are consequences.

## challenge — the whole contract, end to end

**What it tested:** a push producer, a bounded queue, a stream consumer and a
cancellation path, wired so that pressure travels all the way back to the
producer.

**The classic mistake:** applying backpressure at the stream and not at the
subscription. The queue is bounded, so the stream is safe — and the producer,
which is an event emitter that does not know about promises, keeps calling
`emit` and your handler keeps dropping or throwing. A push API that cannot be
slowed must be adapted with an explicit "pause the subscription" call, and if
the API has none, the bound has to be a documented loss policy rather than a
pretend one.

**Model answer:** the bridge from ex6 with the subscription's own pause/resume
wired to the queue's watermarks, an abort path that unsubscribes and destroys,
and a counter of parked pushes as the report.

## review1 — the case pipeline refuses

**What it tested:** that `pipeline` always ends the destination, so
multiplexing several sources into one sink needs the manual version — done
properly.

**The classic mistake:** `source.pipe(dest, { end: false })` and considering
the job done. It handles backpressure and leaves the destination open, and it
still has `pipe`'s error behaviour: a destination failure leaves the source
running. The manual pump has to add what `pipeline` would have added, minus the
ending.

**Model answer:** an async iteration over the source with the write/drain loop
from ex1, a `try`/`catch` that destroys the source on any failure, and an
`end()` call that happens only when the option says so.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `stream.pipeline()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streampipelinesource-transforms-destination-callback) — error propagation, teardown and the `signal` option.
- [Node.js backpressure guide](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) — the write/drain contract in the project's own words.
- [Node.js: `writable.write()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#writablewritechunk-encoding-callback) — what the `false` return does and does not mean.
- [Node.js: buffering and `highWaterMark`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#buffering) — the threshold semantics ex7 pins down.
- [Node.js: `events.once()`](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html#eventsonceemitter-name-options) — the helper that makes waiting for `drain` interruptible.

# V3·A4 — Backpressure and pipeline() (archive)

## What backpressure buys

A producer that emits 100 MB/s into a consumer that absorbs 10 MB/s has to put
90 MB/s somewhere. There are exactly three options: buffer it (memory grows
without bound), drop it (data loss), or slow the producer down. Backpressure is
the third, and Node's streams implement it as two return values and two events.

The consequence worth stating plainly: **a system without backpressure does not
run slower, it runs until it dies.** Latency is the good failure mode and you
have to build for it deliberately.

## The two halves of the contract

```ts
// writable side
const ok = writable.write(chunk);   // false = buffer is at/above highWaterMark
writable.on("drain", () => {});     // buffer fell back below the mark

// readable side
const ok2 = this.push(item);        // false = readable buffer is at/above mark
// _read() is called when the consumer wants more
```

`write()` returning `false` does not reject the chunk. The data is buffered
regardless; the boolean is the only signal you get, and ignoring it is the
whole bug. Likewise `push()` returning `false` does not discard the item.

The high-water mark defaults are worth memorising: **64 KiB** in byte mode
(16 KiB for some older stream types), **16 items** in object mode. Neither is a
memory bound in object mode, because an item can be any size.

## pipe versus pipeline

```ts
// pipe: data + backpressure only
a.pipe(b).pipe(c);

// pipeline: data + backpressure + errors + teardown + completion
await pipeline(a, b, c);
```

What `pipeline` adds, concretely:

1. An `error` listener on every stage, so an unhandled `error` cannot crash the
   process.
2. `destroy()` on every stage when any stage fails or the chain completes.
3. A single completion signal — callback or promise — that fires after the
   *last* stage is genuinely done, not merely finished writing.
4. Support for generator stages and a final async-function sink.
5. `{ signal }` for cancellation.

Point 2 is why `pipe` is a leak rather than merely inconvenient. A failing
destination unpipes the source and leaves it open; nothing closes the file, the
socket or the database cursor behind it.

```ts
// the leak, in the shape people actually write it
res.on("error", log);
fs.createReadStream(path).pipe(res);   // client disconnects → fd leaked
```

Generator stages and function sinks:

```ts
const bytes = await pipeline(
  createReadStream(path),
  async function* (src) {
    for await (const chunk of src) yield chunk.toString().toUpperCase();
  },
  async function (src) {
    let n = 0;
    for await (const s of src) n += s.length;
    return n;      // pipeline resolves with this
  },
);
```

The final function form landed in Node 16 and removes most reasons to build a
Writable by hand.

## Cancellation

```ts
await pipeline(src, gzip, dst, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) });
```

Everything is destroyed; the promise rejects with an `AbortError`. Compose
signals with `AbortSignal.any([userSignal, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)])` when you
need both a deadline and a manual cancel.

The alternative people write — a timer that destroys one stream — produces a
half-torn-down chain. Destroying the source leaves the transform waiting for
input forever; destroying the sink leaves the source pushing into a dead
stream. Only the chain-level abort knows about all the stages.

## Bridging a push API

The recurring real problem: an upstream that emits whenever it likes, a
downstream that can only take so much.

```ts
class BoundedBridge<T> {
  #queue: T[] = [];
  #waiters: (() => void)[] = [];

  push(item: T): Promise<void> {
    this.#queue.push(item);
    if (this.#queue.length < this.limit) return Promise.resolve();
    return new Promise((resolve) => this.#waiters.push(resolve));
  }

  #take(): T | undefined {
    const item = this.#queue.shift();
    if (item !== undefined) this.#waiters.shift()?.();
    return item;
  }
}
```

The promise is the backpressure. A producer that awaits it slows down; a
producer that does not is beyond your help, and that limitation belongs in the
component's documentation rather than in a comment.

## Measuring

Never with a clock. The honest instruments:

- `writable.writableLength` / `readable.readableLength` — current buffered
  amount, sampled under load.
- the `drain` event count — zero means backpressure never engaged.
- `writable.writableNeedDrain` — a boolean saying "I returned false and have
  not drained yet".
- `process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers` — byte-mode buffering that `heapUsed`
  does not show.

A stage whose `writableLength` sits at its mark is the bottleneck. A stage
whose `readableLength` sits at its mark is being throttled from downstream.
Those two sentences diagnose most pipeline performance questions.

## Common mistakes

- Ignoring `write()`'s return value.
- `await once(w, "drain")` without an error path — hangs forever on failure.
- `pipe()` in production code.
- `dest.on("error", ...)` and believing the leak is fixed.
- A timeout that destroys one stream instead of aborting the pipeline.
- Rate limiting by dropping chunks rather than delaying the callback.
- An unbounded array between a push producer and a pull consumer.
- Assuming `highWaterMark: 0` means no read-ahead.
- Leaving object-mode marks at 16 when items are large.
- Resolving on `finish` rather than waiting for the stage to close.
- Testing backpressure with timers instead of counters.
- Using `pipeline` when the destination must stay open — it always ends it.

## The interview answer

*"What is backpressure?"* — The mechanism by which a slow consumer slows a fast
producer, so that the difference in rates is expressed as latency rather than
unbounded memory. In Node it is `write()` returning `false` plus the `drain`
event on the writable side, and `push()` returning `false` on the readable
side. Without it, a fast producer does not overwhelm the consumer — it
overwhelms the process.

*"Why pipeline over pipe?"* — `pipe` relays data and backpressure and nothing
else. It does not forward errors, does not destroy the other stages on failure,
and gives no completion signal, so a failed destination leaves the source open
and holding its resource. `pipeline` adds error listeners on every stage,
destroys them all, and gives one promise. There is no case where `pipe` is
preferable in application code.

*"How would you rate-limit a stream?"* — With a Transform that delays its
callback rather than dropping chunks. The delay stops the machinery delivering
the next chunk, the writable buffer fills, and `write()` upstream returns
`false` — so the limit propagates all the way to the source for free. Dropping
would be a sampler, not a limiter.

## Check yourself

1. What exactly does `write()` returning `false` mean, and what does it not?
2. When does `drain` fire — buffer empty, or buffer below the mark?
3. Why can `await once(w, "drain")` hang, and what fixes it?
4. Name three things `pipeline` does that `pipe` does not.
5. Your handler does `createReadStream(p).pipe(res)` and the client
   disconnects. What leaks, and for how long?
6. Why is destroying only the source a broken timeout?
7. What does `pipeline` do that makes `{ end: false }` impossible?
8. How does delaying a transform's callback produce upstream backpressure?
9. What are the default high-water marks in each mode, and their units?
10. Does `highWaterMark: 0` prevent read-ahead? What actually happens?
11. Which counters prove backpressure engaged, and why not a stopwatch?
12. In a bounded push-to-pull bridge, what is the backpressure signal?
13. What is the failure mode of a producer that ignores that signal?
14. Why must the *first* error win when several stages fail together?
15. Where would you put `AbortSignal.any`, and what would you compose?

# Backpressure: the property, the plumbing, and the four places it leaks

## The idea is older than Node

Flow control is one of the oldest problems in systems engineering, and every
layer of a modern stack has an answer. TCP has a receive window: the receiver
advertises how many bytes it can absorb and the sender may not exceed it.
Unix pipes have a fixed kernel buffer — 64 KiB on Linux — and a `write()` to a
full pipe blocks. Message brokers have prefetch limits. Every one of these is
the same design: *the consumer's capacity is communicated backwards and the
producer is obliged to respect it.*

Node's version is unusual in one respect. In a threaded runtime, backpressure
can be enforced by blocking the producer's thread — the producer literally
cannot continue. Node has one thread and cannot block it, so the obligation is
cooperative: `write()` returns a boolean and *asks* you to stop. Nothing
prevents you from continuing. That single difference is why backpressure is a
recurring Node bug rather than a solved problem, and why so much of this sector
is about noticing the return value you were about to discard.

## What actually happens on a write

`writable.write(chunk)` calls `writeOrBuffer`:

1. `state.length += chunk.length`.
2. If the stream is currently processing a write, or corked, the chunk is
   appended to the buffered request list and that is all.
3. Otherwise `_write(chunk, enc, cb)` is invoked immediately.
4. The return value is `state.length < state.highWaterMark`.

When your `_write` callback fires, `afterWrite` decrements `state.length`,
processes the next buffered request, and — if the length has fallen below the
mark and the stream previously returned `false` — schedules a `drain` emission
on the next tick.

Two things follow. First, `false` is computed *after* the chunk was accepted,
so a single `write` of 10 MB into a stream with a 64 KiB mark buffers all
10 MB and then says "please stop"; the mark bounds the number of chunks in
flight, not the size of any one. Second, `drain` is scheduled rather than
emitted synchronously, so the await in a hand-rolled pump always costs at least
one tick — which is why per-chunk pumping of tiny chunks is slow and why the
chunk size matters more than the mark.

## The libuv floor

Under a file or socket stream, `_write` is a `uv_fs_write` or `uv_write`. For
files, that is a real blocking `write(2)` on the libuv thread pool, whose
default size is 4 (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`). For sockets it is a non-blocking
`write` on the event loop thread, with libuv queueing the remainder if the
kernel's send buffer is full.

That means a Node stream pipeline has at least three buffers stacked: your
stream's internal list, libuv's queue, and the kernel's socket or pipe buffer.
Node's `highWaterMark` bounds only the first. A "correct" 64 KiB mark can still
have several megabytes in flight below it, which is fine — the point is that
all three are bounded, so the total is bounded. What is not bounded is an
application-level array that somebody added between two stages, and that is
where every real backpressure incident originates.

Rough numbers, modern laptop, byte mode: a `pipeline` from a file to a file
moves data at essentially disk speed with a 64 KiB mark; raising the mark to
1 MiB buys a few percent; lowering it to 4 KiB costs 30-50% because per-chunk
overhead starts to dominate. Object mode with trivial items runs at a few
million items per second per stage. Neither number matters as much as the
memory ceiling, which is what you actually chose streams for.

## Four places backpressure quietly does not apply

**Inside your own arrays.** Any `const queue = []` between two stages is an
unbounded buffer that the stream machinery cannot see. This is the number one
cause, and it usually enters the codebase as "just collecting them to batch".

**`for await` over a source with a fast body that fires and forgets.** The loop
respects the source's pace only if the body awaits its work. `for await (const
x of src) void process(x);` reads the entire source at full speed and starts
unbounded concurrent work.

**Event emitters.** `emitter.on("data", handler)` has no flow control at all.
Any adapter from an emitter to a stream must add it — that is ex6 and the
challenge.

**`push()` inside `_read` without checking the return value.** The readable
side has the same contract as the writable one and it is ignored twice as
often, because `push` is usually written in a loop and the loop looks
self-limiting.

A fifth, subtler one deserves a mention because it is invisible in code review:
**a stage that is fast but allocates**. Backpressure bounds the number of items
in flight, not the garbage they produce. A transform that turns each 64 KiB
chunk into a megabyte of intermediate objects keeps memory bounded in the
stream's accounting and unbounded in the heap, because the collector cannot
keep up with the allocation rate. The symptom is a process whose RSS climbs
while every `writableLength` sits comfortably at its mark, and the diagnosis is
allocation profiling rather than stream instrumentation. Backpressure is a
statement about queues and their depth; it says nothing at all about what you
then do with an item once you have taken it out of one.

## When not to use pipeline

When the destination must outlive the source. `pipeline` always ends its
destination, which is correct for a file or a response and wrong for a shared
sink that several sources feed in turn — a log file, a multiplexed socket, an
archive being appended to. There, the manual pump is not a shortcut, it is the
right tool; write it once, carefully, with the error handling `pipeline` would
have given you.

When there is no stream. If the data fits in memory, `await readFile`, an
`Array.prototype.map`, and `await writeFile` are faster to write, faster to
run, and much easier to debug. Streams cost you stack traces that go through
the machinery, error paths that are easy to get wrong, and a mental model that
new team members will not share. Pay that only for the bounded-memory property.

When the concurrency structure is not a chain. A fan-out to five destinations
or a fan-in from twenty sources is not a pipeline; expressing it as nested
pipelines produces teardown semantics nobody can reason about. Use an explicit
coordinator and per-branch pipelines.

And when the "stream" is really a queue with durability requirements. A
bounded in-memory queue loses everything on a crash. If losing it matters, the
bound belongs in a broker, and the Node process should be pulling from it with
a prefetch limit — which is the same design, at a layer that survives a
restart.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `stream.pipeline()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streampipelinesource-transforms-destination-callback) — the teardown and error semantics in normative form.
- [Node.js backpressure guide](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) — the write/drain contract with the project's own worked example.
- [`lib/internal/streams/writable.js`](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/lib/internal/streams/writable.js) — `writeOrBuffer` and `afterWrite`, the twenty lines this whole sector is about.
- [libuv: threadpool](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/threadpool.html) — why file writes have a concurrency of four by default.
- [Node.js: `AbortSignal.any()`](https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#static-method-abortsignalanysignals) — composing a deadline with a user cancel for the `signal` option.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The loop is three lines and everybody writes it correctly. The exercise is the
fourth line, which is about the *wait*: while you are parked on `drain`, the
stream can die, and a dead stream never drains. So the wait must be a race
between two outcomes, not a subscription to one.

## Hint 2

`events.once` already knows about streams:

```ts
import { once } from "node:events";
await once(writable, "drain");   // rejects if the stream emits 'error' first
```

That single behaviour — rejecting on `error` while waiting for something else —
is why you should reach for `once` from `node:events` rather than hand-rolling
`new Promise((res) => w.on("drain", res))`. Check the documentation for what it
does with `AbortSignal` too, because the same argument applies.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `waits` counter, a `for` loop with `if (!writable.write(chunk))
{ waits++; await once(writable, "drain"); }`, then `writable.end()` and an await
on the finished helper, then `return waits`. The decision left to you is what
"finished" means for your sink — `once(writable, "finish")` returns before the
stream has closed its resources, while `finished(writable)` waits for the real
end. One of those is a promise you can rely on when the sink is a file.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the failure the gate constructs, because it is the whole point.
Write the version with `new Promise((resolve) => writable.once("drain",
resolve))`, then make the sink fail on the fourth chunk while your pump is
parked. Nothing happens. No error, no rejection, no exit — the process sits
with an unsettled promise and eventually the test framework times out. That is
what a hung upload looks like in production, and it is one wrong helper away
from the correct code.

## Hint 2

Think about what your return value is measuring and whether it is stable. The
number of `drain` waits depends on the chunk sizes and the high-water mark, and
for the same input it is deterministic — which is why the gate can assert on
it. But it is *not* a measure of slowness; a fast sink with a small mark drains
often and a slow sink with a large mark may drain once. If you were reporting
this as a metric, the useful companion number is total bytes, so the ratio
means something.

## Hint 3

Consider the `end()` placement carefully. Calling it inside the loop's error
path as well as after the loop gives you a double `end`, which emits
`ERR_STREAM_ALREADY_FINISHED` on the second call. Calling it inside a `finally`
looks tidy and ends a stream that has already been destroyed by an error, which
is a different error. The clean structure is: pump, then end, then await — with
the rejection propagating out of the pump before `end` is ever reached.
