exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — what pipe leaves behind

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function transfer(source: Readable, destination: Writable): Promise<void>;
```

Move all the data from `source` to `destination`, and guarantee that **any**
failure destroys both streams.

```ts
await transfer(Readable.from(["a", "b"]), sink);   // resolves when sink finishes

const failing = new Writable({ write(_c, _e, cb) { cb(new Error("disk full")); } });
const src = createSlowSource();
await transfer(src, failing).catch((e) => e.message);   // "disk full"
src.destroyed;                                          // true — the point
```

The gate asserts four things: the promise resolves only after the destination
has finished; a destination failure rejects with that error **and** leaves
`source.destroyed === true`; a source failure rejects and leaves
`destination.destroyed === true`; and destroying the source mid-transfer
rejects with `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` rather than resolving as if the
transfer had succeeded.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The answer is one line and the exercise is knowing *which* line and being able
to defend it. Two functions in the standard library move data between streams.
One of them relays data and backpressure. The other relays data, backpressure,
errors, teardown and completion. The four gate assertions are precisely the
three things the first one is missing plus the completion signal.

## Hint 2

Note the module path, because there are two versions:

```ts
import { pipeline } from "node:stream";           // callback form
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";  // promise form
```

They are different functions with the same name. The callback form takes a
final callback and returns the destination stream; the promise form returns a
promise. Importing the wrong one and awaiting it gives you a promise that
resolves to a stream immediately, which passes a naive test and transfers
nothing.

## Hint 3

Shape: one import and one `return pipeline(source, destination)`. The decision
left to you is whether to add a `try`/`catch` that wraps the error with
context. It would be a reasonable thing to do in a service — knowing *which*
transfer failed matters — and it would break the gate's identity check on the
error object. Decide where wrapping belongs, and note that
`new Error(msg, { cause })` exists precisely so you do not have to choose.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the leak, in the shape people actually write it:

```ts
app.get("/file", (req, res) => {
  const src = createReadStream(path);
  src.on("error", next);
  res.on("error", next);
  src.pipe(res);
});
```

Every error is handled. Nothing crashes. And when a client disconnects
mid-download, `res` emits an error, `pipe` unpipes, and `src` is still open with
its file descriptor held — forever, because nothing else references it. A few
thousand impatient users later the process dies of `EMFILE`, with a stack trace
pointing at whichever unrelated `open` happened to be next.

## Hint 2

The premature-close assertion is the one worth understanding rather than
passing. When the source is destroyed before it ends, the transfer did not
complete — but no stream errored, so there is nothing to propagate. Node
synthesises `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` for exactly this case, and it exists
because the alternative is worse: a transfer that silently resolves after
copying half a file, so the caller writes a success log and deletes the source.

## Hint 3

Think about what "resolves only after the destination has finished" excludes.
It excludes resolving when the source ends — the sink may still be flushing —
and it excludes resolving on `finish`, which fires before the sink has released
its resources. For a file destination, resolving too early means the caller
renames or reads a file whose last block has not been written. The built-in
gets this right; when you write ex8 by hand, this is the assertion that will
fail first.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — a chain that can be cancelled

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function runWithTimeout(
  streams: [Readable, ...Duplex[], Writable],
  ms: number,
): Promise<void>;
```

Run the chain, and if it has not completed within `ms`, tear the **whole thing**
down and reject with an `AbortError` — an `Error` whose `name` is
`"AbortError"`.

```ts
await runWithTimeout([fastSource, gzip, sink], 1000);        // resolves

const stalled = createSourceThatNeverEnds();
await runWithTimeout([stalled, gzip, sink], 50)
  .catch((e) => e.name);                                     // "AbortError"
stalled.destroyed && gzip.destroyed && sink.destroyed;       // true
```

The gate asserts every stage is destroyed after a timeout — including the
middle ones, which is where the naive implementation fails — and that a chain
finishing comfortably inside the limit leaves no timer keeping the process
alive.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Ask where the knowledge lives. A `setTimeout` that calls `destroy()` has to
choose a stream, and no single stream is the right one — killing the source
leaves the middle stages waiting for input, killing the sink leaves the source
pushing into a corpse. The only component that knows about every stage is the
one you already use to wire them together, and it takes an option for this.

## Hint 2

Two pieces from the platform, neither of which needs a `setTimeout`:

```ts
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

await pipeline(a, b, c, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) });
```

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (Node 17.3+) creates a signal that aborts itself, and
its timer is `unref`ed — so it does not hold the event loop open if everything
else finishes first, which is the gate's second assertion.

## Hint 3

Shape: spread the array into `pipeline` and pass the options object. Two lines.
The decision left to you is the rejection's identity: `AbortSignal.timeout`
produces a `TimeoutError`, not an `AbortError`, and the prompt asks for the
latter. So either construct your own controller with a timer, or catch and
translate — and if you translate, think about whether `cause` should carry the
original so the caller can still tell a deadline from a manual cancel.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from what a broken timeout looks like in an incident channel. The
naive implementation destroys the source after five seconds. The source stops.
The gzip stage is holding 30 KB of a partially written deflate block and is
waiting for more input that will never come. The sink is waiting for gzip. The
promise from `pipeline` never settles, so the request handler never responds,
so the load balancer's own timeout fires, so the client sees a 504 with no log
line anywhere in your service. A timeout that produces a hang is worse than
having no timeout at all.

## Hint 2

Think about the difference between the three cancellation vocabularies you now
have. `stream.destroy(err)` is per-stream and immediate. `pipeline`'s `signal`
is per-chain and tears down every stage. `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` composes
several reasons into one — a user cancel and a deadline, which is what a real
request handler needs. Being able to reach for the right one of the three is
most of what this exercise is teaching; the code is short.

## Hint 3

Consider the unref detail, because it is the kind of thing that only shows up
in a CI run. A plain `setTimeout` keeps the event loop alive until it fires, so
a program whose real work finished in 10 ms sits for the full 30-second timeout
before exiting. `AbortSignal.timeout` unrefs its timer for you. If you build
your own controller with `setTimeout`, you need `clearTimeout` in a `finally`
or `timer.unref()`, and forgetting is a bug that looks like "our CLI is slow".

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The mechanism is one sentence: *not calling the callback is the throttle*. The
stream machinery will not hand you another chunk until you call back, so the
writable buffer fills, so `write()` upstream returns `false`, so the producer
stops. You do not have to propagate anything — holding the callback propagates
itself, all the way to the source.

## Hint 2

The parked-work pattern:

```ts
let pending: (() => void) | null = null;

// in transform, when there are not enough tokens:
pending = () => { tokens -= cost; this.push(chunk); callback(); };

// in the refill:
tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + perTick);
if (pending && tokens >= costOfPending) { const go = pending; pending = null; go(); }
```

At most one chunk is ever parked, because the machinery does not deliver
another until the callback fires — which is a genuinely useful simplification
and worth convincing yourself of before you write a queue you do not need.

## Hint 3

Shape: closure state of `tokens` and a single `pending` record; `onTick` is
called once at construction with a `refill` function that tops up and then
tries to release the parked chunk; `transform` either passes through
immediately or parks. The decision left to you is the oversized-chunk rule: a
20-byte chunk into a 10-token bucket can never have enough tokens, so the
condition cannot be `tokens >= cost`. Work out what it has to be instead, and
notice that the answer changes the meaning of `capacity`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through the alternative you are being steered away from. A limiter
that drops chunks when over budget is a *sampler*: the stream still runs at full
speed, the memory is still bounded, and the output is silently missing data.
For a metrics feed that might be acceptable and should be documented; for
anything else it is data loss dressed up as a feature. The distinction — shed
load or slow down — is the first question to ask about any rate limiter, at any
layer, and most incident reports involving one begin with somebody assuming the
other answer.

## Hint 2

The injected clock deserves defending, because it looks like over-engineering.
With `setInterval` inside the component, a test of "does it release the second
chunk after one refill" has to wait real milliseconds, and it becomes flaky on
a loaded CI box, and someone eventually adds a retry. With `onTick` the test
calls `refill()` and asserts. Same production behaviour — the caller passes
`(fn) => setInterval(fn, 100)` — and a deterministic gate. This is dependency
injection earning its keep in ten characters of signature.

## Hint 3

Think about what happens at `end()`. The writable side ends, `_flush` runs, and
if a chunk is still parked waiting for tokens, `_flush`'s callback must not
fire before it is released — otherwise the last chunk is dropped at exactly the
moment nobody is watching. Trace your implementation through "write 20 bytes
into an empty bucket, then immediately `end()`" and check that the byte count
out equals the byte count in.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two instruments and one discipline. The instruments are `sink.writableLength`,
which is the current buffered byte count, and the `drain` event, which fires
when that count falls back below the mark. The discipline is that you must
sample *after* the write and *before* awaiting anything, or you are measuring
the buffer after it has already been drained.

## Hint 2

The sampling point, in context:

```ts
const ok = sink.write(chunk);
maxBuffered = Math.max(maxBuffered, sink.writableLength);   // right here
if (!ok) await once(sink, "drain");
```

Move that line one statement later and every sample is taken from a drained
buffer, so `maxBuffered` reports something close to zero and the test that was
supposed to prove bounded memory proves nothing while passing.

## Hint 3

Shape: attach a `drain` counter to the sink, iterate the source with `for
await`, run ex1's write/drain loop with a sample after each write, then end and
await finished, then return the report. The decision left to you is whether to
remove the `drain` listener afterwards. For a sink that outlives the call it is
mandatory; for one created per transfer it is housekeeping — but you cannot
tell which you were given, and that is the argument.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the test you must not write. The tempting assertion is "with a
slow sink the transfer took more than 200 ms". It passes locally, it passes in
CI ninety times, and on the ninety-first the box is loaded and it takes 4000 ms
and somebody adds a retry, and now the test asserts nothing at all. Every
statement backpressure makes is about *memory*, and memory is an integer you
can read exactly. Assert on the integer.

## Hint 2

Think about why `maxBuffered <= highWaterMark + oneChunk` is the right bound
rather than `<= highWaterMark`. `write()` accepts the chunk first and returns
the boolean afterwards, so the buffer legitimately exceeds the mark by up to one
chunk's worth on every write that returns `false`. A test asserting the tighter
bound fails on correct code, and understanding why is the difference between
knowing the contract and remembering a slogan.

## Hint 3

Consider what `drains === 0` means, because you are asked to report it
honestly. It means the sink kept up: every write returned `true` and the buffer
never reached the mark. That is not a broken measurement and not a missing
feature — it is the answer for a fast sink, and a report that fudges it to look
"more correct" is exactly the instrumentation that misleads someone at 3 a.m.
Report what happened.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — a bridge that pushes back

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface BoundedBridge<T> {
  stream: Readable;                 // object mode
  push(item: T): Promise<void>;     // resolves when there is room for the next
  end(): void;
  fail(err: Error): void;
  parked(): number;                 // how many pushes had to wait, cumulative
}

export function createBoundedBridge<T>(limit: number): BoundedBridge<T>;
```

A push producer on one side, a pull consumer on the other, and a queue between
them that never exceeds `limit` items.

- `push` always accepts the item. It resolves **immediately** while the queue
  is below `limit`, and otherwise resolves only when the consumer has taken an
  item.
- `end()` ends the stream after the queue drains, not immediately.
- `fail(err)` destroys the stream with that error and rejects every parked
  push.
- `parked()` counts pushes that had to wait — the backpressure evidence.

```ts
const bridge = createBoundedBridge<number>(2);
await bridge.push(1);      // resolves at once
await bridge.push(2);      // resolves at once
const third = bridge.push(3);   // does NOT resolve yet
// after the consumer reads one item, `third` resolves
bridge.parked();           // 1
```

The gate pushes 1000 items into a bridge with `limit` 2 from a producer that
awaits, reads slowly, and asserts the queue length never exceeded 2 and that
every item arrived in order.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex6
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the failure you are replacing. Somebody has an emitter and a
stream and writes:

```ts
emitter.on("row", (row) => stream.push(row));
```

It works. It is also unbounded: `push` returning `false` is ignored, and the
stream's internal buffer absorbs the entire feed. The instinct then is to add
`const queue: T[] = []` — which moves the unbounded buffer from a place you
cannot see into a place you can, and changes nothing else. The bound only
becomes real when *something makes the producer wait*, and a promise is the only
tool JavaScript gives you for that.

## Hint 2

Think about `fail()` and the parked pushes. If a producer is awaiting
`push(item)` when the consumer dies, that promise must reject — otherwise the
producer sits forever holding whatever it holds, which for a database cursor is
a transaction. So `fail` rejects every waiter, and each rejection must be with
the *same* error object so a caller catching it can compare identities. Note
also that rejecting an array of waiters while iterating it is one of the
classic mutation-during-iteration bugs; take a copy first.

## Hint 3

Consider the interaction between `end()` and the queue. Ending immediately
truncates whatever the consumer has not taken yet — a silent data loss that
tests never catch, because in a test the queue is always empty when `end` is
called. The correct behaviour is to set a flag and let the drain path push
`null` at the moment the queue empties, which means `end()` on an already-empty
queue must also trigger that path directly.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — the high-water mark, exactly

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface LazySource {
  stream: Readable;
  produced(): number;   // how many items the generator has actually yielded
}

export function createLazySource<T>(
  items: readonly T[],
  highWaterMark: number,
): LazySource;
```

An object-mode Readable built from an async generator over `items`, where
`produced()` reports what the generator has genuinely yielded so far — the
evidence for how far ahead of the consumer it ran.

```ts
const src = createLazySource([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 1);
src.produced();                       // 0 — nothing has been asked for
const it = src.stream[Symbol.asyncIterator]();
await it.next();                      // { value: 1 }
src.produced();                       // 2 — one delivered, one buffered
```

With `highWaterMark: 0`, `produced()` after the same single `next()` is **1**,
not 0. A mark of zero does not mean "produce nothing until asked" — `push()`
always returns `false`, but the machinery still primes the stream with one
`_read`. Document that in a comment; the gate asserts the number.

The gate reads three of a hundred items with `highWaterMark: 1` and asserts
`produced()` is at most 5 — proving the generator did not run to completion.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na04_backpressure_pipeline ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The counter has to live inside the generator, because that is the only place
that knows what was actually produced. A counter in the stream's `data` handler
measures consumption; a counter outside the generator measures nothing. Put
`produced++` immediately before the `yield` and you have an honest instrument.

## Hint 2

`Readable.from` takes options, which people rarely pass:

```ts
Readable.from(gen(), { objectMode: true, highWaterMark: 1 });
```

Without the second argument you get the object-mode default of 16, and a
generator whose every item is a database round trip will make sixteen of them
before your consumer has looked at the first. That is the whole practical
consequence of this exercise.

## Hint 3

Shape: a `let produced = 0`, an async generator that increments and yields,
`Readable.from` with the options, and an accessor. Six lines. The decision left
to you is what to do about the `highWaterMark: 0` surprise — the honest answer
is a comment explaining that zero still primes one read, because the next
person to read the code will assume otherwise and "fix" it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it as an experiment rather than an implementation. Write the source,
then print `produced()` after zero, one and two `next()` calls, for
`highWaterMark` values of 0, 1, 2 and 16. The table you get is the actual
semantics of the option, and it contains one number that contradicts what
almost everyone expects. Finding that number yourself is worth more than being
told it.

## Hint 2

Think about why the machinery primes. A stream with nothing buffered cannot
answer a synchronous `read()`, and the design goal was that a consumer
attaching a `data` listener gets data without a round trip. So `_read` is
called once when the stream is constructed and flowing is requested,
regardless of the mark. With `highWaterMark: 0` every subsequent `push` returns
`false`, so it never runs more than one item ahead — which is the useful
property, just not the one the number suggests.

## Hint 3

Consider what this costs in a real system. An object-mode stage over a paginated
API with the default mark of 16 fetches sixteen pages before the consumer sees
page one. If the consumer then filters and takes the first match, fifteen of
those fetches were wasted — and if the consumer breaks out of the loop early,
they were wasted *and* charged. The fix is one options object, and knowing to
pass it is the entire value of this exercise.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Separate the two jobs completely: *wiring* and *watching*. Wiring is a `reduce`
of `pipe` calls and takes one line. Watching is attaching a completion callback
to every stage, deciding what the first failure means, and tearing everything
down. Almost all the difficulty is in the second job, which is exactly why
`pipeline` exists.

## Hint 2

`finished` is the per-stage watcher, and it hands back its own cleanup:

```ts
import { finished } from "node:stream";

const cleanups = streams.map((s) =>
  finished(s, (err) => { /* err is null on a clean end */ }),
);
// later, on settle:
for (const c of cleanups) c();
```

`finished` fires for every ending — `end`, `finish`, `error`, `destroy` — and
synthesises `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` when a stream is destroyed without
having completed. That single behaviour covers two of the gate's assertions.

## Hint 3

Shape: validate the count; wire with `reduce((a, b) => a.pipe(b))`; keep
`firstError` and a `settled` flag; attach `finished` to each stage with a
handler that records the first error and destroys every *other* stage; resolve
when the last stage reports a clean finish. The decision left to you is what
"destroy every other stage" passes as its argument — `destroy()` with no error
avoids a cascade of duplicate rejections, while `destroy(err)` propagates a
reason. The built-in does one of them, and knowing which tells you something
about how it thinks.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the direction `pipe` cannot see. `a.pipe(b)` means "when `a` has
data, write it to `b`". Errors in `b` are not `a`'s business, and `a` has no
reference to `b` at all except through the pipe bookkeeping. So a failure in
stage two must be propagated to stage one *by you*, from outside, because
nothing in the chain looks upstream. That asymmetry is the reason a naive
implementation leaks exactly the resources the pipeline was holding.

## Hint 2

Think about "the first error wins" as a debugging property rather than a rule.
When a transform fails, it destroys itself; the pipe from the source then hits
a destroyed destination and produces `ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED`; the sink is
destroyed and reports premature close. Three errors, one cause. Reporting the
last one — which is what happens if you overwrite a variable each time — gives
the caller a message about a stream they have never heard of. Reporting the
first gives them the failure.

## Hint 3

Consider the resolve condition carefully, because it is where a working
implementation still fails the gate. The last stage emitting `finish` means it
has flushed its buffers to its own `_write`; it does not mean the file is
closed or the socket is flushed. `finished()` waits for `close`, and for a file
sink the difference is the last block on disk. Resolving early means a caller
who immediately reads the file back sees a truncated one, on some platforms,
some of the time.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the honest limitation, because it is what separates a component
from a demo. Your bound is only real if the producer *awaits* what `onItem`
returns. A producer written as `emitter.on("row", (r) => handlers.onItem(r))`
ignores the promise, and your queue grows without limit no matter how carefully
you built it. There are exactly three options: document the requirement, offer
an explicit `pause()`/`resume()` on the subscription for producers that support
it, or adopt a loss policy and say so. Pretending is not on the list.

## Hint 2

The "exactly once" clauses are not busywork; each one is a real leak. Consider
the paths: normal end, producer error, sink error, abort before subscribing,
abort mid-flow, and an abort that races with a sink failure. `unsubscribe` must
happen on all six and only once on each. The way to get this right is a single
guarded helper — `let done = false; const stop = () => { if (done) return; done
= true; sub.unsubscribe(); }` — called from every path, rather than an
`unsubscribe()` sprinkled through six branches that you will get wrong the
first time and again after the next refactor.

## Hint 3

Think about the ordering of teardown on abort. If you destroy the sink first,
the pipeline rejects with a sink error rather than an `AbortError`, and the
caller cannot tell a cancellation from a failure — which matters, because one
is retried and the other is not. If you unsubscribe first, the producer stops
and the pipeline drains what is queued, which the prompt forbids. The signal on
the pipeline handles the ordering for you; your own abort listener should
handle only the parts the pipeline does not know about.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves that you have already written separately: iterate the source with
`for await`, and run ex1's write/drain loop inside it. What is new is the
teardown policy, and it is genuinely different from `pipeline`'s — because a
destination that other writers still hold must survive your failure.

## Hint 2

The `for await` loop gives you more than it looks:

```ts
for await (const chunk of source) {
  if (!destination.write(chunk)) await once(destination, "drain");
}
```

Breaking out of that loop, or throwing from inside it, calls the iterator's
`return()`, which destroys the source. So the source's teardown is handled by
the language; the destination's is the part you must decide.

## Hint 3

Shape: an options default, the loop above inside a `try`, a `catch` that
destroys the source (and the destination only when you own it) and rethrows,
and an ending branch that either `end()`s and awaits `finished` or simply
returns. The decision left to you is what "every byte has been accepted" means
in the `end: false` case: the last `write` returning `true` is not the same as
the sink having processed it, and there is no `finish` to wait for. Work out
what you can honestly promise a caller who is about to call `pump` again with a
different source.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from why the option exists, because that shapes the error policy. A
shared destination — one log file, one archive, one framed socket carrying
several logical streams — is owned by the caller, not by the transfer. So when
your source blows up mid-write, destroying the destination would take out three
other transfers that did nothing wrong. `pipeline`'s "destroy everything" is
correct precisely because `pipeline` owns everything, and the moment it does
not, the policy has to change.

## Hint 2

Think about interleaving, which is the failure this API invites. Two concurrent
`pump` calls into the same destination will interleave their chunks, producing
a corrupted archive and a log file where half-lines from two sources alternate.
Nothing in the signature prevents it. If you were shipping this, the honest
answer is either a documented "one at a time" contract or a mutex inside the
sink wrapper — and choosing the first without saying so is how the bug reaches
production.

## Hint 3

Consider the resolve condition in the `end: false` case once more, because it
is the subtle one. `write()` returning `true` means "buffered, and there is
room for more" — the sink may not have touched the data. To know it has been
processed you need the per-write callback: `write(chunk, cb)` calls `cb` when
that chunk has been handled. Awaiting the last one gives you a stronger promise
than the drain loop does, at the cost of a tick. Decide which promise your
caller actually needs.

lessons.title: V3·A5 — File handles, atomic writes and watching
lessons.summary: The filesystem as an API with failure modes: FileHandle and positional reads, the write-temp-fsync-rename dance that makes a write atomic, mkdtemp and guaranteed cleanup, exclusive creation as a lock, opendir for trees that do not fit, bounded concurrency against EMFILE, debounced watching, and rotation.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·A5 — File handles, atomic writes and watching

`05_fs_path` and `d12_fs_ops` covered the vocabulary: `readFile`, `writeFile`,
`stat`, `readdir`, and the path module. That is enough to write a build script.
It is not enough to write something that survives a power cut, a concurrent
process, a symlink, a directory with two million entries, or a user-supplied
path — and each of those is one exercise here.

The framing that makes this sector cohere: **the filesystem is a shared mutable
database with no transactions, accessed by processes you do not control.**
Every technique below is a way of getting a guarantee out of a system that
offers almost none.

## Concept — FileHandle, and why `readFile` is not always enough

```ts
import { open } from "node:fs/promises";

const handle = await open(path, "r");
try {
  const buffer = Buffer.alloc(20);
  const { bytesRead } = await handle.read(buffer, 0, 20, 0);   // position 0
} finally {
  await handle.close();
}
```

`fsPromises.open` returns a `FileHandle` — an object wrapping a file
descriptor, with `read`, `write`, `stat`, `truncate`, `sync`,
`createReadStream` and `close`. Three reasons to reach for it over the
whole-file helpers:

1. **Positional I/O.** Reading twenty bytes from the middle of a 4 GB file
   costs twenty bytes.
2. **One descriptor, many operations.** `stat` then `read` through the same
   handle cannot race with a rename between the two calls, because the handle
   refers to the *inode*, not the path.
3. **`sync()`**, which is the only way to know your bytes reached the disk.

And one obligation: **a `FileHandle` that is not closed leaks a descriptor**.
Node will warn you when the garbage collector eventually finds one, and by then
you are several thousand descriptors into an `EMFILE`. `try`/`finally` is not
optional here, which is why the standard shape above has the `finally` before
the interesting code is even written.

## Concept — atomic writes

`await writeFile(path, data)` is not atomic. It opens with `O_TRUNC`, so the
file is empty for a while, and if the process dies mid-write the file is a
prefix of the new content — which is worse than either the old or the new
version, because it looks valid. Any reader that runs concurrently may see it.

The portable technique is four steps:

```ts
const tmp = join(dirname(path), `.${basename(path)}.${randomUUID()}.tmp`);
const handle = await open(tmp, "wx");     // exclusive create
try {
  await handle.writeFile(data);
  await handle.sync();                    // the bytes are on the disk
} finally {
  await handle.close();
}
await rename(tmp, path);                  // atomic on POSIX and on NTFS
```

Three details carry all the weight. The temp file must be **in the same
directory**, because `rename` is only atomic within a filesystem and `/tmp` is
frequently a different one — cross-device gives you `EXDEV`. The `sync()` must
happen before the rename, or a crash can leave a renamed file full of zeroes,
which several filesystems will cheerfully do. And on Windows, `rename` over an
existing file fails if any process holds it open, which is the one place this
recipe is genuinely less reliable than on POSIX.

Fully durable means also fsyncing the *directory*, so the rename itself is on
disk. Node cannot do that portably — you would open the directory and call
`sync` on the handle, which works on Linux and throws `EISDIR` on Windows — so
production code either accepts the gap or platform-branches.

## Concept — exclusive creation is your only lock

There is no `flock` in Node's standard library. What there is:

```ts
await open(path, "wx");    // O_CREAT | O_EXCL — fails with EEXIST if it exists
```

`O_EXCL` create is atomic against other processes, which makes it a mutex — and
a bad one, because a process that crashes leaves the lock file behind forever.
A usable lock therefore needs a staleness policy, which is ex8.

## Concept — watching is advisory

`fs.watch` is a thin wrapper over `inotify` (Linux), `FSEvents` (macOS) and
`ReadDirectoryChangesW` (Windows), and the three disagree about almost
everything: whether you get one event or three for a single save, whether
`rename` means create or delete, whether recursive works (only macOS and
Windows, plus Linux since Node 20), and whether the filename is included. Any
watcher you ship must debounce and must re-`stat` rather than trusting the
event.

## Problem 1 — read the middle of a big file

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `readAt(path, offset, length)` reads exactly the bytes
you asked for using a `FileHandle`, returning a short buffer at end-of-file and
closing the handle on every path.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a write that cannot be half-done

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `writeFileAtomic(path, data)` writes via a temp file in
the same directory, fsyncs, renames, and removes the temp file if anything
fails — so a reader never sees a partial file.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a temp directory that always goes away

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `withTempDir(fn)` creates a unique directory under the
OS temp dir, passes it to `fn`, returns `fn`'s result, and removes the
directory recursively whether `fn` resolved or threw.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex3
```

## Problem 4 — create, but only if absent

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createIfAbsent(path, data)` writes a file only when it
does not exist, returning `true` or `false`, using exclusive creation rather
than an `exists` check — because between the check and the write is a race.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a tree that does not fit in memory

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `walk(root)` is an async generator yielding the
relative path of every regular file beneath `root`, using `opendir` so a
directory with a million entries does not become a million-element array, and
never following symlinks.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a watcher you can actually use

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `watchDebounced(dir, options)` collects raw watch
events, coalesces them per filename over a window, and stops cleanly on an
`AbortSignal` — driven by an injected scheduler so it is testable.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex6
```

## Problem 7 — EMFILE is a design error, not bad luck

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `totalSize(paths, concurrency)` stats many files with a
bounded number of operations in flight, because `Promise.all` over ten thousand
paths opens ten thousand descriptors and the process dies.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex7
```

## Problem 8 — a lock that survives a crash

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `acquireLock(path, options)` uses exclusive creation
plus a staleness policy, so a lock left behind by a killed process is
recoverable rather than permanent.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex8
```

## Challenge — a rotating log writer

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createRotatingWriter(options)` appends lines
through a held handle, rotates atomically when the file exceeds a size, keeps a
fixed number of generations, and never loses a line across a rotation.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic challenge
```

## Review

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. `resolveWithin(root, userPath)` turns
attacker-controlled input into a path guaranteed to be inside a root — the
other half of filesystem safety, where the enemy is a `..` and a symlink rather
than a crash.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic review1
```

# Reading - node/v3na05_fs_handles_atomic

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The through-line is **the gap between two calls**. Almost every bug in this
sector lives in the interval between checking something and acting on it: the
`exists` before the `write`, the `stat` before the `read`, the resolve before
the open, the read of a file another process is halfway through writing. The
filesystem is shared mutable state with no transactions, so the fix is always
the same shape — do it in *one* operation that the kernel makes atomic
(`O_EXCL`, `rename`), or hold a handle so the thing you checked is the thing
you act on.

The second theme is **resources are finite and Node hides that from you**.
Descriptors run out, the libuv thread pool has four slots, and `Promise.all`
over an array of paths is an unbounded fan-out wearing the clothes of a
one-liner.

## ex1 — the handle refers to the inode

**What it tested:** positional reads through a `FileHandle`, and the
`try`/`finally` that must surround every one.

**The classic mistake:** `(await readFile(path)).subarray(offset, offset + n)`.
It is correct, it is one line, and it reads the whole file — 4 GB into memory
to get twenty bytes. The second mistake is opening the handle and closing it
only on the success path, so every error leaks a descriptor and the leak is
invisible until the thousandth failure.

**Model answer:** `open`, then `read(buffer, 0, length, position)`, and trust
`bytesRead` rather than the buffer's length, because a read near end-of-file
returns short and the tail of your buffer is still zeroes.

## ex2 — a prefix of the new file is the worst outcome

**What it tested:** the write-temp-fsync-rename sequence, and the two details
that make it actually atomic.

**The classic mistake:** writing the temp file to `os.tmpdir()`. `rename`
across filesystems fails with `EXDEV`, and `/tmp` is very often tmpfs while the
target is not — so the code works on the developer's machine and fails in the
container. The second is skipping `sync()`: several filesystems will happily
persist the rename before the data, so a crash leaves a correctly named file
full of zeroes.

**Model answer:** temp file in `dirname(path)`, `handle.sync()` before
`close()`, `rename` after, and an `unlink` of the temp in the failure path that
itself ignores `ENOENT` — because the failure may have been the create.

## ex3 — cleanup is the whole exercise

**What it tested:** the resource-scoped-function pattern, applied to a
directory.

**The classic mistake:** `mkdtemp` in a fixed location, or worse a fixed name.
Two concurrent test runs then share a directory and delete each other's files,
which produces failures that only happen on CI and only sometimes. `mkdtemp`
exists precisely because generating a unique name yourself is a race.

**Model answer:** `mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), "prefix-"))`, the call in a `try`,
`rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true })` in the `finally`, and the result
returned from the `try` — so a throwing `fn` still cleans up and still throws
the original error rather than a cleanup error.

## ex4 — check-then-act is a race

**What it tested:** that `O_EXCL` is a single atomic operation and
`if (!exists) write()` is two.

**The classic mistake:** `existsSync(path) || writeFile(path, data)`. Between
the check and the write, another process can create the file, and you overwrite
it — the classic TOCTOU. `fs.exists` was deprecated for exactly this reason.
The subtler mistake is catching every error rather than only `EEXIST`, which
turns a permission problem into a silent `false`.

**Model answer:** `open(path, "wx")`, `catch` and re-throw unless
`err.code === "EEXIST"`, and close the handle in a `finally`. Branch on `code`,
never on the message.

## ex5 — readdir returns an array

**What it tested:** streaming a directory tree, and the symlink decision every
walker has to make explicitly.

**The classic mistake:** `readdir` recursively. It materialises every entry of
every directory as an array before you look at one, which is fine for a source
tree and fatal for a mail spool. `opendir` gives you an async iterable over the
same data with one entry resident. The second mistake is following symlinks
without thinking: a link pointing at its own ancestor is an infinite walk, and
`isDirectory()` on a `Dirent` reports the *link's* type only because `opendir`
does not follow — which is the behaviour you want, once you know it.

**Model answer:** an async generator over `opendir`, recursing with `yield*`
into `entry.isDirectory()`, yielding `relative(root, full)` for
`entry.isFile()`, and skipping `entry.isSymbolicLink()` explicitly so the
decision is visible in the code.

## ex6 — the events are lies

**What it tested:** that a raw watcher is unusable and what turning it into a
usable one requires.

**The classic mistake:** acting on each event. One editor save produces between
one and five events depending on the platform and whether the editor writes in
place or writes-and-renames; a naive rebuild therefore runs five times, and
because the file is momentarily absent during a rename, two of those runs read
nothing. The other mistake is `recursive: true` as a portability assumption —
it has only worked everywhere since Node 20.

**Model answer:** a `Map` from filename to a pending timer, reset on each
event, firing once per filename per window; an `AbortSignal` passed straight to
`fs.watch`, which supports it natively; and an injected scheduler so the gate
does not need a real clock.

## ex7 — Promise.all is a fan-out

**What it tested:** that concurrency limits are a filesystem concern, not a
network one.

**The classic mistake:** `await Promise.all(paths.map((p) => stat(p)))`. For
ten thousand paths that is ten thousand operations queued at once; the libuv
thread pool serialises them four at a time, so it is not even faster, and on
some platforms the descriptor pressure produces `EMFILE`. The mistake feels
safe because `Promise.all` looks like a loop.

**Model answer:** a worker pool — `concurrency` workers each pulling the next
index from a shared cursor — which is bounded, order-preserving in its output
array, and stops on the first failure. The default worth knowing is
`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, which is 4, so a concurrency above about 8 buys nothing
for disk-bound work.

## ex8 — a lock nobody can release is worse than no lock

**What it tested:** the staleness policy that turns `O_EXCL` into a usable
mutex.

**The classic mistake:** the lock without an expiry. The process is killed with
`SIGKILL`, the file remains, and every subsequent run fails until a human
deletes it — which is exactly the incident you were trying to prevent. The
opposite mistake is a stale timeout so short that a slow but healthy holder
gets its lock stolen, and now two processes believe they own it.

**Model answer:** write the pid and a timestamp into the lock file; on
`EEXIST`, read it, and if its `mtime` is older than the staleness window,
`unlink` and retry **once** — the single retry matters, because a loop makes
two racing processes steal from each other indefinitely.

## challenge — rotation is a rename with bookkeeping

**What it tested:** the whole sector in one component: a held handle, size
tracking, atomic rename, generation cleanup and the no-lost-lines guarantee.

**The classic mistake:** rotating by checking the size with `stat` before each
write. That is an extra syscall per line and it is wrong under concurrency
anyway; track the bytes you have written yourself, because you are the only
writer. The other is renaming while writes are in flight — the handle follows
the inode, so writes issued before the rename land in the *old* file, which is
correct only if you meant it.

**Model answer:** a serialised write queue so a rotation cannot interleave with
a write, a byte counter rather than a `stat`, `rename` of the current file to
`.1` after shifting the older generations down, and a fresh `open` with `"a"`.

## review1 — the enemy has a keyboard

**What it tested:** path containment, which is the other half of filesystem
safety and the one with a CVE list.

**The classic mistake:** `resolved.startsWith(root)`. It accepts
`/data/uploads-evil` for a root of `/data/uploads`, because string prefixes do
not respect path boundaries. The fix is `relative(root, resolved)` and a check
that the result neither starts with `..` nor is absolute. The second mistake is
checking before resolving symlinks — a path inside the root can point outside
it, so a system that must be safe uses `realpath` and accepts that the file has
to exist.

**Model answer:** `resolve(root, userPath)`, then the `relative` test, then
optionally `realpath` on both sides for the symlink case, with the `ENOENT`
branch documented rather than swallowed.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `fsPromises.open` and FileHandle](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#class-filehandle) — positional reads, `sync()`, and the closing obligation.
- [Node.js: `fsPromises.mkdtemp`](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#fspromisesmkdtempprefix-options) — why unique temp directories are a library call and not a `Math.random`.
- [Node.js: file system flags](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#file-system-flags) — `wx`, `ax`, `r+` and the rest of the `O_*` vocabulary behind ex4 and ex8.
- [Node.js: `fs.watch` caveats](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#caveats) — the platform differences ex6 exists to absorb.
- [Node.js: `fsPromises.opendir`](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#fspromisesopendirpath-options) — the streaming directory iterator.
- [libuv: threadpool](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/threadpool.html) — the four-slot pool that bounds real filesystem concurrency.

# V3·A5 — File handles, atomic writes and watching (archive)

## Three APIs, one filesystem

Node offers the same operations three times: `node:fs` callbacks, `node:fs`
synchronous, and `node:fs/promises`. Use the promises API everywhere except
startup configuration loading, where sync is genuinely simpler and the blocking
does not matter because nothing else is running yet. The callback API exists
for history and for the few functions that have no promise equivalent
(`fs.watch`, `fs.createReadStream`).

The promises API also gives you `FileHandle`, which the others do not — they
hand you a numeric descriptor you must remember to close.

## FileHandle

```ts
import { open } from "node:fs/promises";

const handle = await open("data.bin", "r");
try {
  const stats = await handle.stat();
  const buf = Buffer.alloc(64);
  const { bytesRead } = await handle.read(buf, 0, 64, stats.size - 64);  // tail
  const stream = handle.createReadStream({ start: 0, end: 1023 });
} finally {
  await handle.close();
}
```

Why a handle rather than a path:

- **Positional reads and writes** — `read(buffer, offset, length, position)`
  where `position` is where in the *file* to start; pass `null` to continue
  from the current position.
- **Stability across renames.** The handle refers to the inode. Once open, a
  rename or delete by another process does not affect your reads — on POSIX the
  inode survives until the last descriptor closes, which is why you can delete
  a file a process is still reading.
- **`sync()` and `datasync()`** — the durability primitives.
- **`createReadStream({ start, end })`** for byte-range serving.

The obligation is `close()`. A leaked handle is a leaked descriptor, and Node's
warning arrives whenever the GC gets round to it, which is far too late to
attribute.

## Atomic writes

```ts
import { open, rename, unlink } from "node:fs/promises";
import { dirname, basename, join } from "node:path";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

export async function writeFileAtomic(path: string, data: Buffer | string) {
  const tmp = join(dirname(path), `.${basename(path)}.${randomUUID()}.tmp`);
  let handle;
  try {
    handle = await open(tmp, "wx");
    await handle.writeFile(data);
    await handle.sync();           // durability: bytes on the platter
    await handle.close();
    handle = undefined;
    await rename(tmp, path);       // atomicity: readers see old or new
  } catch (err) {
    await handle?.close().catch(() => {});
    await unlink(tmp).catch(() => {});
    throw err;
  }
}
```

Atomicity and durability are different properties and this gives you both.
`rename` gives atomicity: any reader sees the complete old file or the complete
new one, never a prefix. `sync` gives durability: the content is on disk before
the name points at it.

Three caveats to carry:

- **Same directory, always.** `rename` across devices is `EXDEV`.
- **Windows.** `rename` onto an open file fails with `EPERM` or `EBUSY`.
- **Directory fsync.** Full durability requires fsyncing the directory too,
  which is not portable from Node. Most applications accept the gap.

## Flags

| flag | meaning |
|---|---|
| `r` | read; fails if absent |
| `r+` | read/write; fails if absent |
| `w` | write, create, **truncate** |
| `wx` | write, create, fail with `EEXIST` if present |
| `a` | append, create |
| `ax` | append, create, fail if present |

`wx` and `ax` are `O_EXCL`, which the kernel guarantees is atomic against other
processes. That is the only mutual-exclusion primitive Node gives you and it is
the basis of every lock-file implementation.

## Directories

```ts
const dir = await opendir(root);
for await (const entry of dir) {
  entry.name; entry.isFile(); entry.isDirectory(); entry.isSymbolicLink();
}
```

`readdir` returns an array; `opendir` streams. For a directory with a million
entries the difference is a hundred megabytes of `Dirent` objects. `readdir`
with `{ withFileTypes: true }` avoids a `stat` per entry, which is the more
common performance win.

Symlinks: `Dirent.isDirectory()` reports the link's own type because
`readdir`/`opendir` use `lstat` semantics. Deciding whether to follow is
therefore an explicit choice, and the safe default for a walker is not to —
a link into an ancestor is an infinite loop and a link out of the tree is a
security boundary crossed.

## Watching

```ts
const ac = new AbortController();
const watcher = watch(dir, { recursive: true, signal: ac.signal });
for await (const event of watcher) {
  event.eventType;   // "rename" | "change"
  event.filename;    // may be null
}
```

Every field there is unreliable in some way:

- `eventType` is `"rename"` for creation *and* deletion *and* actual renames.
- `filename` can be `null` on some platforms.
- One logical change produces one to five events.
- `recursive` was macOS/Windows only until Node 20.
- Events can arrive for a file that no longer exists by the time you look.

So a usable watcher debounces per filename and re-`stat`s rather than trusting
the event. For anything cross-platform and important, polling with
`fs.watchFile` is slower but predictable, and libraries like chokidar exist
because absorbing all of this is genuinely tedious.

## Concurrency

`Promise.all(paths.map(stat))` is an unbounded fan-out. The libuv thread pool
has **four** threads by default (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`), so filesystem
operations are serialised four at a time regardless — the fan-out buys no
speed and costs descriptors and memory. A bounded worker pool of 4-16 is both
faster and safe.

## Common mistakes

- Not closing a `FileHandle` on the error path.
- `readFile` to extract a few bytes from a large file.
- `writeFile` where a torn file would matter.
- A temp file in `os.tmpdir()` followed by a `rename` — `EXDEV`.
- Skipping `sync()` and calling the result durable.
- `existsSync` before a write instead of `wx`.
- Catching all errors where you meant to catch `EEXIST`.
- Branching on `err.message` instead of `err.code`.
- Recursive `readdir` on a tree of unknown size.
- Following symlinks in a walker by accident.
- Acting on every `fs.watch` event.
- `Promise.all` over thousands of paths.
- `resolved.startsWith(root)` as a containment check.
- A lock file with no staleness policy.

## The interview answer

*"How do you write a file atomically in Node?"* — Write to a temp file in the
**same directory**, `fsync` it, then `rename` over the target. `rename` within
a filesystem is atomic, so a concurrent reader sees the whole old file or the
whole new one. Same directory because cross-device rename fails with `EXDEV`;
fsync first because otherwise a crash can leave the renamed file empty. Full
durability also wants a directory fsync, which is not portable.

*"How do you avoid a race when creating a file only if it does not exist?"* —
`open(path, "wx")` and catch `EEXIST`. Checking with `exists` and then writing
is two operations with a gap, which is a TOCTOU race; `O_EXCL` is one operation
the kernel makes atomic.

*"Why is `Promise.all` over ten thousand `stat` calls a bug?"* — It queues ten
thousand operations at once. The libuv pool runs four at a time, so there is no
speed benefit, and the pending operations hold memory and descriptors until
`EMFILE`. Bound it with a worker pool.

## Check yourself

1. Name three things a `FileHandle` gives you that `readFile` does not.
2. Why does a handle survive the file being renamed by another process?
3. What are the four steps of an atomic write, and what does each guarantee?
4. Why must the temp file live in the same directory as the target?
5. What can happen if you `rename` before `fsync`?
6. What breaks about the atomic-write recipe on Windows?
7. Which flag gives you atomic exclusive creation, and what error does it
   produce?
8. Why was `fs.exists` deprecated?
9. When is `opendir` worth the extra ceremony over `readdir`?
10. What does `Dirent.isDirectory()` report for a symlink to a directory?
11. Give three ways `fs.watch` events lie about what happened.
12. What is `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, its default, and why does it cap useful
    filesystem concurrency?
13. Why is `startsWith` the wrong containment check, and what is the right one?
14. What goes wrong with a lock file that has no staleness window? With one
    whose window is too short?
15. During a log rotation, where do writes issued just before the `rename` end
    up, and why?

# The filesystem: what the syscalls actually promise

## Node's fs is libuv's fs is POSIX

Almost every function in `node:fs` maps to one libuv call which maps to one or
two syscalls. `fsPromises.open` is `uv_fs_open` is `open(2)`. `readFile` is
`open`, a loop of `read`, and `close`. `rename` is `rename(2)`. The abstraction
is thin on purpose, and it means the guarantees you get are POSIX's guarantees
— which are narrower than most people assume.

The consequential ones:

**`rename(2)` is atomic within a filesystem.** POSIX requires that a rename
onto an existing path either succeeds completely or leaves the target
untouched; there is no window in which the name refers to nothing. This is the
only transactional primitive the filesystem offers, and every "atomic write"
recipe in every language is built on it.

**`open(2)` with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` is atomic.** The check and the create happen
under the inode lock. This is the only mutual-exclusion primitive, and it is
famously broken over NFS versions before v3, which is why old lock-file code
does the link-and-count dance.

**`write(2)` promises nothing about durability.** It copies into the page
cache and returns. `fsync(2)` is what pushes the pages to the device, and even
that has a history of lying — the 2018 "fsyncgate" discussion around PostgreSQL
established that on Linux a failed writeback could be reported once and then
forgotten, so a retry would see success on data that never landed.

**Nothing is atomic across two calls.** There is no way to check and then act.
Every check-then-act pattern in filesystem code is a race, and the fix is
always to find the single call that does both.

## The thread pool

Node's event loop is single-threaded and filesystem calls block, so libuv runs
them on a thread pool. The default size is **4**, configurable only via the
`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` environment variable and only before the process starts.
The pool is shared with `dns.lookup`, `crypto.pbkdf2`, and zlib's async
functions.

Two practical consequences. First, filesystem concurrency above about 8 buys
nothing for disk-bound work and can hurt — the operations queue in the pool
regardless, and the only thing more concurrency adds is memory and descriptors.
Second, a long `pbkdf2` or a big `zlib` call can starve your file I/O, because
they share the four slots. If a service does both, raising the pool size is one
of the few environment variables genuinely worth setting.

Order of magnitude: a `stat` on a warm cache is a few microseconds; on a cold
one it is a disk seek. Reading a 1 MB file with `readFile` is around a
millisecond warm. Opening and closing a handle is a couple of microseconds. An
`fsync` is 0.1 ms on an NVMe SSD with a write cache, and 5-10 ms on spinning
rust — which is why the atomic-write recipe is genuinely expensive and why you
do not use it for every write, only for the ones where a torn file matters.

## Watching, and why everyone uses a library

The three backends have almost nothing in common.

**inotify** (Linux) is per-directory, gives you a file descriptor you read
events from, and has a per-user watch limit (`max_user_watches`, historically
8192, now often 65536 or higher). Recursive watching means walking the tree and
adding a watch per directory, which is why it was not supported natively for so
long and why it can fail on large trees with `ENOSPC` — an error that means
"out of watches", not "out of disk", and confuses everybody the first time.

**FSEvents** (macOS) is a system-wide event stream with coalescing and a
latency parameter, natively recursive, and reports directory-level changes
rather than file-level ones by default.

**ReadDirectoryChangesW** (Windows) is per-directory with an optional recursive
flag, and delivers events in a buffer that can overflow under load — after
which you have to rescan.

On top of that, editors differ. Vim writes a temp file and renames. VS Code
writes in place. Some tools truncate then write, which produces a `change`
event for a file that is momentarily empty — so a rebuild triggered on the
first event reads nothing and reports a syntax error that vanishes on retry.

The takeaway is not "watching is impossible" but "the event is a hint". Debounce
per path, then `stat` and read; treat the event as an invalidation signal
rather than as data.

## Windows

Node smooths over a lot, but four differences leak into application code:

- **Open files cannot be renamed over or deleted** by default, so the atomic
  write recipe can fail with `EPERM`/`EBUSY` if any process has the target
  open — including a virus scanner.
- **Path separators and case.** `path.sep` is `\`, comparisons are
  case-insensitive but case-preserving, and `path.resolve` normalises
  differently. Containment checks must normalise before comparing.
- **`MAX_PATH`** is 260 characters unless long paths are enabled; Node uses the
  `\\?\` prefix internally for some operations but not all.
- **No `fsync` on a directory handle** — `open` on a directory throws `EISDIR`,
  so the last durability step is simply unavailable.

## When not to use the filesystem this way

When you need transactions across more than one file. Two atomic writes are not
one atomic write, and a crash between them leaves an inconsistent pair. That is
a database, even if the database is SQLite in the same directory.

When several processes coordinate. Lock files work and are miserable: they need
staleness policies, they break on NFS, and the failure mode is a permanently
stuck system. If you control the deployment, a real lock service — Redis,
Postgres advisory locks, the orchestrator's leader election — is less code and
far fewer incidents.

When you are watching for changes in order to react quickly. Watching is fine
for a dev-server rebuild and wrong for anything where a missed event matters:
the event streams drop, overflow and coalesce. A queue or a database
notification gives you the delivery guarantee that the filesystem does not.

And when the data does not need to be a file. A cache in `/tmp` that must
survive nothing, a queue that must survive a crash, a config that several
processes edit — each of those has a better home. The filesystem's appeal is
that it is always there; its cost is that it offers one atomic operation and no
way to compose two.

## A note on containers

Two things change enough in a container to be worth stating separately. The
first is that the writable layer of an overlay filesystem is not the same
filesystem as a mounted volume, so a temp file in `/tmp` and a target in
`/data` are cross-device by construction and `rename` fails with `EXDEV` — the
scenario the atomic-write exercise is built around, and the reason it fails in
production and not on the laptop. The second is that a copy-on-write layer
turns the first write to any pre-existing file into a full copy of that file,
so appending one line to a 2 GB log inherited from the image costs two
gigabytes of I/O and disk. Both are invisible locally and obvious in
production, which is the worst combination a failure mode can have.

Descriptor limits differ too. A container's `RLIMIT_NOFILE` is frequently 1024
where a developer machine offers 256K, so the unbounded fan-out in ex7 is not a
theoretical concern — 1024 concurrent opens is an ordinary directory listing,
and `EMFILE` under load is one of the most common first production incidents
for a service that reads files per request.

Finally, watching. Container filesystems layered over overlayfs have
historically not propagated inotify events for files in lower layers at all,
and bind mounts from a host running a different OS — the Docker Desktop case —
deliver events unreliably or not at all. A dev-server rebuild loop that works
natively and silently stops working in a container is almost always this, and
the workaround is polling, which is exactly the trade `fs.watchFile` exists to
offer.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: File system](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html) — the flags table, the FileHandle class, and the `fs.watch` caveats section in particular.
- [libuv: threadpool](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/threadpool.html) — the four-slot pool shared with dns, crypto and zlib.
- [`rename(2)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html) — the atomicity guarantee every safe-write recipe rests on.
- [`open(2)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html) — `O_EXCL`, `O_TRUNC`, `O_APPEND` and the NFS caveat.
- [PostgreSQL fsync errors discussion (2018)](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Fsync_Errors) — why "I called fsync" is not the end of the durability story.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — read the middle of a big file

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function readAt(
  path: string,
  offset: number,
  length: number,
): Promise<Buffer>;
```

Read `length` bytes starting at byte `offset`, using a `FileHandle` and a
positional read — not by loading the file.

```ts
// file contains "0123456789"
await readAt(p, 3, 4);        // <Buffer 33 34 35 36>   ("3456")
await readAt(p, 8, 10);       // <Buffer 38 39>          — short at EOF
await readAt(p, 99, 4);       // <Buffer >               — empty, not an error
await readAt(p, 0, 0);        // <Buffer >
```

Requirements:

- the returned buffer's length is the number of bytes actually read, never
  padded with zeroes;
- the handle is closed on **every** path, including when the read throws;
- a negative `offset` or `length` throws before opening anything;
- a missing file propagates the `ENOENT` error unchanged.

The gate opens a thousand handles through your function against a file that
does not exist and asserts the process's descriptor count is unchanged
afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two things to look up rather than guess. First, the argument order of
`handle.read` — there are four numbers and only one of them is the position in
the file; the others describe where in *your* buffer to put the data. Second,
what the call resolves to, because it is not the buffer.

## Hint 2

The shape of a positional read:

```ts
const buffer = Buffer.alloc(length);
const { bytesRead } = await handle.read(buffer, 0, length, offset);
//                                       ^buf  ^into ^count ^file position
return buffer.subarray(0, bytesRead);
```

That last line is the one people omit. `Buffer.alloc` zero-fills, so a read
that returns 2 bytes into a 10-byte buffer leaves eight zeroes that look
exactly like real data — and for a binary format they will parse as valid.

## Hint 3

Shape: validate the numbers, `const handle = await open(path, "r")`, then a
`try` containing the read and a `finally` containing `await handle.close()`.
The decision left to you is where the validation goes relative to the `open`.
Validating first means a bad argument never touches the filesystem, which is
both faster and gives a cleaner stack; validating inside the `try` is one line
shorter and opens a file in order to immediately fail.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the leak. Write the version without the `finally`, point it at
a path that does not exist, and call it in a loop:

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 5000; i++) await readAt("/nope", 0, 4).catch(() => {});
```

For a missing file this passes, because `open` threw before there was anything
to leak. Now make the *read* fail instead — a directory, or a file you cannot
read — and watch the descriptors climb. Node will eventually print
`Warning: Closing file descriptor N on garbage collection`, which is the
runtime telling you it cleaned up a bug for you, some unknowable time later.

## Hint 2

Think about why this is a handle exercise and not a `readFile` exercise, in
numbers. A 4 GB file, twenty bytes wanted: `readFile` allocates 4 GB (and on a
64-bit build hits `ERR_FS_FILE_TOO_LARGE` above 2 GiB anyway), reads 4 GB from
disk, and slices. The positional read does one `pread(2)` of a single page. The
difference is not a micro-optimisation; it is the difference between a function
that works and one that cannot.

## Hint 3

Consider the short-read contract more carefully than the prompt requires. POSIX
`read(2)` may return fewer bytes than asked for even in the *middle* of a file
— on a pipe, on a network filesystem, or when interrupted by a signal. Node's
`handle.read` does not loop for you. For a regular local file a short read
means EOF in practice, but if this function ever pointed at a FIFO the
"correct" implementation would loop until `bytesRead` is zero or the count is
satisfied. Know which assumption you are shipping.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — a write that cannot be half-done

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function writeFileAtomic(
  path: string,
  data: Buffer | string,
): Promise<void>;
```

A reader running concurrently must see either the complete old file or the
complete new one — never a prefix.

The sequence:

1. create a uniquely named temp file **in the same directory** as `path`, with
   exclusive creation;
2. write the data;
3. `sync()` the handle;
4. close it;
5. `rename` the temp over the target.

On any failure, close the handle if it is open, unlink the temp file (ignoring
`ENOENT`, because the failure may have been the create itself), and rethrow the
**original** error.

```ts
await writeFileAtomic(join(dir, "config.json"), '{"a":1}');
// a concurrent reader at any moment sees the old content or '{"a":1}'
```

The gate replaces a 4 MB file while a reader loops reading it, and asserts
every observed read parsed as one of the two complete versions. It also asserts
that no `.tmp` files remain after a forced failure, and that a temp file
written to `os.tmpdir()` would have failed — so keep it local.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two guarantees with two different mechanisms, and conflating them is the usual
mistake. *Atomicity* — a reader never sees a partial file — comes from
`rename`, which the kernel performs as one indivisible operation.
*Durability* — the bytes survive a power cut — comes from `fsync`. You need
both, and the order matters: sync the content before the name points at it.

## Hint 2

Constructing the temp path:

```ts
import { dirname, basename, join } from "node:path";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const tmp = join(dirname(path), `.${basename(path)}.${randomUUID()}.tmp`);
```

`dirname(path)`, not `os.tmpdir()`. A leading dot so it is hidden from casual
listing and from most build-tool globs. A UUID rather than a counter or a pid,
because two processes with the same pid in different containers is not
hypothetical.

## Hint 3

Shape: build the temp path, `open(tmp, "wx")`, then a `try` with write, sync,
close, rename; a `catch` that closes and unlinks defensively before rethrowing.
The decision left to you is how to avoid a double close — you close inside the
happy path before the rename, and the `catch` must not close again. A
`let handle: FileHandle | undefined` set to `undefined` after the successful
close is the usual answer; convince yourself the alternative (closing only in a
`finally`) does not let you rename while the handle is open, which matters on
Windows.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter through the failure this prevents, because it is more specific than
"corruption". Consider `writeFile(configPath, JSON.stringify(config))` on a
process that is killed halfway. `writeFile` opens with `O_TRUNC`, so the file
is *first* emptied and then filled. The crash leaves valid JSON's opening brace
and half a key. On restart the service reads it, `JSON.parse` throws, and the
service will not start — with the original config gone, because you truncated
it. That is a bad night, and it is three lines of prevention.

## Hint 2

The `EXDEV` trap deserves reproducing once so you never forget it. On Linux,
`/tmp` is frequently `tmpfs` — a different filesystem from `/var/lib/yourapp`.
`rename("/tmp/x", "/var/lib/yourapp/x")` fails with
`EXDEV: cross-device link not permitted`. It works on a Mac where everything is
one volume, and fails in the container. This is why every "atomic write"
library takes the directory from the target path and why a `tmpdir` option is
usually a mistake in that API.

## Hint 3

Think about what `sync()` costs, because you should not do this everywhere. An
`fsync` is roughly 0.1 ms on NVMe with a write cache and 5-10 ms on a spinning
disk — a thousand times the cost of the write itself. Atomic writes are for
files where a torn version is a disaster: configuration, state, indexes,
anything read at startup. For a log line or a cache entry the cost is not
justified, and using this function everywhere is how a service ends up
disk-bound writing files nobody reads.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two library calls do almost all of it: one that creates a uniquely named
directory for you, and one that removes a tree. The interesting part is the
control flow between them — specifically, what happens to `fn`'s error when the
cleanup also fails, which is the same precedence question as V3·A2 ex3's
`_destroy`.

## Hint 2

`mkdtemp` takes a *prefix*, not a path, and appends six random characters:

```ts
import { mkdtemp, rm } from "node:fs/promises";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";

const dir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), "ipskill-"));
// -> /tmp/ipskill-Xf3a9K
await rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
```

Note the trailing separator problem: `join(tmpdir(), "ipskill-")` is right, and
`tmpdir() + "ipskill-"` is right on Linux and wrong on Windows. `force: true`
makes `rm` ignore a directory that is already gone.

## Hint 3

Shape: `mkdtemp`, a `try` that returns `await fn(dir)`, and a `finally` that
removes the tree. Six lines. The decision left to you is whether the `finally`
swallows its own failure. Letting a cleanup error escape replaces the caller's
real error with an `EBUSY` about a directory they have never heard of;
swallowing it silently means a leaked temp directory nobody ever learns about.
One of those is clearly worse, and the other deserves a log line this
signature gives you nowhere to put.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it through the race you are being protected from. The version people
write by hand is:

```ts
const dir = join(tmpdir(), `run-${Date.now()}`);
await mkdir(dir);
```

Two processes started in the same millisecond — which is normal for a test
runner spawning workers — get the same path, and the second `mkdir` either
throws `EEXIST` or, with `recursive: true`, silently succeeds and they share a
directory. Then they delete each other's files. The failure appears only under
parallelism, only sometimes, and gets labelled "flaky test" for a year.
`mkdtemp` is a syscall that creates-and-names atomically for exactly this
reason.

## Hint 2

Think about the error-precedence rule concretely. `fn` throws "record 47 is
malformed". Cleanup then throws `EBUSY` because a file is still open on
Windows. If you let the cleanup error escape, the caller sees `EBUSY` — a
message about a temp directory they never heard of, for a bug that has nothing
to do with it. The first error explains the second; the second explains
nothing. `finally` with a swallowed cleanup error is the standard answer, and
logging the swallowed one is the polite refinement.

## Hint 3

Consider what happens if the process is killed inside `fn`. Nothing runs; the
directory stays. That is unavoidable and worth knowing, because it means temp
directories accumulate on a machine where processes are killed — CI runners,
mostly. The mitigations are a distinctive prefix (so a sweeper can find yours),
and putting the sweep in the *start* of the program rather than the end. Neither
belongs in this function, but the limitation belongs in your head.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — create, but only if absent

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function createIfAbsent(
  path: string,
  data: Buffer | string,
): Promise<boolean>;
```

Write the file only if it does not already exist. Resolve `true` if you created
it and `false` if it was already there. Every other failure — a missing parent
directory, no permission, a path that is a directory — propagates.

```ts
await createIfAbsent(p, "first");    // true
await createIfAbsent(p, "second");   // false
await readFile(p, "utf8");           // "first" — never overwritten

await createIfAbsent("/nonexistent-dir/x", "y");   // rejects with ENOENT
```

You may not use `existsSync`, `access`, or a `stat` to decide. The check and
the create must be a single operation, because between two operations another
process can act.

The gate spawns twenty concurrent calls against the same path with different
contents and asserts exactly one returned `true` and the file's content matches
that one.

```
uv run dojo test node v3na05_fs_handles_atomic ex4
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through the name of the bug, because it will come up in a review.
This is TOCTOU — time-of-check to time-of-use. The pattern
`if (!exists(p)) write(p)` has a window between the two calls in which the
world can change, and the window is not small: it is however long the event
loop takes to get back to you, which under load is milliseconds. `fs.exists`
was deprecated in Node 1.0 explicitly because its very existence encourages
this, and the deprecation notice says so.

## Hint 2

Think about what "exactly one returned `true`" is actually testing. Twenty
concurrent calls hit `open(path, "wx")`. The kernel serialises them on the
inode; one gets the file, nineteen get `EEXIST`. There is no lock in your code
and no coordination between the processes — the atomicity is entirely the
syscall's. That is the pattern worth taking away: when you need mutual
exclusion on a filesystem, you are not building a lock, you are borrowing the
kernel's.

## Hint 3

Consider the error branch you are about to write too broadly. A bare
`catch { return false }` turns `EACCES`, `EISDIR`, `ENOSPC` and `ENOENT` into
"the file already existed" — so a permission problem in production looks like a
successful no-op, and the file that should exist never does. Branching on
exactly `EEXIST` and rethrowing everything else is three characters more and
the difference between a diagnosable failure and a silent one.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Recursion plus `yield*` is the whole structure. An async generator that yields
files and delegates to itself for directories reads almost like the description
of the problem. The two decisions that are not structural are how you classify
each entry, and what you do when a directory refuses to open.

## Hint 2

`opendir` gives you an async iterable of `Dirent`s:

```ts
import { opendir } from "node:fs/promises";

const dir = await opendir(path);
for await (const entry of dir) {
  entry.name;                 // just the basename
  entry.isFile();
  entry.isDirectory();
  entry.isSymbolicLink();     // true for a link, whatever it points at
}
```

`entry.name` is a basename, so you must `join` it yourself. And the type
predicates are `lstat` semantics — a symlink to a directory reports
`isSymbolicLink() === true` and `isDirectory() === false`, which is exactly the
behaviour that makes skipping links a one-line decision.

## Hint 3

Shape: an inner recursive generator taking an absolute path, a `for await` over
`opendir`, an `if` chain testing symlink first, then directory (recurse), then
file (yield the relative path). The decision left to you is the order of those
tests. Testing `isDirectory()` before `isSymbolicLink()` happens to work
because of `lstat` semantics — but relying on that means the code is correct
for a reason a reader has to know, and reordering it later silently introduces
the loop.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it through the memory difference, with a real number. `readdir` on a
directory with a million entries allocates a million strings — or a million
`Dirent` objects with `withFileTypes` — before your first line of logic runs.
That is roughly 100-200 MB resident for a listing you were going to consume one
at a time. `opendir` holds one entry. Mail spools, object-store mirrors and CI
artefact directories routinely reach those sizes, and the failure is an OOM
kill with no useful stack.

## Hint 2

Think about the `EACCES` requirement as a policy decision rather than an edge
case. A walk over `/` as a non-root user hits dozens of unreadable directories.
Aborting means the tool is useless; skipping silently means the output is
incomplete and nobody knows. The honest designs are: skip and *report* (yield a
diagnostic, or take an `onError` callback), or abort with a clear message. This
exercise picks skip-silently for simplicity, and if you were shipping it the
`onError` option is the version that does not lose information.

## Hint 3

Consider what "relative to root" costs on Windows. `path.relative` produces
`sub\b.txt`, not `sub/b.txt`, so any consumer matching against a glob or
comparing to a stored value has to normalise. The choice is to yield
platform-native separators (correct for passing back into `fs`) or
forward-slashed (correct for display, config and cross-platform comparison).
Pick one deliberately; the bug is picking neither and having both appear.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The state you need is one timer per filename, so the natural structure is a
